W-36 Supplement 8-A A Useful Theorem

Consider, for example, the one-dimensional simple harmonic oscillator, for which the
Hamiltonian is

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{H} = \frac{\mathrm{p}^2}{2\mathrm{m}} + \frac{1}{2}\, \mathrm{m}\omega^2 \mathrm{x}^2 \tag{8A-5}
\end{equation}

The eigenvalues are known to be

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{n}} = \hbar\omega( \mathrm{n} + \textstyle\frac{1}{2} ) \tag{8A-6}
\end{equation}

If we differentiate $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{n}}$ with respect to $\omega$, and if we note that

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial \mathrm{H}}{\partial \omega} = \mathrm{m}\omega \mathrm{x}^2
\end{equation*}

we can immediately make the identification

\begin{equation*}
\hbar ( \mathrm{n} + \textstyle\frac{1}{2} ) = \mathrm{m}\omega \langle \mathrm{x}^2 \rangle_{\mathrm{n}}
\end{equation*}

or

\begin{equation}
\langle \mathrm{x}^2 \rangle_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{\hbar}{\mathrm{m}\omega} \left( \mathrm{n} + \frac{1}{2} \right) = \frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{n}}}{\mathrm{m}\omega^2} \tag{8A-7}
\end{equation}

Examples of relevance to the hydrogen atom are of particular interest. In the Hamiltonian,
the factor

\begin{equation*}
\frac{-\mathrm{e}^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 \mathrm{r}} = -\frac{\hbar\mathrm{c}\alpha}{\mathrm{r}}
\end{equation*}

appears. The eigenvalue has the form

\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{n}\mathrm{l}} = -\frac{1}{2} \frac{\mathrm{m}\mathrm{c}^2\alpha^2}{\mathrm{n}^2}
\end{equation*}

If we take as our parameter to be $\alpha$, then we get

\begin{equation}
-\hbar\mathrm{c}\left\langle \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{n},\mathrm{l}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha}\,\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{n}\mathrm{l}} = -\frac{\mathrm{m}\mathrm{c}^2\alpha}{\mathrm{n}^2} \tag{8A-8}
\end{equation}

so that

\begin{equation}
\left\langle \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{n}\mathrm{l}} = \frac{\mathrm{m}\mathrm{c}\alpha}{\hbar\mathrm{n}^2} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{a}_0\mathrm{n}^2} \tag{8A-9}
\end{equation}

In the radial Hamiltonian, there is a term

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mathrm{m}} \frac{\mathrm{l}(\mathrm{l}+1)}{\mathrm{r}^2}
\end{equation*}

If we treat $\mathrm{l}$ as the parameter and recall that $\mathrm{n} = \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{r}} + \mathrm{l} + 1$, we get

\begin{equation}
\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mathrm{m}}\left\langle \frac{2\mathrm{l}+1}{\mathrm{r}^2} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{m}\mathrm{c}^2\alpha^2 \frac{2}{\mathrm{n}^3} \tag{8A-10}
\end{equation}

which is equivalent to

\begin{equation}
\left\langle \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{n}\mathrm{l}} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{a}_0^2\mathrm{n}^3(\mathrm{l} + \frac{1}{2})} \tag{8A-11}
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 197 -->
A Useful Theorem W-37

Using an observation of J. Schwinger that the average force in a stationary state must van-
ish, we can proceed from

\begin{align}
\rm F &= - \frac{d V(r)}{dr} = - \frac{d}{dr} \left( - \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} + \frac{\hbar^2 l(l+1)}{2 m r^2} \right) \\
&= - \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} + \frac{\hbar^2 l(l+1)}{m r^3}
\tag{8A-12}
\end{align}

to $\langle \rm F(r) \rangle = 0$ and thus obtain

\begin{equation}
\left\langle \frac{1}{r^3} \right\rangle_{\rm nl} = \frac{m}{\hbar^2 l(l+1)} \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left\langle \frac{1}{r^2} \right\rangle_{\rm nl} = \frac{1}{a_0^3 n^3 l(l + \frac{1}{2})(l+1)}
\tag{8A-13}
\end{equation}

\section*{The Square Well, Continuum Solutions}

We saw in eq. (8-69) that asymptotically the free-particle solution has the form

\[ R_l(r) \rightarrow -\frac{1}{2ikr} [\text{e}^{-i(kr - l\pi/2)} - \text{e}^{i(kr - l\pi/2)}] \]

We now assert that the first term is an incoming spherical wave, and the second is an outgoing spherical wave. The description is arrived at in the following way.

Consider the three-dimensional probability flux

\[ j = \frac{\hbar}{2i\mu} (\psi^*(r)\nabla\psi(r) - \nabla\psi^*(r)\psi(r)) \]

We shall see that it is only the radial flux that is of interest for large r. The radial flux, integrated over all angles, is thus

\[ \int \text{d}\Omega\text{i}_r \cdot j(r) = \frac{\hbar}{2i\mu} \int \text{d}\Omega \left( \psi^* \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r} - \frac{\partial\psi^*}{\partial r}\psi \right) \tag{8B-1} \]

For a solution of the form

\[ \psi(r) = \text{C}\frac{\text{e}^{\pm ikr}}{r} \text{Y}_{lm}(\theta, \varphi) \tag{8B-2} \]

with $\int \text{d}\Omega |\text{Y}_{lm}(\theta, \varphi)|^2 = 1$ the right-hand side of (8B-1) can easily be evaluated, and we find that

\[ \int \text{d}\Omega \text{j}_r = \pm \frac{\hbar\text{k}|C|^2}{\mu} \frac{1}{r^2} \tag{8B-3} \]

The $\pm$ sign describes outgoing/incoming flux. The factor $1/r^2$ that emerges from our calculation is actually necessary for flux conservation, since the flux going through a spherical surface of radius r is

\[ \int r^2 \text{d}\Omega \text{j}_r = \pm \frac{\hbar\text{k}|C|^2}{\mu}, \quad \text{independent of r} \]

We therefore see that for the free-particle solution the incoming flux is equal in magnitude to the outgoing flux, which is what it should be, because there are no sources of flux.

We now note that in the presence of a potential flux is still conserved. Any solution will asymptotically consist of an incoming spherical wave and an outgoing spherical

\textbf{The Plane Wave in Terms of Spherical Harmonics}

The solution of the free-particle equation

\begin{equation}
\nabla^2\psi(\mathbf{r}) + \mathrm{k}^2\psi(\mathbf{r}) = 0 \tag{8B-15}
\end{equation}

can be written in two ways. One is simply the plane wave solution

\begin{equation}
\psi(\mathbf{r}) = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} \tag{8B-16}
\end{equation}

The other way is to write it as a linear superposition of the partial wave solutions—that is,

\begin{equation}
\sum\sum A_{\mathrm{lm}} \mathrm{j}_{\mathrm{l}}(\mathrm{kr}) \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{lm}}(\theta, \phi) \tag{8B-17}
\end{equation}

We may therefore find $\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{lm}}$ such that $\psi(\mathbf{r}) = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$ in (8B-17). Note that the spherical angles
$(\theta, \phi)$ are the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{r}$ relative to some arbitrarily chosen z-axis. If we
define the z-axis by the direction of $\mathbf{k}$ (until now an arbitrary direction), then

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{ikr}\cos\theta} \tag{8B-18}
\end{equation}

Thus the left side of (8B-18) has no azimuthal angle, $\phi$, dependence, and thus on the right
side only terms with $\mathrm{m} = 0$ can appear; hence, making use of the fact that

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{l}0}(\theta, \phi) = \left( \frac{2\mathrm{l} + 1}{4\pi} \right)^{1/2} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{l}}(\cos\theta) \tag{8B-19}
\end{equation}

where the $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{l}}(\cos\theta)$ are the Legendre polynomials, we get the relation

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{ikr}\cos\theta} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}=0}^\infty \left( \frac{2\mathrm{l} + 1}{4\pi} \right)^{1/2} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{l}} \mathrm{j}_{\mathrm{l}}(\mathrm{kr}) \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{l}}(\cos\theta) \tag{8B-20}
\end{equation}

We may use the relation

\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{2} \int_{-1}^1 \mathrm{d}(\cos\theta) \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{l}}(\cos\theta) \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{l}'}(\cos\theta) = \frac{\delta_{\mathrm{ll}'}}{2\mathrm{l} + 1} \tag{8B-21}
\end{equation}

which is a direct consequence of the orthonormality relation for the $\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{lm}}$ and (8B-19) to obtain

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{l}}\mathrm{j}_{\mathrm{l}}(\mathrm{kr}) = \frac{1}{2} [4\pi(2\mathrm{l} + 1)]^{1/2} \int_{-1}^1 \mathrm{dz} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{l}}(\mathrm{z}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{ikrz}} \tag{8B-22}
\end{equation}

Compare the two sides of the equation as $\mathrm{kr} \rightarrow 0$. The first term on the left-hand side is

\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{l}} \frac{(\mathrm{kr})^{\mathrm{l}}}{1, 3, 5, \dots, (2\mathrm{l} + 1)}
\end{equation*}

and the corresponding power of $(\mathrm{kr})^{\mathrm{l}}$ on the right-hand side has

\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2} [4\pi(2\mathrm{l} + 1)]^{1/2} (\mathrm{ikr})^{\mathrm{l}} \int_{-1}^1 \mathrm{dz} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{l}}(\mathrm{z}) \mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{l}} / \mathrm{l}!
\end{equation*}

The integral can be evaluated by noting that $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{l}}(\mathrm{z})$ is an lth-degree polynomial in $\mathrm{z}$. The coef
ficient of the leading power, $\mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{l}}$, can be easily obtained from eq. (7-47) as the power of $\mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{l}}$ in

\begin{equation*}
(-1)^{\mathrm{l}} \frac{1}{2^{\mathrm{l}}\mathrm{l}!} \left( \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{dz}} \right)^{\mathrm{l}} (1 - \mathrm{z}^2)^{\mathrm{l}} = \frac{2\mathrm{l}(2\mathrm{l} - 1)(2\mathrm{l} - 1) \cdots (\mathrm{l} + 1)}{2^{\mathrm{l}}\mathrm{l}!} \mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{l}} + 0(\mathrm{z}^{\mathrm{l}-1})
\end{equation*}


<!-- Page 202 -->
W-42 Supplement 8-B The Square Well, Continuum Solutions

We can rewrite this in the form

\[
z^1 = \frac{2^1 l!}{21(21 - 1)(21 - 2) \cdots (1 + 1)} P_{1}(z) + \text{terms involving P}_{1+1}(z) \text{ and higher}
\]

With the help of (8B-21) we finally get

\[
A_{1} \frac{(kr)^1}{1, 3, 5, \dots, (21 + 1)} = \frac{1}{2} [4\pi(21 + 1)]^{1/2} (ikr)^1 \frac{1}{l!} \frac{2^1 l!}{21(21 - 1)(21 - 2) \cdots (1 + 1)} \frac{2}{21 + 1} \tag{8B-23}
\]

What results is the expansion

\[
e^{ikr \cos\theta} = \sum_{1=0}^{\infty} (21 + 1) i^1 j_{1}(kr) P_{1}(\cos\theta)
\]

which we will find exceedingly useful in discussions of collision theory.

\chapter*{Chapter 9}
\hrulefill

\section*{Matrix Representation\n\n of Operators}

\textbf{T}he original discovery of quantum mechanics is due to W. Heisenberg. He associated physical quantities like $x$ and $p$ with square \textit{arrays} of numbers for which he proposed multiplication rules, so as to be able to talk about quantities like $x^2$ and the like. Max Born immediately recognized these arrays as \textit{matrices}, and the formulation of the fundamentals of quantum mechanics was carried by M. Born and P. Jordan with Heisenberg. The discovery of the Schr\"odinger equation came soon after, followed by the more abstract formulation in terms of operators and states by Paul Dirac. The formulation in terms of matrices is very useful in that it allows us to deal with quantities that have no classical counterpart. This applies particularly to a nonclassical property of particles, their \textit{intrinsic spin}, which will be discussed in the next chapter.

\section*{9-1 \quad MATRICES IN QUANTUM MECHANICS}

In Chapter 8 we solved the eigenvalue problem posed by the equations
\begin{align}
\mathbf{L}^2 |l,m\rangle &= \hbar^2 l(l+1)|l,m\rangle \nonumber \\
L_z|l,m\rangle &= \hbar m|l,m\rangle \tag{9-1}
\end{align}
by operator methods. We also found that for the harmonic oscillator we could do the same, and even found the complete set of eigenstates in the form
\begin{equation}
|n\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n!}} (A^+)^n |0\rangle \tag{9-2}
\end{equation}
for which
\begin{equation}
H|n\rangle = \hbar\omega(n + \textstyle{\frac{1}{2}}) |n\rangle \tag{9-3}
\end{equation}
We could also calculate the action of the raising and lowering operators on $|n\rangle$,
\begin{align}
A^+|n\rangle &= \sqrt{n+1} |n+1\rangle \nonumber \\
A|n\rangle &= \sqrt{n} |n-1\rangle \tag{9-4}
\end{align}
We also showed that
\begin{equation}
\langle m|n \rangle = \delta_{mn} \tag{9-5}
\end{equation}
a statement that can be made about the eigenstates of \textit{any} hermitian operator.

146


<!-- Page 204 -->
9-1 Matrices in Quantum Mechanics \textbf{147}

The expansion theorem was seen to be equivalent to what we called the \textit{completeness} relation
\begin{equation}
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |n\rangle\langle n| = \mathbf{1}
\end{equation}
where \textbf{1} is the unit operator.

We start on the form of matrix representations of operators by practicing on the harmonic oscillator problem. If we take the scalar products of (9-3) and (9-4) with $\langle m|$, we get
\begin{align}
\langle m|H|n\rangle &= \hbar\omega\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\delta_{mn} \\
\langle m|A^{+}|n\rangle &= \sqrt{n+1} \, \delta_{m,n+1} \\
\langle m|A|n\rangle &= \sqrt{n} \, \delta_{m,n-1}
\end{align}
These quantities may be arranged in arrays called \textit{matrices}. The conventional notation for a matrix $M_{ij}$ has the first index labeling the row and the second labeling the column of the array. Thus if we write the scalar produce $\langle m|H|n\rangle$ as $H_{mn}$, we find that
\begin{equation}
H = \hbar\omega 
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 3/2 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & 5/2 & 0 &  \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 7/2 & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}
We may also construct matrices for the operator $A^{+}$ and $A$.
\begin{equation}
A^{+} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
\sqrt{1} & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & \sqrt{3} & 0 & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
A = 
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & \sqrt{1} & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \sqrt{3} & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & \sqrt{0} & 0 & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots
\end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}

Without restricting ourselves to the harmonic oscillator problem, we shall call the array $\langle m|F|n\rangle$, where $F$ is any operator and the $|n\rangle$ any complete set of states, a matrix representation of $F$ in the basis provided by the complete set of states $|n\rangle$. The appellation needs some justification. The product of two matrices, for example, is given by
\begin{equation}
(FG)_{ij} = \sum_{k} (F)_{ik} (G)_{kj} = (F)_{ik} (G)_{kj}
\end{equation}
[In the last step we have introduced the convention that if a subscript appears twice, it is to be summed over].


<!-- Page 205 -->
**148** Chapter 9 Matrix Representation of Operators

We need to verify that this relation holds for the *matrix representations* of the operators $F$ and $G$. To do this, let us consider some complete set $|n\rangle$. The state $G|j\rangle$ may, with the help of the completeness relation, be written in the form

\[
G|j\rangle = \sum_n C_n|n\rangle
\]

with

\[
C_n = \langle n|G|j\rangle
\]

so that

\[
G|j\rangle = \sum_n |n\rangle\langle n|G|j\rangle \tag{9-12}
\]

Hence

\[
\langle i|FG|j\rangle = \sum_n \langle i|F|n\rangle\langle n|G|j\rangle \tag{9-13}
\]

This is the same as (9-11), provided we write

\[
\langle i|F|n\rangle = F_{in} \tag{9-14}
\]

This identification gives rise to the name given to the left-hand side of the above equation. It is called the *matrix element* of the operator $F$. Further justification for the matrix connection comes from the relation

\[
\langle m|F|n\rangle^* = \langle F(n)|m\rangle = \langle n|F^+|m\rangle \tag{9-15}
\]

which shows that if the operator $F$ is represented by a matrix, then the hermitian conjugate operator $F^+$ will be represented by the hermitian conjugate matrix, since the latter is defined by

\[
(F^+)_{nm} = F_{mn}^* \tag{9-16}
\]

If the complete set of kets are the eigenkets of some operator $A$, then the matrix representation of that operator is

\[
\langle a_n|A|a_m\rangle = a_m\langle a_n|a_m\rangle = a_m \delta_{mn} \tag{9-17}
\]

as is the case in (9-8). Finding the eigenvalues of a hermitian operator is tantamount to *diagonalizing* it.

How do we diagonalize a matrix? Let us consider the operator $A$, whose eigenkets are $|a_n\rangle$. Suppose we know the *matrix elements* of $A$ in a basis $|u_n\rangle$; that is, we know each entry in the square matrix

\[
A_{mn} = \langle u_m|A|u_n\rangle \tag{9-18}
\]

We know from the completeness of the basis $|u_n\rangle$ that an arbitrary eigenket $|a_n\rangle$ may be expanded in terms of the $|u_n\rangle$. We write

\[
|a_n\rangle = \sum_k |u_k\rangle\langle u_k|a_n\rangle \tag{9-19}
\]

and similarly

\[
\langle a_n| = \sum_l \langle a_n|u_l\rangle\langle u_l| \tag{9-20}
\]

It follows that

\[
\langle a_m|A|a_n\rangle = a_m \delta_{mn} = \sum_l \langle a_m|u_l\rangle\langle u_l|A|u_k\rangle\langle u_k|a_n\rangle \tag{9-21}
\]


<!-- Page 206 -->
9-1 Matrices in Quantum Mechanics \textbf{149}

Let us now define the matrix $U$ by the matrix elements

\begin{equation}
U_{kn} \equiv \langle u_{k}|a_{n}\rangle
\label{eq:9-22}
\end{equation}

Then

\begin{equation}
\langle a_{m}|u_{l}\rangle = \langle u_{l}|a_{m}\rangle * = U_{lm}^{*} = (U^{+})_{ml}
\label{eq:9-23}
\end{equation}

Thus, in matrix form the equation reads

\begin{equation}
a_{m}\delta_{mn} = \sum_{k,l} (U^{+})_{ml} A_{lk} U_{kn}
\label{eq:9-24}
\end{equation}

The matrix $U$ has the property that

\begin{equation}
\sum_{k} \langle a_{m}|u_{k}\rangle \langle u_{k}|a_{n}\rangle = (U^{+}U)_{mn} = \delta_{mn}
\label{eq:9-25}
\end{equation}

that is,

\begin{equation}
U^{+}U = 1
\label{eq:9-26}
\end{equation}

Such a matrix is called a \emph{unitary} matrix. Finding the matrix $U$ for finite-dimensional matrices $A$ is an exercise in solving algebraic equations. Finding it for infinite-dimensional $A$'s is equivalent to solving the Schr\"{o}dinger equation.

We shall find it useful to introduce the \emph{trace} of a matrix. This is defined by

\begin{equation}
\text{Tr } M = \sum_{k} M_{kk}
\label{eq:9-27}
\end{equation}

The trace of a product of two matrices has the interesting property that

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\text{Tr } MN &= \sum_{k} (MN)_{kk} = \sum_{kl} M_{kl}N_{lk} = \sum_{kl} N_{lk}M_{kl} \\
&= \text{Tr } NM
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:9-28}
\end{equation}

Note that we were allowed to order the matrix elements differently because each one of the $M_{kl}$ and $N_{kl}$ are plain (complex) numbers. It is easy to show that

\begin{equation}
\text{Tr } ABC = \text{Tr } BCA = \text{Tr } CAB
\label{eq:9-29}
\end{equation}

and similarly for products of larger number of matrices. A consequence of this is that

\begin{equation}
\text{Tr } [A, B] = 0
\label{eq:9-30}
\end{equation}

\emph{unless} the series in (9-27) diverges, in which case no useful statement can be made. Thus, for finite-dimensional matrices, such as the matrix representation of angular momentum,

\begin{equation*}
[L_{x}, L_{y}] = i\hbar L_{z} \quad \text{ (and cycl.)},
\end{equation*}

implies that the traces of the matrices for $\textbf{L}$ must vanish. We can turn such an argument around and argue that for operators such as $x_{\text{op}}$ and $p_{\text{op}}$, the relation

\begin{equation*}
[p_{\text{op}}, x_{\text{op}}] = \frac{\hbar}{i} \textbf{1}
\end{equation*}

implies that these operators \emph{must} be represented by infinite-dimensional matrices. For example in the harmonic oscillator basis, we have seen that $A$ and $A^{+}$ are represented by infinite-dimensional matrices, and therefore so are the $x$ and $p$ operators.


<!-- Page 207 -->
\textbf{150}\quad Chapter 9\quad Matrix Representation of Operators

\section*{9-2 MATRIX REPRESENTATIONS\newline OF ANGULAR MOMENTUM OPERATORS}

It is often convenient and, as we shall see in the next chapter, sometimes \textit{essential}, to represent operators as matrices. Let us do this for the angular momentum operators. Consider the matrix elements of $L_z$. As a consequence of

\[ [\mathbf{L}^2, L_z] = 0 \]

we have

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \langle l', m' | [\mathbf{L}^2, L_z] | l, m \rangle \\
&= \langle \mathbf{L}^2 (l', m') | L_z | l, m \rangle - \langle l', m' | L_z \mathbf{L}^2 | l, m \rangle \\
&= \hbar^2 [l'(l' + 1) - l(l + 1)] \langle l', m' | L_z | l, m \rangle
\end{aligned}
\tag{9-31}
\end{equation}

From this we conclude that if $l' \neq l$ then $\langle l' m' | L_z | l, m \rangle$ vanishes. Thus $L_z$ (and all other operators that commute with $\mathbf{L}^2$) only have matrix elements between states that have the same total angular momentum quantum numbers. If we stay with fixed $l$, then we use the second of the relations in (9-1) to get

\begin{equation}
\langle l, m' | L_z | l, m \rangle = \hbar m \, \delta_{m'm}
\tag{9-32}
\end{equation}

Furthermore, (9-16) and (9-18) imply that

\begin{equation}
\langle l, m' | L_{\pm} | l, m \rangle = \hbar \sqrt{l(l + 1) - m(m \pm 1)} \delta_{m', m \pm 1}
\tag{9-33}
\end{equation}

For the angular momentum $l = 1$ operators, this leads to the matrix representations

\begin{equation}
L_z = \hbar \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{9-34}
\end{equation}

We also get

\begin{equation}
L_+ = \hbar \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{9-35}
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
L_- = \hbar \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \sqrt{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{9-36}
\end{equation}

From these we get

\begin{equation}
L_x = \frac{1}{2}(L_+ + L_-) = \frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{9-37}
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
L_y = -\frac{i}{2}(L_+ - L_-) = \frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i & 0 \\ i & 0 & -i \\ 0 & i & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{9-38}
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 208 -->
9-3 General Relations in Matrix Mechanics\hfill 151

The rows and columns are labeled with $m = 1, 0, -1$ in order from left to right and top to
bottom. The matrices satisfy the commutation relations: for example,

\begin{align*}
[L_x, L_y] &= i \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \left[ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \right] \\
&= i \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \left[ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \right] = i \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix} \\
&= i \hbar L_z
\end{align*}

\subsection*{9-3 GENERAL RELATIONS IN MATRIX MECHANICS}

Consider, for example, a relation between state vectors that reads as follows:
\begin{equation}
| \psi \rangle = A | \phi \rangle \tag{9-39}
\end{equation}

If we take the scalar product of this with any member of a complete set $| i \rangle$, we have
\begin{equation}
\langle i | \psi \rangle = \langle i | A | \phi \rangle \tag{9-40}
\end{equation}

Furthermore, the insertion of the unit operator in the form (6-16) between $A$ and $| \phi \rangle$ yields
\begin{equation}
\langle i | \psi \rangle = \sum_n \langle i | A | n \rangle \langle n | \phi \rangle \tag{9-41}
\end{equation}

If we write $\langle n | \phi \rangle$ as a column vector $\alpha_n$, so that
\begin{equation}
\langle n | \phi \rangle \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \langle 1 | \phi \rangle \\ \langle 2 | \phi \rangle \\ \langle 3 | \phi \rangle \\ \vdots \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_1 \\ \alpha_2 \\ \alpha_3 \\ \vdots \end{pmatrix} \tag{9-42}
\end{equation}

and similarly
\begin{equation}
\langle n | \psi \rangle \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \langle 1 | \psi \rangle \\ \langle 2 | \psi \rangle \\ \langle 3 | \psi \rangle \\ \vdots \end{pmatrix} \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \\ \beta_3 \\ \vdots \end{pmatrix} \tag{9-43}
\end{equation}

then the matrix representation of (9-39) is
\begin{equation}
\beta_i = \sum_n A_{in} \alpha_n \tag{9-44}
\end{equation}

Thus matrices represent operators, and column vectors represent kets. The scalar product
$\langle \phi | n \rangle = \langle n | \phi \rangle^*$ is conventionally written in the form of a row,
\begin{equation}
\langle \phi | n \rangle \rightarrow (\alpha_1^*, \alpha_2^*, \alpha_3^*, \ldots) \tag{9-45}
\end{equation}

so that the scalar product $\langle \phi | \psi \rangle$, for example, can be written as
\begin{equation}
\langle \phi | \psi \rangle = \sum_n \langle \phi | n \rangle \langle n | \psi \rangle = \sum_n \alpha_n^* \beta_n \tag{9-46}
\end{equation}

154 Chapter 9 Matrix Representation of Operators

We get $-i\alpha_2 = \lambda \alpha_1$, $i\alpha_1 = \lambda\alpha_2$, and $\lambda\alpha_3 = 0$. From the third of these, we see that if $\lambda \neq 0$, then
$\alpha_3 = 0$. Since the product of the first two relations implies $(\lambda^2 - 1)\alpha_1 \alpha_2 = 0$, we see that unless
$\lambda = +1, -1, \text{or } 0$, all the $\alpha$'s must vanish. So, for $\lambda = 0$, we get $\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = 0$, and $\alpha_3 = 1$ since
the normalization condition implies that $|\alpha_1|^2 + |\alpha_2|^2 + |\alpha_3|^2 = 1$. For $\lambda = 1$, we get $\alpha_1 = u$,
$\alpha_2 = iu$, and $\alpha_3 = 0$. Normalization implies that $|u|^2 + |iu|^2 = 2|u|^2 = 1$ so we may choose $u = 1/\sqrt{2}$. For $\lambda = -1$, we do the same thing, or we recognize that eigenvectors corresponding to dif
ferent eigenvalues are orthogonal. We thus write $\alpha_1 = 1/\sqrt{2}$, $\alpha_2 = -i/\sqrt{2}$, $\alpha_3 = 0$. So for the
eigenstates corresponding to the three eigenvalues we get

$$
\lambda = 1, \quad \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ i/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}; \quad \lambda = 0, \quad \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}; \quad \lambda = -1, \quad \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ -i/\sqrt{2} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix};
$$

We may use this to find $U$ according to the rule given in (9-55):

$$
U = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ i & 0 & -i \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$

We check:

\begin{align*}
U^\dagger M_3 U &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -i & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & i & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i & 0 \\ i & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ i & 0 & -i \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{L_z}{\hbar}
\end{align*}

Equivalently, $M_3$ may be seen to be a unitary transform of $L_z$.

---

If we can solve the eigenvalue problem for some hermitian operator $H$, which is easy (and
useful) for $2 \times 2$ and $3 \times 3$ matrices, then it is straightforward to find an expression for
any function of $H$. In general, if

$$
U^\dagger H U = D \eqno{(9-58)}
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix, then

$$
\sum_n a_n H^n = \sum_n a_n (UDU^\dagger)^n = \sum_n a_n (UDU^\dagger)(UDU^\dagger)(UDU^\dagger) \ldots
$$

$$
= U \sum_n a_n D^n U^\dagger = U \begin{pmatrix} \sum_n a_n h_1^n & 0 & 0 & \ldots \\ 0 & \sum_n a_n h_2^n & 0 & \ldots \\ 0 & 0 & \sum_n a_n h_3^n & \ldots \\ \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \end{pmatrix} U^\dagger \eqno{(9-59)}
$$

Here the $h_k$ are the eigenvalues of $H$ and therefore the diagonal elements of the matrix $D$.
A simple diagonalization of $H$ yields the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, which are used
to construct the $U$ matrix. We illustrate this in the next example.


<!-- Page 212 -->
9-3 General Relations in Matrix Mechanics\quad\textbf{155}

\textbf{EXAMPLE 9-2}
Use the procedure of the previous example to calculate the matrix representation of

\[ e^{i\alpha M_3} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(i\alpha)^k}{k!} (M_3)^k \]

\textit{SOLUTION}\quad We have

\[ e^{i\hbar\alpha M_3} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(i\hbar\alpha)^k}{k!} (M_3)^k \]

We know that

\[ U^+M_3U = L_z/\hbar \]

It follows that

\begin{align*}
(L_z/\hbar)^k &= (U^+M_3U)^k = U^+M_3UU^+M_3U \ldots U^+M_3U \\
&= U^+(M_3)^kU
\end{align*}

Equivalently,

\[ (M_3)^k = U(L_z/\hbar)^kU^+ \]

Now for $k$ even,

\[ (L_z/\hbar)^k = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \]

While for $k$ odd,

\[ (L_z/\hbar)^k = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = (L_z/\hbar) \]

We use this to evaluate the sum

\[ \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(i\alpha M_3)^k}{k!} = U \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(i\alpha L_z/\hbar)^k}{k!} U^+ \]

The calculation of the sum is straightforward:

\begin{align*}
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(i\alpha L_z/\hbar)^k}{k!} &= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{2!} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \alpha^2 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{4!} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha^4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \alpha^4 \end{pmatrix} - \cdots \\
&\quad + i \left[ \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\alpha \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{3!} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha^3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\alpha^3 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{5!} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha^5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\alpha^5 \end{pmatrix} + \cdots \right] \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} \cos \alpha & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \cos \alpha \end{pmatrix} + i \begin{pmatrix} \sin \alpha & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\sin \alpha \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\alpha} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & e^{-i\alpha} \end{pmatrix}
\end{align*}

What remains is the calculation of

\[ U \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\alpha} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & e^{-i\alpha} \end{pmatrix} U^+ \]

an exercise left to the reader.

\chapter*{Chapter 10}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Chapter 10}

\section*{Spin}

\textbf{A} proper discussion of atomic and subatomic physics is not possible without taking into account a new degree of freedom for the electron\textemdash the \textit{spin} of the electron. In spite of its suggestive name, this property of the electron does not have a classical analog. The picture of an electron rotating about its own axis is wrong. Thus there is no counterpart to the orbital angular momentum operator $\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}$, and the treatment must necessarily be more abstract. It turns out that the operator treatment of angular momentum, which depends \textit{only} on the commutation relations, also applies to spin. It is only the step of representing the states by wave functions whose variables are real coordinates (such as $\theta, \phi$) that cannot be carried out here. Rather, the operators are represented by matrices.

The discovery of spin was rooted in experiment. There were many mysterious patterns that appeared in the pre-quantum analysis of spectral lines. Among them was the appearance of doublets of lines when radiating alkali atoms were placed in a magnetic field. The semiclassical understanding of what was called the \textit{Zeeman effect} after its discoverer did not allow for such splittings, and it took a while before W. Pauli in 1924 (i.e., before quantum mechanics) saw through the fog and proposed that an electron in an atom, besides being described by a set of quantum numbers such as ($n, l, m$), had another nonclassical two-valued ``index'' associated with it. Within a year Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck, at the time graduate students in Holland, proposed that the electron had an intrinsic angular momentum that had the value $s = 1/2$. The electron is pointlike, and there is nothing that rotates. The spin of the electron is just an intrinsic property like its mass, and the \textit{spin operators} in analogy with the orbital angular momentum discussed in Chapter 7 are defined by the commutation relations

\begin{equation}
[S_x, S_y] = i\hbar S_z \quad \text{(and cycl.)}
\tag{10-1}
\end{equation}

\subsection*{10-1 EIGENSTATES OF SPIN 1/2}

We recall that eqs. (9-32) and (9-33) were derived solely from the commutation relations like those of (10-1). Applying them to the spin case, where $s = 1/2$, we can write

\begin{equation}
S_z = \hbar
\begin{pmatrix}
1/2 & 0 \\
0 & -1/2
\end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-2}
\end{equation}

and (9-33) gives

\begin{equation}
S_+ = \hbar
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1 \\
0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\quad
S_- = \hbar
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 0 \\
1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-3}
\end{equation}

We may write this representation as

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{2}\hbar\boldsymbol{\sigma}
\tag{10-4}
\end{equation}

158


<!-- Page 216 -->
10-1 Eigenstates of Spin 1/2 \hfill 159

where
\begin{equation}
\sigma_x = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \sigma_y = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \sigma_z = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-5}
\end{equation}

are the \textit{Pauli matrices}. They satisfy the commutation relations
\begin{equation}
[\sigma_x, \sigma_y] = 2i\sigma_z
\tag{10-6}
\end{equation}
and so on, as they must, to satisfy (10-1), and they also satisfy
\begin{equation}
\sigma_x^2 = \sigma_y^2 = \sigma_z^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 1
\tag{10-7}
\end{equation}
The Pauli matrices also anticommute:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_x \sigma_y &= -\sigma_y \sigma_x \\
\sigma_z \sigma_x &= -\sigma_x \sigma_z \\
\sigma_y \sigma_z &= -\sigma_z \sigma_y
\end{aligned}
\tag{10-8}
\end{equation}
These relations are peculiar to the spin $1/2$ representations and do not hold for the $l = 1$
matrices, for example.

The eigenstates of $S_z$ will be represented by a two-component column vector, which
we call \textit{spinor}. To find these eigenspinors, we solve
\begin{equation}
S_z \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix} = \pm \frac{1}{2}\hbar \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-9}
\end{equation}
that is, using (10-4),
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix} = \pm \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}
\]
or
\[
\begin{pmatrix} u \\ -v \end{pmatrix} = \pm \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}
\]
The plus eigensolution has $v = 0$, and the minus eigensolution has $u = 0$. We thus write
\begin{equation}
\chi_+ = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \chi_- = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-10}
\end{equation}
for the eigenspinors corresponding to spin up [$S_z = +(1/2)\hbar$] and spin down [$S_z = -(1/2)\hbar$], respectively.

An arbitrary spinor can be expanded in this complete set
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha_+ \\ \alpha_- \end{pmatrix} = \alpha_+ \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha_- \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-11}
\end{equation}
and the expansion postulate yields the interpretation that $|\alpha_+|^2$ and $|\alpha_-|^2$, when properly
normalized, so that
\begin{equation}
|\alpha_+|^2 + |\alpha_-|^2 = 1
\tag{10-12}
\end{equation}
yield the probabilities that a measurement of $S_z$ on the state $\begin{pmatrix} \alpha_+ \\ \alpha_- \end{pmatrix}$ yields $+(1/2)\hbar$ and
$-(1/2)\hbar$, respectively.


<!-- Page 217 -->
**160** Chapter 10 Spin

It is not necessary to keep $S_z$ diagonal. If we look for eigenstates of the operator $S_x \cos \phi + S_y \sin \phi$, we must solve

\begin{equation}
(S_x \cos \phi + S_y \sin \phi) \binom{u}{v} = \frac{1}{2} \hbar \lambda \binom{u}{v} \tag{10-13}
\end{equation}

that is,

$$\begin{pmatrix}
0 & \cos \phi - i \sin \phi \\
\cos \phi + i \sin \phi & 0
\end{pmatrix} \binom{u}{v} = \lambda \binom{u}{v}$$

This implies that

\begin{align}
v e^{-i \phi} &= \lambda u \nonumber \\
u e^{i \phi} &= \lambda v \tag{10-14}
\end{align}

Taking the products of the left- and right-hand sides in the two equations we find that

\begin{equation}
u v(\lambda^2 - 1) = 0 \tag{10-15}
\end{equation}

Hence

\begin{equation}
\lambda = \pm 1 \tag{10-16}
\end{equation}

The eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda = 1$ satisfies

$$v = e^{i \phi} u$$

so that the normalized form is

$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \binom{1}{e^{i \phi}}$$

We take advantage of the fact that we can multiply a state vector by an arbitrary phase factor, which we choose to be $e^{-i \phi/2}$. This yields

\begin{equation}
u_+ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \binom{e^{-i \phi/2}}{e^{i \phi/2}} \tag{10-17}
\end{equation}

and similarly, the eigenstate corresponding to $\lambda = -1$ can be written in the form

\begin{equation}
u_- = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \binom{e^{-i \phi/2}}{-e^{i \phi/2}} \tag{10-18}
\end{equation}

which is easily seen to be orthogonal to $u_+$:

\begin{align}
u_+^* u_- &= \frac{1}{2} \left( e^{i \phi/2}, e^{-i \phi/2} \right) \binom{e^{-i \phi/2}}{-e^{i \phi/2}} \nonumber \\
&= 0 \tag{10-19}
\end{align}

Given an arbitrary state $\alpha$, the expectation value of $\mathbf{S}$ can be calculated. We have

$$\langle \alpha | \mathbf{S} | \alpha \rangle = \sum_i \sum_j \langle \alpha | i \rangle \langle i | \mathbf{S} | j \rangle \langle j | \alpha \rangle$$

or, equivalently,

$$(\alpha_+^*, \alpha_-^*) \mathbf{S} \binom{\alpha_+}{\alpha_-}$$


<!-- Page 218 -->
10-1 Eigenstates of Spin 1/2 \hfill 161

Thus

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\langle S_x \rangle &= (\alpha_+^*, \alpha_-^*) \frac{1}{2}\hbar \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_+ \\ \alpha_- \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\hbar (\alpha_+^*, \alpha_-^*) \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_- \\ \alpha_+ \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\hbar (\alpha_+^*\alpha_- + \alpha_-^*\alpha_+) \\
\langle S_y \rangle &= \frac{1}{2}\hbar (\alpha_+^*, \alpha_-^*) \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_+ \\ \alpha_- \end{pmatrix} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}\hbar (\alpha_+^*, \alpha_-^*) \begin{pmatrix} -i\alpha_- \\ i\alpha_+ \end{pmatrix} = -\frac{i\hbar}{2} (\alpha_+^*\alpha_- - \alpha_-^*\alpha_+) \\
\langle S_z \rangle &= \frac{1}{2}\hbar (\alpha_+^*, \alpha_-^*) \begin{pmatrix} \alpha_+ \\ -\alpha_- \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\hbar (|\alpha_+|^2 - |\alpha_-|^2)
\end{aligned}
\tag{10-20}
\end{equation*}

Note that all of these are real, as expected for hermitian operators.

\textbf{EXAMPLE 10-1}
\begin{quote}
A measurement of $S_x$ for a spin 1/2 system leads to the eigenvalue $+\hbar/2$. Subsequently, a measure
ment of $S_x \cos \phi + S_y \sin \phi$ is carried out. What is the probability that the result is $+\hbar/2$?
\end{quote}

\textit{SOLUTION}\quad After the initial measurement, the system must be in the eigenstate of $S_x$ with eigenvalue $+\hbar/2$.
This means that

$$\frac{\hbar}{2} \sigma_x \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix} = + \frac{\hbar}{2} \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}$$

that is,

$$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix}$$

Since $|u|^2 + |v|^2 = 1$ results from normalization, it is convenient to choose the numbers $u$ and $v$ to
be real. Thus

$$\begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

This state may be expanded in eigenstates of the operator $S_x \cos \phi + S_y \sin \phi$, which were obtained
before. They are given in (10-17) and (10-18). Writing

$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \alpha_+ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\phi/2} \\ e^{i\phi/2} \end{pmatrix} + \alpha_- \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\phi/2} \\ -e^{i\phi/2} \end{pmatrix}$$

we get

$$\alpha_+ = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^{i\phi/2} \ e^{-i\phi/2} \right) \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \cos \frac{\phi}{2}$$

The result is that $P_+ = |\alpha_+|^2 = \cos^2 \phi/2$.

10-2 The Intrinsic Magnetic Moment of Spin 1/2 Particles \textbf{163}

Suppose that at time $t = 0$ the spin is in an eigenstate of $S_x$ with eigenvalue $\hbar/2$, so that it
“points in the $x$-direction.” This means that
\[
\frac{\hbar}{2} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2} \begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}
\]
that is,
\[
\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-26}
\]
At a later time,
\[
\psi(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\omega_0t} \\ e^{i\omega_0t} \end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-27}
\]
At the time $t$,
\[
\langle S_x \rangle = \frac{\hbar}{2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(e^{i\omega_0t} \ e^{-i\omega_0t}\right) \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\omega_0t} \\ e^{i\omega_0t} \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2} \cos 2\omega_0t
\tag{10-28}
\]
Similarly,
\[
\langle S_y \rangle = \frac{\hbar}{2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(e^{i\omega_0t} \ e^{-i\omega_0t}\right) \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} e^{-i\omega_0t} \\ e^{i\omega_0t} \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2} \sin 2\omega_0t
\tag{10-29}
\]
Thus the spin precesses about the direction of $B$ with a frequency
\[
2\omega_0 = \frac{egB}{2m_e} \equiv g\omega_c
\tag{10-30}
\]
$\omega_c = eB/2m_e$ is called the \textit{cyclotron frequency}. The same frequency of precession occurs
if the spin makes an angle $\theta$ with the $z$-axis, rather than lying in the $x$-plane. For a mag
netic field of 1T, the magnitude of $\omega_c = 0.9 \times 10^{11}$ radians/s.

It is worth commenting that the “motion” of the spin can easily be interpreted when
written in the Heisenberg picture. There we have
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{S}}{dt} = \frac{i}{\hbar} [H, \mathbf{S}(t)]
\tag{10-31}
\]
With
\[
H = \frac{eg}{2m_e} \mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{B} \equiv \gamma \mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{B}
\tag{10-32}
\]
we can calculate
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS_1(t)}{dt} &= \frac{i\gamma}{\hbar} [B_1[S_1, S_1] + B_2[S_2, S_1] + B_3[S_3, S_1]] \\
&= \frac{i\gamma}{\hbar} [-i\hbar B_2S_3 + i\hbar B_3S_2] = \gamma(\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{S})_1
\end{aligned}
\]
Similar calculation for the other components yields
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{S}(t)}{dt} = \gamma(\mathbf{S} \times \mathbf{B})
\tag{10-33}
\]
This, however, is exactly the equation for the precession of a classical angular momentum
vector (associated with a magnetic dipole) subject to a torque due to a magnetic field. In this
form we easily see that the precession is not restricted to the case of spin 1/2. Given that the
magnetic moment of a system with angular momentum $\mathbf{J}$ is $\gamma\mathbf{J}$, the same equation holds.

10-3 PARAMAGNETIC RESONANCE

In a solid the gyromagnetic factor $g$ of an electron is affected by the nature of the forces acting in the solid. A knowledge of $g$ provides very useful constraints on what these forces could be, and it is therefore important to be able to measure $g$. This can be done by the *paramagnetic resonance method*. The principle of the method is the following: We have a magnetic field pointing in the $z$-direction, and the electron spin precesses about that direction. How fast does it do so? If we could introduce a magnetic field that is perpendicular to the $z$-axis and rotates with the spin, then the field would "see" an electron spin at rest. The component of the electron spin that points in the $x$-$y$ plane would preferentially align in a direction opposite to the magnetic field to reach the minimum energy state. For those electrons not already aligned in the minimum energy direction, a transition to the lowest energy will take place, and in the process, energy-in the form of radiation-is given up. This can be detected and measured.

It is not practical to have a magnetic field rotating with a frequency of the order of $10^{11}$ radians per second. If, however, we have a magnetic field that points in the $x$-direction, say, and oscillates with a frequency $\omega$, it may be viewed as a superposition of a field rotating in the $x$-$y$ plane clockwise with frequency $\omega$, and a field rotating counter-clockwise with the same frequency, with the phase arranged so that the net effect is in the $x$-direction. (This is analogous to obtaining a linear polarization out of the sum of two circular polarizations.) Only one of the components will travel in the same direction as the precessing spin. The other component will move in a direction opposite to the spin precession, and its effect on the electron spin averages out to zero.

Consider an electron whose only degrees of freedom are the spin states, under the influence of a large magnetic field $B_0$ pointing in the $z$-direction and constant in time, and a small oscillating field $B_1 \cos \omega t$ pointing in the $x$-direction. The Schrödinger equation now reads

\begin{equation}
i\hbar \frac{d}{dt} \begin{pmatrix} a(t) \\ b(t) \end{pmatrix} = \frac{eg\hbar}{4m_e} \begin{pmatrix} B_0 & B_1 \cos \omega t \\ B_1 \cos \omega t & -B_0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a(t) \\ b(t) \end{pmatrix} \tag{10-34}
\end{equation}

If $B_1 = 0$,

\begin{align*}
i \frac{da(t)}{dt} &= \frac{egB_0}{4m_e} a(t) \equiv \omega_0 a(t) \\
i \frac{db(t)}{dt} &= -\omega_0 b(t)
\end{align*}

so that $a(t) = a(0)e^{-i\omega_0 t}$ and $b(t) = b(0)e^{i\omega_0 t}$. This suggests that if $B_1 \neq 0$ then we introduce $A(t)$ and $B(t)$ as follows:

\begin{align*}
A(t) &= a(t)e^{i\omega_0 t} \\
B(t) &= b(t)e^{-i\omega_0 t} \tag{10-35}
\end{align*}

where $a(t)$ and $b(t)$ obey (10-34).
If we also introduce the notation

\begin{equation}
\omega_1 = \frac{egB_1}{4m_e} \tag{10-36}
\end{equation}

then the equations for $A(t)$ and $B(t)$ read as follows

\begin{align*}
i \frac{dA(t)}{dt} &= -\omega_0 A(t) + i \frac{da(t)}{dt} e^{i\omega_0 t} \\
&= -\omega_0 A(t) + (\omega_0 a(t) + \omega_1 b(t) \cos \omega t) e^{i\omega_0 t} \tag{10-37} \\
&= \omega_1 B(t) \cos \omega t e^{2i\omega_0 t} \\
&\approx \frac{1}{2} \omega_1 B(t) e^{i(2\omega_0 - \omega) t}
\end{align*}


<!-- Page 222 -->
10-3 Paramagnetic Resonance \hspace{10pt} \textbf{165}

In exactly the same way we obtain
\begin{equation}
i \frac{dB(t)}{dt} \approx \frac{1}{2} \, \omega_1 A(t) e^{-i(2\omega_0 - \omega)t}
\tag{10-38}
\end{equation}

To obtain these equations in their final form we made use of the \textit{rotating wave} approximation
\begin{equation}
\cos\omega t e^{2i\omega_0 t} = \frac{1}{2} \, (e^{2i\omega_0 t + i\omega t} + e^{2i\omega_0 t - i\omega t}) \approx \frac{1}{2} \, e^{i(2\omega_0 - \omega)t}
\tag{10-39}
\end{equation}

The resonance condition $\omega = 2\omega_0$ implies that the first term above will oscillate very rapidly, and it contributes nothing on the average. We only used the second term in the rotating wave approximation.

The two first-order differential equations can be combined into a single second-order equation. We differentiate (10-37) and get
\begin{align}
\frac{d^2A(t)}{dt^2} &= - \frac{i\omega_1}{2} \frac{d}{dt}(e^{i(2\omega_0 - \omega)t} B(t)) \nonumber \\
&= \frac{\omega_1}{2}(2\omega_0 - \omega) e^{i(2\omega_0 - \omega)t} B(t) - \frac{i\omega_1}{2} \, e^{i(2\omega_0 - \omega)t} \frac{dB(t)}{dt} \tag{10-40} \\
&= (2\omega_0 - \omega)i \frac{dA(t)}{dt} - \left(\frac{\omega_1}{2}\right)^2 A(t) \nonumber
\end{align}

To solve this differential equation, let us try the solution $A(t) = A(0)e^{i\Omega t}$. We get
\[
-\Omega^2 = -(2\omega_0 - \omega)\Omega - \left(\frac{\omega_1}{2}\right)^2
\]

This quadratic equation has two roots:
\begin{equation}
\Omega_{\pm} = \left(\omega_0 - \frac{\omega}{2}\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(\omega_0 - \frac{\omega}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{\omega_1^2}{4}}
\tag{10-41}
\end{equation}

We now write
\begin{equation}
A(t) = A_+ e^{i\Omega_+ t} + A_- e^{i\Omega_- t}
\tag{10-42}
\end{equation}

After a couple of lines of algebra this leads to
\begin{equation}
B(t) = - \frac{2}{\omega_1}(\Omega_+ A_+ e^{-i\Omega_- t} + \Omega_- A_- e^{-i\Omega_+ t})
\tag{10-43}
\end{equation}

We can now finally write the solutions for $a(t)$ and $b(t)$. They are
\begin{align}
a(t) &= A(t) e^{-i\omega_0 t} \nonumber \\
b(t) &= B(t) e^{i\omega_0 t}
\tag{10-44}
\end{align}

Suppose that at time $t = 0$ the spin is in the "up" spin state $\chi_+$. This means that $a(0) = 1$, $b(0) = 0$, which translates into
\begin{align}
A_+ + A_- &= 1 \nonumber \\
\Omega_+ A_+ + \Omega_- A_- &= 0
\tag{10-45}
\end{align}

The solution is
\begin{align}
A_+ &= \frac{\Omega_-}{\Omega_- - \Omega_+} \nonumber \\
A_- &= -\frac{\Omega_+}{\Omega_- - \Omega_+}
\tag{10-46}
\end{align}


<!-- Page 223 -->
**166** Chapter 10 Spin

We may now calculate the probability that at a time $t$, the system is in the "down" spin state $\chi_{-}$. That probability is

\begin{align}
P_{-}(t) &= |b(t)|^2 = \frac{4}{\omega_1^2} |\Omega_{+}A_{+}e^{i\Omega_{+}t} + \Omega_{-}A_{-}e^{i\Omega_{-}t}|^2 \nonumber \\
&= \frac{4}{\omega_1^2} \left( \frac{\Omega_{+}\Omega_{-}}{\Omega_{-} - \Omega_{+}} \right)^2 |e^{i\Omega_{+}t} - e^{i\Omega_{-}t}|^2 \tag{10-47} \\
&= \frac{8}{\omega_1^2} \left( \frac{\Omega_{+}\Omega_{-}}{\Omega_{-} - \Omega_{+}} \right)^2 (1 - \cos(\Omega_{-} - \Omega_{+})t) \nonumber
\end{align}

At resonance, when

\begin{equation}
\omega = 2\omega_0 \tag{10-48}
\end{equation}

(10-41) yields

\begin{equation}
\Omega_{\pm} = \pm \frac{\omega_1}{2} \nonumber
\end{equation}

This means that

\begin{equation}
P_{\text{res}}(t) = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \cos \omega_1 t) \tag{10-49}
\end{equation}

Off-resonance we have

\begin{equation}
P_{-}(t) = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\omega_1^2}{(2\omega_0 - \omega)^2 + \omega_1^2} (1 - \cos \sqrt{(2\omega_0 - \omega)^2 + \omega_1^2} t) \tag{10-50}
\end{equation}

which is small, since $\omega \gg \omega_1$. At resonance the probability becomes of the order of unity. Since the energy of the "up" state is different from that of the "down" state, this energy difference, absorbed from the external field, is enhanced at resonance, when it matches $2\omega_0$. This allows us to determine $g$.

**10-4 ADDITION OF TWO SPINS**

In classical mechanics, angular momenta add vectorially. For example, if the angular momentum of the moon about the earth's axis is $\mathbf{S}$ and the orbital angular momentum of the earth about the sun is $\mathbf{L}$, then there is meaning to the statement that the total angular momentum of the moon about the sun is

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{L} + \mathbf{S} \tag{10-51}
\end{equation}

Does this carry over to quantum mechanics? We will show that we can "add" two angular momenta, but that the addition is not vectorial in the usual sense. We begin by considering the *addition of two spins*. An example of a two-spin system might be the ground state of helium, which has two electrons, both with zero orbital angular momentum in the lowest state. Thus the only contribution to the total angular momentum comes from the spins. We ignore all other aspects of the problem and deal only with the spins.

Suppose we have two electrons, whose spins are described by the operators $\mathbf{S}_1$ and $\mathbf{S}_2$. Each of these sets of operators satisfies the standard angular momentum commutation relations

\begin{equation}
[S_{1x}, S_{1y}] = i\hbar S_{1z} \quad \text{(and cycl.)} \tag{10-52}
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
[S_{2x}, S_{2y}] = i\hbar S_{2z} \quad \text{(and cycl.)} \tag{10-53}
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 224 -->
10-4 Addition of Two Spins \textbf{167}

but the two sets of operators commute with each other, since the degrees of freedom associated with different particles are independent; that is,

\[ [\mathbf{S}_1, \mathbf{S}_2] = 0 \]

Let us now define the total spin $\mathbf{S}$ by

\[ \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{S}_2 \tag{10-54} \]

The commutation relations obeyed by the components of $\mathbf{S}$ are

\begin{align}
[S_x, S_y] &= [S_{1x} + S_{2x}, S_{1y} + S_{2y}] \notag \\
&= [S_{1x}, S_{1y}] + [S_{2x}, S_{2y}] \tag{10-55} \\
&= i\hbar(S_{1z} + S_{2z}) = i\hbar S_z \notag
\end{align}

and so on. We are therefore justified in calling $\mathbf{S}$ the total \textit{spin}. We may now determine the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of $\mathbf{S}^2$ and $S_z$.

The two-spin system actually has four states. If we denote the spinor of the first electron by $\chi^{(1)}_{\pm}$, so that

\begin{align}
\mathbf{S}_1^2\chi^{(1)}_{\pm} &= \frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2} + 1)\hbar^2\chi^{(1)}_{\pm} \tag{10-56} \\
S_{1z}\chi^{(1)}_{\pm} &= \pm \frac{1}{2}\hbar\chi^{(1)}_{\pm} \notag
\end{align}

and similarly for the spinor $\chi^{(2)}_{\pm}$ of the second electron, then the four states are

\[ \chi^{(1)}_{+}\chi^{(2)}_{+}, \quad \chi^{(1)}_{+}\chi^{(2)}_{-}, \quad \chi^{(1)}_{-}\chi^{(2)}_{+}, \quad \chi^{(1)}_{-}\chi^{(2)}_{-} \tag{10-57} \]

The eigenvalues of $S_z$ for the four states are

\begin{align*}
S_z\chi^{(1)}_{\pm}\chi^{(2)}_{\pm} &= (S_{1z} + S_{2z})\chi^{(1)}_{\pm}\chi^{(2)}_{\pm} \\
&= (S_{1z}\chi^{(1)}_{\pm})\chi^{(2)}_{\pm} + \chi^{(1)}_{\pm}(S_{2z}\chi^{(2)}_{\pm})
\end{align*}

that is,

\begin{align}
S_z\chi^{(1)}_{+}\chi^{(2)}_{+} &= \hbar\chi^{(1)}_{+}\chi^{(2)}_{+} \notag \\
S_z\chi^{(1)}_{+}\chi^{(2)}_{-} &= S_z\chi^{(1)}_{-}\chi^{(2)}_{+} = 0 \tag{10-58} \\
S_z\chi^{(1)}_{-}\chi^{(2)}_{-} &= -\hbar\chi^{(1)}_{-}\chi^{(2)}_{-}
\end{align}

There are two states with $m$-value $0$. One might expect that one linear combination of them will form an $S=1$ state, to form a triplet with the $m=1$ and $m=-1$ states, and the orthogonal combination will form a singlet $S=0$ state. To check this expectation, let us construct the lowering operator

\[ S_{-} = S_{1-} + S_{2-} \tag{10-59} \]

and apply this to the $m=1$ state. This should give us the $m=0$ state that belongs to the $S=1$ triplet, aside from a coefficient in front. Indeed, using the fact that

\[ S_{-}^{(i)}\chi^{(i)}_{+} = \hbar\chi^{(i)}_{-} \tag{10-60} \]

which can be established by noting that

\[ \frac{1}{2}\hbar \left[ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} - i \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{pmatrix} \right] \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \hbar \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \tag{10-61} \]

we get

\begin{align}
S_{-} \chi^{(1)}_{+}\chi^{(2)}_{+} &= (S_{1-}\chi^{(1)}_{+}) \chi^{(2)}_{+} + \chi^{(1)}_{+} S_{2-}\chi^{(2)}_{+} \notag \\
&= \hbar\chi^{(1)}_{-}\chi^{(2)}_{+} + \hbar\chi^{(1)}_{+}\chi^{(2)}_{-} \tag{10-62} \\
&= \sqrt{2}\hbar \frac{\chi^{(1)}_{+}\chi^{(2)}_{-} + \chi^{(1)}_{-}\chi^{(2)}_{+}}{\sqrt{2}} \notag
\end{align}


<!-- Page 225 -->
168 Chapter 10 Spin

The linear combination has been normalized, and the compensating factor in front, $\sqrt{2}\hbar$, agrees with what one would expect from (7-20) and (7-24) with $l = m = 1$. If we now apply $S_-$ to this linear combination, and note that

\begin{equation}
S_-^{(i)}\chi_-^{(i)} = 0 \tag{10-63}
\end{equation}

we get

\begin{align}
S_- \frac{\chi_+^{(1)}\chi_+^{(2)} + \chi_-^{(1)}\chi_+^{(2)}}{\sqrt{2}} &= \frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2}} (\chi_-^{(1)}\chi_+^{(2)} + \chi_-^{(1)}\chi_-^{(2)}) \nonumber \\
&= \sqrt{2}\hbar\chi_-^{(1)}\chi_-^{(2)} \tag{10-64}
\end{align}

as we should, for an angular momentum state $S = 1$. The remaining state, constructed to be orthogonal to (10-62) and properly normalized, is

\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\chi_+^{(1)}\chi_-^{(2)} - \chi_-^{(1)}\chi_+^{(2)}) \tag{10-65}
\end{equation}

and because it has no partners, we conjecture that it is an $S = 0$ state. In order to check this, we compute $\mathbf{S}^2$ for the two states

\begin{equation}
X_\pm = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\chi_+^{(1)}\chi_-^{(2)} \pm \chi_-^{(1)}\chi_+^{(2)}) \tag{10-66}
\end{equation}

We have

\begin{align}
\mathbf{S}^2 &= (\mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{S}_2)^2 = \mathbf{S}_1^2 + \mathbf{S}_2^2 + 2\mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{S}_2 \nonumber \\
&= \mathbf{S}_1^2 + \mathbf{S}_2^2 + 2S_{1z}S_{2z} + S_{1+}S_{2-} + S_{1-}S_{2+} \tag{10-67}
\end{align}

First,

\begin{align}
\mathbf{S}_1^2 X_\pm &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\chi_-^{(2)} \mathbf{S}_1^2 \chi_+^{(1)} \pm \chi_+^{(2)} \mathbf{S}_1^2 \chi_-^{(1)}) \nonumber \\
&= \frac{3}{4}\hbar^2 X_\pm \tag{10-68}
\end{align}

and similarly,

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{S}_2^2 X_\pm = \frac{3}{4}\hbar^2 X_\pm \tag{10-69}
\end{equation}

Next, we calculate

\begin{equation}
2S_{1z}S_{2z} X_\pm = 2(\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar)(-\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar) X_\pm = -\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar^2 X_\pm \tag{10-70}
\end{equation}

Finally,

\begin{align}
(S_{1+}S_{2-} + S_{1-}S_{2+}) X_\pm &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (S_{1+}\chi_+^{(1)} S_{2-}\chi_-^{(2)} + S_{1-}\chi_+^{(1)} S_{2+}\chi_-^{(2)} \nonumber \\
&\quad \pm S_{1+}\chi_-^{(1)} S_{2-}\chi_+^{(2)} \pm S_{1-}\chi_-^{(1)} S_{2+}\chi_+^{(2)}) \nonumber
\end{align}

which, with the help of (10-60) and (10-63), yields

\begin{equation}
(S_{1+}S_{2-} + S_{1-}S_{2+}) X_\pm = \pm \hbar X_\pm \tag{10-71}
\end{equation}

Thus

\begin{align}
\mathbf{S}^2 X_\pm &= \hbar^2 (\tfrac{3}{4} + \tfrac{3}{4} - \tfrac{1}{2} \pm 1) X_\pm = \binom{2}{0} \hbar^2 X_\pm \nonumber \\
&= \hbar^2 S(S+1) X_\pm \tag{10-72}
\end{align}

with $S = 1$ and $0$ corresponding to the $\pm$ states.


<!-- Page 226 -->
10-4 Addition of Two Spins  169

What we have shown is that the totality of the four states of two spin 1/2 particles
may be recombined into a triplet and into a singlet total spin state. It is important to note
that the two descriptions are entirely equivalent. In one case we have as our complete set
of commuting observables $\mathbf{S}_1^2, \mathbf{S}_2^2, S_{1z},$ and $S_{2z}$. In the other case we have as our complete
set of commuting observables $\mathbf{S}^2, S_z, \mathbf{S}_1^2, \mathbf{S}_2^2$. By the expansion theorem, any function can
be expanded in terms of a complete set of eigenstates. *What we have demonstrated here is*
*the expansion of the eigenstates of the second set of observables in terms of the complete*
*set of states of the first set of observables.* This is quite analogous to the expression of the
eigenstates of the hydrogen atom in terms of the eigenstates of the momentum operator, in
which the coefficients (the analogs of the $1/\sqrt{2}$'s here) are the momentum-space wave
functions. It is a simple exercise to invert the process and to find the products of the
$\chi^{(1)}\chi^{(2)}$ in terms of triplet and singlet combinations.

In physical problems it frequently happens that to first approximation two sets of
completely commuting observables are equally useful in the construction of eigenstates.
In the next approximation, when additional terms in the Hamiltonian are taken into ac
count, only one of these sets remains useful. A simple example occurs in low-energy nu
clear physics.

In early studies of the potential $V(r)$ that describes the interaction between neutrons
and protons at low energies, it became clear that the strength of the interaction depended
on whether the two interacting particles were in a total spin $S=1$ state or a spin $S=0$
state. For example, a deuteron had $S=1$, while the corresponding $S=0$ state of a neu
tron and a proton did not bind. This can be described in terms of a spin-dependent poten
tial. Suppose we have

\begin{equation}
V(r) = V_1(r) + \frac{1}{\hbar^2} \mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{S}_2 V_2(\mathbf{r}) \tag{10-73}
\end{equation}

we can easily see that $S_{1z}$ and $S_{2z}$ do not commute with the second term, so that the eigen
states of $H$ containing this potential cannot just be simple products of eigenstates of $S_{1z}$
and $S_{2z}$. If we observe, however, that

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{S}_2 = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{S}^2 - \mathbf{S}_1^2 - \mathbf{S}_2^2) \tag{10-74}
\end{equation}

so that this term can be replaced by the eigenvalue, when acting on an eigenfunction of $\mathbf{S}^2$,
$\mathbf{S}_1^2$, and $\mathbf{S}_2^2$, then

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
V(r) &= V_1(r) + \frac{1}{2} V_2(r) \left[ S(S+1) - \frac{3}{2} \right] \\
&= V_1(r) + \frac{1}{4} \binom{1}{-3} V_2(r) \begin{cases} S = 1 \\ S = 0 \end{cases}
\end{aligned} \tag{10-75}
\end{equation}

Such a spin-dependent potential is actually observed in the neutron-proton system. The
bound state is an $S=1$ state-this is the deuteron-but there is also an unbound $S=0$
state. This implies that $V_1 - (3/4)V_2$ is a less attractive potential than $V_1 + (1/4)V_2$. This is
only possible if $V_2(r) \neq 0$.

The spin singlet wave function (10-65) implies that if in a measurement electron
(1) is found in a spin "up" state, then electron (2) *must* be in a spin "down" state. Consider
a singlet state in which the electrons are moving to the right and left, respectively, with
equal and opposite momenta, so that the two-electron system is still at rest in the center of
mass. We may *define* the right-moving electron as labeled with (1) and the left-moving
electron as labeled with (2). Suppose we now make a measurement of the $S_x$ component
of the right-moving electron. From what we have learned so far, the eigenvalues $\pm \hbar/2$


<!-- Page 227 -->
**170** Chapter 10 Spin

will turn up with equal probabilities. Suppose that a particular measurement yields the ($+$) eigenvalue. This projects the eigenstate of electron (1) into the state $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$. One might expect that a simultaneous measurement of $S_x$ carried out on electron (2) is unpredictable, leading to the eigenvalues $\pm\hbar/2$ with equal probability, on the ground that the information about the state of electron (1) cannot propagate to the apparatus measuring electron (2) with infinite speed. *This is false!* In quantum mechanics, the two-electron system is described by a single state vector in which the spins are *entangled*. The system is still a singlet system, and the measurement of $S_x$ must yield the ($-$) eigenvalue. We can see this directly. The singlet state has the wave function

\begin{equation}
\psi(1, 2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}_{\!1} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}_{\!2} - \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}_{\!1} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}_{\!2} \right)
\tag{10-76}
\end{equation}

We now project the state of electron (1) onto the $S_x$ eigenstate with eigenvalue $+\hbar/2$. The projection operator for the positive eigenvalue of $S_x$ for electron (1) is given by

\begin{equation}
P_1(+) = \xi^{(1)}_+ \xi^{(1)*}_{+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\tag{10-77}
\end{equation}

When this acts on the (1) component of the state (10-76) we get

\begin{align}
&P_1(+)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}_{\!1} \left\{ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}_{\!2} \right\} - P_1(+)\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}_{\!1} \left\{ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}_{\!2} \right\} \notag \\
&\qquad= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1/2 \\ 1/2 \end{pmatrix}_{\!1} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}_{\!2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1/2 \\ 1/2 \end{pmatrix}_{\!1} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}_{\!2} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left\{ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}_{\!1} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} \phantom{-}1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}_{\!2} \right\}
\tag{10-78}
\end{align}

This, aside from the numerical factor $-1/\sqrt{2}$ in front, is just the product that describes electron (1) in an eigenstate of $S_x$ with eigenvalue $\hbar/2$ and electron (2) in an eigenstate of $S_x$ with eigenvalue $-\hbar/2$, as expected as a result of the *entanglement* of the two spins.

Another way of seeing this is to expand the spinor eigenstates $\chi_\pm$ of $S_z$ in terms of the spinor eigenstates $\xi_\pm$ of $S_x$. We have [cf. (10-17) and (10-18) with $\phi = 0$]

\begin{equation*}
\xi_\pm = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\chi_+ \pm \chi_-)
\end{equation*}

or, equivalently

\begin{equation*}
\chi_\pm = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\xi_+ \pm \xi_-)
\end{equation*}

If we substitute these into

\begin{equation*}
\psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\chi^{(1)}_+ \chi^{(2)}_- - \chi^{(1)}_- \chi^{(2)}_+)
\end{equation*}

we get, after a little algebra,

\begin{equation*}
\psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\xi^{(1)}_+ \xi^{(2)}_- - \xi^{(1)}_- \xi^{(2)}_+)
\end{equation*}

which clearly shows the correlation of spins in the $x$-direction.


<!-- Page 228 -->
1-5 The Addition of Spin 1/2 and Orbital Angular Momentum \textbf{171}

\textbf{10-5 THE ADDITION OF SPIN 1/2 AND ORBITAL ANGULAR MOMENTUM}

The addition of a spin angular momentum with an orbital angular orbital momentum is of great importance in atomic and nuclear physics. The procedure for doing this is exactly the same as the one we used to add two spins. The algebraic details are worked out in Supplement 10-A [www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz], where we also give a superficial discussion of the addition of two arbitrary angular momenta. Here, we will just write down the results.

For
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{L} \tag{10-79}
\end{equation}
we can find linear combinations of the spin eigenstates $\chi_{\pm}$ and the orbital angular momentum eigenstates $Y_{lm}(\theta, \varphi)$ that are eigenstates of the total angular momentum. We find
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbf{J}^2 \psi_{j,m_j} &= \hbar^2 j(j + 1) \psi_{j,m_j} \\
J_z \psi_{j,m_j} &= \hbar m_j \psi_{j,m_j}
\end{split} \tag{10-80}
\end{equation}
where $j$ can take on the values $j = l \pm \frac{1}{2}$. In both cases,
\begin{equation}
m_j = j, j - 1, j - 2, \dots, -j \tag{10-81}
\end{equation}
The suitably normalized linear combinations are
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\psi_{l+1/2, m+1/2} &= \sqrt{\frac{l + m + 1}{2l + 1}} Y_{l,m} \chi_+ + \sqrt{\frac{l - m}{2l + 1}} Y_{l, m+1} \chi_- \\
\psi_{l-1/2, m+1/2} &= \sqrt{\frac{l - m}{2l + 1}} Y_{l,m} \chi_+ - \sqrt{\frac{l + m + 1}{2l + 1}} Y_{l, m+1} \chi_-
\end{split} \tag{10-82}
\end{equation}
These eigenfunctions are orthogonal to each other.

\textbf{General Rules for Addition of Angular Momenta}

For $\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{L}_1 + \mathbf{L}_2$ we can find linear combinations of the eigenstates $Y_{l_1m_1}$ and the eigenstates $Y_{l_2m_2}$ that are eigenstates of the total angular momentum. We find, as expected, that
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
\mathbf{J}^2 \psi_{j,m_j} &= \hbar^2 j(j + 1) \psi_{j,m_j} \\
J_z \psi_{j,m_j} &= \hbar m_j \psi_{j,m_j}
\end{split} \tag{10-83}
\end{equation}
where $j$ can take on the values
\begin{equation}
j = l_1 + l_2, l_1 + l_2 - 1, l_1 + l_2 - 2, \dots, |l_1 - l_2| \tag{10-84}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
m_j = j, j - 1, j - 2, \dots, -j \tag{10-85}
\end{equation}

We associated angular momentum with integer values with orbital angular momentum. This is not always so. There are particles that have an \textit{intrinsic} spin 1, just as electrons have an intrinsic spin 1/2. The states of these particles in isolation will be described by matrices, except that these are now $3 \times 3$ matrices. We saw these in equations (9-34), (9-37), and (9-38). For an interesting digression on this subject, see Supplement 10-B [www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz].

Of great importance for future applications is the combination of a spin with an orbital angular momentum. Since $\mathbf{L}$ depends on spatial coordinates and $\mathbf{S}$ does not, they commute
\begin{equation}
[\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{S}] = 0 \tag{10A-1}
\end{equation}
It is therefore evident that the components of the total angular momentum $\mathbf{J}$ , defined by
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{L} + \mathbf{S} \tag{10A-2}
\end{equation}
will satisfy the angular momentum commutation relations.

In asking for linear combinations of the $\text{Y}_{\text{lm}}$ and the $\chi_{\pm}$ that are eigenstates of
\begin{equation}
\text{J}_z = \text{L}_z + \text{S}_z \tag{10A-3}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{align}
\mathbf{J}^2 &= \mathbf{L}^2 + \mathbf{S}^2 + 2\mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{S} \nonumber \\
&= \mathbf{L}^2 + \mathbf{S}^2 + 2\text{L}_z\text{S}_z + \text{L}_+\text{S}_- + \text{L}_-\text{S}_+ \tag{10A-4}
\end{align}
we are again looking for the expansion coefficients of one complete set of eigenfunctions in terms of another set of eigenfunctions.

Let us consider the linear combination
\begin{equation}
\psi_{\text{j},\text{m}+1/2} = \alpha \text{Y}_{\text{lm}}\chi_+ + \beta \text{Y}_{\text{l},\text{m}+1}\chi_- \tag{10A-5}
\end{equation}
It is, by construction, an eigenfunction of $\text{J}_z$ with eigenvalue $(\text{m} + \frac{1}{2})\hbar$. We now determine $\alpha$ and $\beta$ such that it is also an eigenfunction of $\mathbf{J}^2$. We shall make use of the fact that
\begin{align}
\text{L}_+\text{Y}_{\text{lm}} &= [\text{l}(\text{l} + 1) - \text{m}(\text{m} + 1)]^{1/2} \hbar \text{Y}_{\text{l},\text{m}+1} \nonumber \\
&= [(\text{l} + \text{m} + 1)(\text{l} - \text{m})]^{1/2} \hbar \text{Y}_{\text{l},\text{m}+1} \nonumber \\
\text{L}_-\text{Y}_{\text{lm}} &= [(\text{l} - \text{m} + 1)(\text{l} + \text{m})]^{1/2} \hbar \text{Y}_{\text{l},\text{m}-1} \tag{10A-6} \\
\text{S}_+\chi_+ &= \text{S}_-\chi_- = 0 \quad \text{S}_{\pm}\chi_{\mp} = \hbar\chi_{\pm} \nonumber
\end{align}
Then
\begin{align}
\mathbf{J}^2\psi_{\text{j},\text{m}+1/2} &= \alpha\hbar^2 \{ [\text{l}(\text{l} + 1) \text{Y}_{\text{lm}}\chi_+ + \tfrac{3}{4}\text{Y}_{\text{lm}}\chi_+ + 2\text{m}(\tfrac{1}{2}) \text{Y}_{\text{lm}}\chi_+ \nonumber \\
&\quad + [(\text{l} - \text{m})(\text{l} + \text{m} + 1)]^{1/2} \text{Y}_{\text{l},\text{m}+1}\chi_- \} + \beta\hbar^2 \{ [\text{l}(\text{l} + 1) \text{Y}_{\text{l},\text{m}+1}\chi_- \nonumber \\
&\quad + \tfrac{3}{4}\text{Y}_{\text{l},\text{m}+1}\chi_- + 2(\text{m} + 1)(-\tfrac{1}{2}) \text{Y}_{\text{l},\text{m}+1}\chi_- \nonumber \\
&\quad + [(\text{l} - \text{m})(\text{l} + \text{m} + 1)]^{1/2} \text{Y}_{\text{lm}}\chi_+ \} \tag{10A-7}
\end{align}

This will be of the form
\[ \hbar^2 \mathrm{j}(\mathrm{j} + 1) \psi_{\mathrm{j}, \mathrm{m}+1/2} = \hbar^2 \mathrm{j}(\mathrm{j} + 1)(\alpha \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{lm}} \chi_{+} + \beta \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{l, m+1}} \chi_{-}) \]  (10A-8)

provided that
\[ \alpha[\mathrm{l}(\mathrm{l} + 1) + \frac{3}{4} + \mathrm{m}] + \beta[(\mathrm{l} - \mathrm{m})(\mathrm{l} + \mathrm{m} + 1)]^{1/2} = \mathrm{j}(\mathrm{j} + 1)\alpha \]
\[ \beta[\mathrm{l}(\mathrm{l} + 1) + \frac{3}{4} - \mathrm{m} - 1] + \alpha[(\mathrm{l} - \mathrm{m})(\mathrm{l} + \mathrm{m} + 1)]^{1/2} = \mathrm{j}(\mathrm{j} + 1)\beta \]  (10A-9)

This requires that
\[ (\mathrm{l} - \mathrm{m})(\mathrm{l} + \mathrm{m} + 1) = [ \mathrm{j}(\mathrm{j} + 1) - \mathrm{l}(\mathrm{l} + 1) - \frac{3}{4} - \mathrm{m}] \]
\[ \times [ \mathrm{j}(\mathrm{j} + 1) - \mathrm{l}(\mathrm{l} + 1) - \frac{3}{4} + \mathrm{m} + 1] \]

which evidently has two solutions,
\[ \mathrm{j}(\mathrm{j} + 1) - \mathrm{l}(\mathrm{l} + 1) - \frac{3}{4} = \begin{cases} -\mathrm{l} - 1 \\ \mathrm{l} \end{cases} \]  (10A-10)

that is,
\[ \mathrm{j} = \begin{cases} \mathrm{l} - \frac{1}{2} \\ \mathrm{l} + \frac{1}{2} \end{cases} \]  (10A-11)

For $\mathrm{j} = \mathrm{l} + 1/2$, we get, after a little algebra
\[ \alpha = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{l} + \mathrm{m} + 1}{2\mathrm{l} + 1}} \quad \beta = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{l} - \mathrm{m}}{2\mathrm{l} + 1}} \]  (10A-12)

(Actually we just get the ratio; these are already normalized forms.) Thus
\[ \psi_{\mathrm{l}+1/2, \mathrm{m}+1/2} = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{l} + \mathrm{m} + 1}{2\mathrm{l} + 1}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{lm}} \chi_{+} + \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{l} - \mathrm{m}}{2\mathrm{l} + 1}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{l}, \mathrm{m}+1} \chi_{-} \]  (10A-13)

We can guess that the $\mathrm{j} = \mathrm{l} - 1/2$ solution must have the form
\[ \psi_{\mathrm{l}-1/2, \mathrm{m}+1/2} = \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{l} - \mathrm{m}}{2\mathrm{l} + 1}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{lm}} \chi_{+} - \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{l} + \mathrm{m} + 1}{2\mathrm{l} + 1}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{l}, \mathrm{m}+1} \chi_{-} \]  (10A-14)

in order to be orthogonal to the $\mathrm{j} = \mathrm{l} + 1/2$ solution.

General Rules for Addition of Angular Momenta,
and Implications for Identical Particles

These two examples illustrate the general features that are involved in the addition of angular momenta: If we have the eigenstates $\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{l}_1 \mathrm{m}_1}^{(1)}$ of $\mathrm{L}_1^2$ and $\mathrm{L}_{1\mathrm{z}}$, and the eigenstates $\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{l}_2 \mathrm{m}_2}^{(2)}$ of $\mathrm{L}_2^2$ and $\mathrm{L}_{2\mathrm{z}}$, then we can form $(2\mathrm{l}_1 + 1)(2\mathrm{l}_2 + 1)$ product wave functions
\[ \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{l}_1 \mathrm{m}_1}^{(1)} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{l}_2 \mathrm{m}_2}^{(2)} \begin{cases} -\mathrm{l}_1 \le \mathrm{m}_1 \le \mathrm{l}_1 \\ -\mathrm{l}_2 \le \mathrm{m}_2 \le \mathrm{l}_2 \end{cases} \]  (10A-15)

These can be classified by the eigenvalue of
\[ \mathrm{J}_{\mathrm{z}} = \mathrm{L}_{1\mathrm{z}} + \mathrm{L}_{2\mathrm{z}} \]  (10A-16)

which is $\mathrm{m}_1 + \mathrm{m}_2$, and which ranges from a maximum value of $\mathrm{l}_1 + \mathrm{l}_2$ down to $-\mathrm{l}_1 - \mathrm{l}_2$.
As in the simple cases discussed earlier, different linear combinations of functions with

m-value & $m_1, m_2$ combinations & numbers \\

6 & (4, 2) & 1 \\

There are a total of 45 combinations, consistent with $(2l_1 + 1) (2l_2 + 1)$.

The highest state has total angular momentum $l_1 + l_2$ as can easily be checked by applying $J^2$ to $Y_{l_1l_1}^{(1)} Y_{l_2l_2}^{(2)}$:
\begin{align}
J^2Y_{l_1l_1}^{(1)}Y_{l_2l_2}^{(2)} &= (L_1^2 + L_2^2 + 2L_{1z}L_{2z} + L_{1+}L_{2-} + L_{1-}L_{2+})~Y_{l_1l_1}^{(1)}Y_{l_2l_2}^{(2)} \nonumber \\
&= \hbar^2[l_1(l_1 + 1) + l_2(l_2 + 1) + 2l_1l_2]~Y_{l_1l_1}^{(1)}Y_{l_2l_2}^{(2)} \tag{10A-17} \\
&= \hbar^2(l_1 + l_2)(l_1 + l_2 + 1)~Y_{l_1l_1}^{(1)}Y_{l_2l_2}^{(2)} \nonumber
\end{align}
This is $j = 6$ in the example discussed in the table. Successive applications of
\begin{equation}
J_- = L_{1-} + L_{2-} \tag{10A-18}
\end{equation}
will pick out one linear combination from each row in the table. These will form the 13 states that belong to j = 6. When this is done, there remains a single state with m = 5, two with m = $4, \ldots ,$ one with m = $-5$. It is extremely plausible, and can, in fact, be checked, that the m = 5 state belongs to j = 5. Again, successive applications of $J_-$ pick out another linear combination from each row in the table, forming 11 states that belong to j = 5. Repetition of this procedure shows that we get, after this, sets that belong to j = 4, j = 3, and finally j = 2. The multiplicities add up to 45:

\[
13 + 11 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 45
\]

We shall not work out the details of this decomposition, as it is beyond the scope of this book. We merely state the results.

(a) The produces $Y_{l_1m_1}^{(1)}Y_{l_2m_2}^{(2)}$ can be decomposed into eigenstates of $J^2$, with eigenvalues $j(j + 1) \hbar^2$, where j can take on the values

\begin{equation}
j = l_1 + l_2, l_1 + l_2 - 1, \ldots, |l_1 - l_2| \tag{10A-19}
\end{equation}

Supplement 10-B


The Levi-Civita Symbol
and Maxwell's Equations


A very useful mathematical device is the use of the Levi-Civita symbol. The symbol $\text{e}_{\text{ijk}}$ is
defined by the following properties:


(a) It is antisymmetric under the interchange of any two of its indices. For example,

$$\text{e}_{123} = -\text{e}_{213} = -(-\text{e}_{231}) \quad\quad (\text{10B-1})$$

and so on. Two consequences of this rule are


(i) When any two indices are equal, the value of $\text{e}_{\text{ijk}}$ is zero.


(ii) $\text{e}_{123} = \text{e}_{231} = \text{e}_{312}$


(b) $\text{e}_{123} = 1 \quad\quad (\text{10B-2})$

Some consequences of this definition are

$$\begin{align*} \text{e}_{\text{ijk}}\text{e}_{\text{ijm}} & = 2\delta_{\text{km}} \\ \text{e}_{\text{ijk}}\text{e}_{\text{imn}} & = \delta_{\text{jm}}\delta_{\text{kn}} - \delta_{\text{jn}}\delta_{\text{km}} \\ \text{e}_{\text{ijk}}\text{A}_{\text{j}}\text{B}_{\text{k}} & = (\text{A} \times \text{B})_{\text{i}} \quad\quad (\text{10B-3}) \\ [\text{L}_{\text{i}}, \text{L}_{\text{j}}] & = \text{i}\text{e}_{\text{ijk}}\text{L}_{\text{k}} \end{align*}$$

We may use this to write out Maxwell's equations in a particularly interesting way.

Maxwell's equations in empty space have the form

$$\begin{align*} \boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \text{B} & = 0 \\ \boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \text{E} & = 0 \\ \boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \text{B} & = \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial\text{E}}{\partial\text{t}} \quad\quad (\text{10B-4}) \\ \boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \text{E} & = -\frac{\partial\text{B}}{\partial\text{t}} \end{align*}$$

They may be rewritten in the form

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\text{t}} (\text{E} + \text{icB}) = -\text{ic}\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times (\text{E} + \text{icB}) \quad\quad (\text{10B-5})$$

Which bears some resemblance to the Schrödinger equation in that the "wave function" is
complex, and that the first-order time derivative enters into the equation.


We may write the equation in a very suggestive way by using the Levi-Civita symbol
in two contexts. First, the symbol may be used to give a matrix representation of the spin
1 angular momentum $\text{S}$. (We are actually working with the angular momentum matrix di
vided by $\hbar$—that is, with the analog of $\boldsymbol{\sigma}/2$.)

W-47


<!-- Page 236 -->
W-48 Supplement 10-B The Levi-Civita Symbol and Maxwell's Equations

To see this, we postulate
\[
(S_i)_{jk} = -i e_{ijk} \tag{10B-6}
\]
The square of the matrix is easily calculated. We have
\[
(S^2)_{jl} = (S_i)_{jk}(S_i)_{kl} = -e_{ijk}e_{ikl} = e_{ijk}e_{ikl} = 2\delta_{jl} \tag{10B-7}
\]
We next need to check the commutation relations
\[
\begin{aligned}
(S_a)_{jk}(S_b)_{kl} - (S_b)_{jk}(S_a)_{kl} &= -e_{ajk}e_{bkl} + e_{bjk}e_{akl} \\
&= e_{ajk}e_{blk} - e_{bjk}e_{alk} = \delta_{ab}\delta_{jl} - \delta_{al}\delta_{jb} - \delta_{ab}\delta_{jl} + \delta_{bl}\delta_{aj} \\
&= \delta_{bl}\delta_{aj} - \delta_{al}\delta_{jb} = e_{bam}e_{ljm} = ie_{abm}(-ie_{mjl}) = ie_{abm}(S_m)_{jl}
\end{aligned}
\]
that is,
\[
[S_a, S_b] = ie_{abm}S_m \tag{10B-8}
\]
Let us now rewrite our version of Maxwell's equations. It reads
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} (E_i + icB_i) &= -ice_{imn} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_m} (E_n + iB_n) \\
&= -c(S_m)_{in} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_m} (E_n + iB_n)
\end{aligned}
\]
or equivalently,
\[
i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} (E_i + icB_i) = c(S_m)_{in} \frac{\hbar}{i} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_m} (E_n + iB_n) \tag{10B-9}
\]
With the notation $\psi_i = (E_i + icB_i)$, we get
\[
i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi_i}{\partial t} = c(S \cdot p_{op})_{im} \psi_m \tag{10B-10}
\]
The operator on the right side is the projection of the photon spin along the direction of motion. The complex conjugate wave function is easily seen to satisfy
\[
i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi_i^*}{\partial t} = -c(S \cdot p_{op})_{im} \psi_m^* \tag{10B-11}
\]
where the right side represents the opposite projection (helicity). We need both equations to obtain separate equations for E and B.
