\chapter{16}

\section*{The Interaction of Charged Particles with the Electromagnetic Field}

\textbf{T}he most important application of quantum mechanics dealt with in this book involves the interaction between electrons (or other charged particles) and the electromagnetic field. In this chapter we deal with the formulation of the Schr\"{o}dinger equation in the presence of a general electromagnetic field, and then study the special case of electrons in a constant, uniform magnetic field.

\section*{16-1 CLASSICAL ELECTRODYNAMICS}

Maxwell's equations read
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}, t) & = 0 \\
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t) & = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0} \rho(\mathbf{r}, t) \\
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}, t) - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} & = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r}, t) \\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t) + \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} & = 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{16-1}
\end{equation}

These equations lead to
\begin{equation}
\frac{\partial \rho(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r}, t) = 0
\tag{16-2}
\end{equation}
which expresses charge conservation. If we integrate (16-2) over an arbitrary volume $V$, then this reads
\begin{equation*}
\frac{d}{dt} \int\limits_V d^3r \, \rho(\mathbf{r}, t) = - \int\limits_S dS \, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r}, t)
\end{equation*}
which states that the rate of change of charge in the volume $V$ is equal to the net current flowing out through the surface $S$ that bounds the volume $V$.

A point electron of mass $m_e$ and charge $-e$ obeys the Lorentz force equation
\begin{equation}
m_e \frac{d^2 \mathbf{r}}{dt^2} = -e[\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t) + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}, t)]
\tag{16-3}
\end{equation}

246


<!-- Page 336 -->
16-1 Classical Electrodynamics 247

The transition to quantum mechanics requires the construction of a Hamiltonian. To do
this, it is necessary to introduce the \textit{potentials} for the electromagnetic system. We intro
duce $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)$ and $\phi(\mathbf{r}, t)$ as follows
\begin{align}
\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}, t) &= \boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) \nonumber \\
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t) &= -\frac{\partial \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} - \boldsymbol{\nabla} \phi(\mathbf{r}, t) \label{16-4}
\end{align}

so that the first and last of the equations (16-1) are automatically satisfied. The potentials
are not uniquely defined. The first of the above equations is unchanged if we make a
transformation to a new \textit{vector potential}
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{A}'(\mathbf{r}, t) = \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) - \boldsymbol{\nabla} g(\mathbf{r}, t) \label{16-5}
\end{equation}

since $\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \boldsymbol{\nabla} g(\mathbf{r}, t) = 0$. The electric field will be unchanged if, in addition to making the
change in (16-5), we change $\phi$ to $\phi'$ according to
\begin{equation}
\phi'(\mathbf{r}, t) = \phi(\mathbf{r}, t) + \frac{\partial g(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} \label{16-6}
\end{equation}

This invariance, known as \textit{invariance under gauge transformations}, gives us the freedom
to define the potentials in various ways, to suit out convenience. The Maxwell equations
now read
\begin{equation}
-\nabla^2 \phi(\mathbf{r}, t) - \frac{\partial}{\partial t} (\boldsymbol{\nabla} \boldsymbol{\cdot} \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)) = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0} \rho(\mathbf{r}, t) \label{16-7}
\end{equation}

and
\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times (\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)) + \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t^2} + \frac{1}{c^2} \boldsymbol{\nabla} \frac{\partial \phi(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r}, t) \label{16-8}
\end{equation}

where we have used $\varepsilon_0 \mu_0 = 1/c^2$. This may be rewritten as
\begin{equation}
-\nabla^2 \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) + \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t^2} + \boldsymbol{\nabla} \left( \boldsymbol{\nabla} \boldsymbol{\cdot} \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) + \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial \phi(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} \right) = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r}, t) \label{16-9}
\end{equation}

If the charge distribution is static---that is, $\rho(\mathbf{r})$ is independent of time---it is convenient to
choose the function $g(\mathbf{r}, t)$ such that
\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\nabla} \boldsymbol{\cdot} \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) = 0 \label{16-10}
\end{equation}

This choice is given the name of \textit{Coulomb gauge}. In this case we have
\begin{equation}
\nabla^2 \phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0} \rho(\mathbf{r}) \label{16-11}
\end{equation}

a time-independent scalar potential. The equation for the vector potential in this gauge
reads
\begin{equation}
-\nabla^2 \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) + \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t^2} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}(\mathbf{r}, t) \label{16-12}
\end{equation}

When the charge distribution is not static, it is more convenient to choose the so-called
\textit{Lorentz gauge}, for which
\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\nabla} \boldsymbol{\cdot} \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) + \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial \phi(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} = 0 \label{16-13}
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 337 -->
**248** Chapter 16 The Interaction of Charged Particles with the Electromagnetic Field

This leaves the equation for the vector potential (16-12) unaltered. The scalar potential
now also obeys a wave equation. A technical point worth noting is that the vector identity.

$$\nabla \times (\nabla \times \textbf{A}) = -\nabla^2 \textbf{A} + \nabla(\nabla \cdot \textbf{A})$$

used to obtain (16-9) is only valid in cartesian coordinates. This means that $\nabla^2 \textbf{A}(\textbf{r},t)$ as it
appears, must be calculated in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$.

The transition to quantum mechanics requires a Hamiltonian formulation of the equa
tion of motion. In the absence of interaction with the electromagnetic field, it is easily
seen that the Hamiltonian equations

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dx_i}{dt} & = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} \\
\frac{dp_i}{dt} & = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_i}
\end{aligned}
\tag{16-14}
\end{equation}

with

\begin{equation}
H = \frac{p^2}{2m_e} + V(r)
\tag{16-15}
\end{equation}

yields

\begin{equation}
m_e \frac{d^2x_i}{dt^2} = -\frac{\partial V(r)}{\partial x_i}
\tag{16-16}
\end{equation}

The Hamiltonian for the interaction of an electron with an external electromagnetic field,
represented by the potentials $(\textbf{A}(\textbf{r},t), \phi(\textbf{r},t))$, is taken to be

\begin{equation}
H = \frac{1}{2m_e} (\textbf{p} + e\textbf{A}(\textbf{r},t))^2 - e\phi(\textbf{r},t)
\tag{16-17}
\end{equation}

The Hamiltonian equations of motion are

\begin{equation}
\frac{dx_i}{dt} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} = \frac{1}{m_e} (p_i + eA_i(\textbf{r},t))
\tag{16-18}
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
\frac{dp_i}{dt} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_i} = -\frac{1}{m_e} (p_k + eA_k) \frac{\partial A_k}{\partial x_i} + e\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x_i}
\tag{16-19}
\end{equation}

From this it follows that

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
m_e \frac{d^2x_i}{dt^2} & = \frac{d}{dt}(p_i + eA_i(\textbf{r},t)) = \frac{dp_i}{dt} + e \left(\frac{\partial A_i}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial A_i}{\partial x_k} \frac{dx_k}{dt} \right) \\
& = -\frac{e}{m_e} \left(m_e \frac{dx_k}{dt} \right) \frac{\partial A_k}{\partial x_i} + e \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x_i} + e \frac{\partial A_i}{\partial t} + e \frac{\partial A_i}{\partial x_k} \frac{dx_k}{dt} \\
& = e \left(\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x_i} + \frac{\partial A_i}{\partial t} \right) + e \frac{dx_k}{dt} \left(\frac{\partial A_i}{\partial x_k} - \frac{\partial A_k}{\partial x_i} \right) \\
& = -eE_i + e(\textbf{v} \times (-\nabla \times \textbf{A}))_i \\
& = -eE_i - e(\textbf{v} \times \textbf{B})_i
\end{aligned}
\tag{16-20}
\end{equation}

This confirms that the Hamiltonian in (16-7) correctly describes the classical motion.


<!-- Page 338 -->
16-2 The Schrödinger Equation for an Electron in Interaction with an Electromagnetic Field 

**16-2 THE SCHRÖDINGER EQUATION FOR AN ELECTRON IN INTERACTION WITH AN ELECTROMAGNETIC FIELD**

The Schrödinger equation takes the form

$$
i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} = H\psi = \left[ \frac{1}{2m_e} (-i\hbar \mathbf{\nabla} + e\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t))^2 - e\phi(\mathbf{r}, t) \right] \psi(\mathbf{r}, t) \quad (16-21)
$$

where we have replaced the operator **$p$** by $-i\hbar\mathbf{\nabla}$. Let us first check what happens to this equation when we make a gauge transformation on the potentials, such as (16-5) and (16-6). In terms of the primed potentials the equation becomes

$$
i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} = \left[ \frac{1}{2m_e} (-i\hbar \mathbf{\nabla} + e\mathbf{A}'(\mathbf{r}, t) + e\mathbf{\nabla} g(\mathbf{r}, t))^2 - e\phi'(\mathbf{r}, t) - e \frac{\partial g(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} \right] \psi(\mathbf{r}, t)
$$

This looks like a different equation. We now show that by making an appropriate change from $\psi$ to a newly defined $\psi'$ we can restore the equation to its original form, and thus show the _gauge invariance_ of the Schrödinger equation. Since we want to preserve the absolute square of the wave function, we define

$$
\psi'(\mathbf{r}, t) = e^{i\Lambda(\mathbf{r}, t)} \psi(\mathbf{r}, t) \quad (16-22)
$$

We see that

$$
\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} (e^{-i\Lambda} \psi') = -i \frac{\partial \Lambda}{\partial t} \psi + e^{-i\Lambda} \psi'
$$

and

$$
-i\hbar\mathbf{\nabla}\psi = -i\hbar\mathbf{\nabla}(e^{-i\Lambda} \psi') = -\hbar(\mathbf{\nabla}\Lambda)\psi - e^{-i\Lambda}\mathbf{\nabla}\psi'
$$

We see from this that we recover the original Schrödinger equation in terms of $\mathbf{A}'$, $\phi'$, $\psi'$, provided we choose

$$
\Lambda(\mathbf{r}, t) = \frac{e}{\hbar} g(\mathbf{r}, t) \quad (16-23)
$$

To continue, we assume that the scalar potential is independent of time. We work in the _Coulomb gauge_ specified by

$$
\mathbf{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) = 0 \quad (16-24)
$$

Thus (16-21), which has the form

$$
i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e} \mathbf{\nabla}^2 \psi - \frac{ie\hbar}{m_e} \mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{\nabla} \psi - \frac{ie\hbar}{m_e} (\mathbf{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{A}) \psi + \frac{e^2}{2m_e} \mathbf{A}^2 \psi - e\phi \psi
$$

becomes

$$
i\hbar \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e} \mathbf{\nabla}^2 \psi - \frac{ie\hbar}{m_e} \mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{\nabla} \psi + \frac{e^2}{2m_e} \mathbf{A}^2 \psi - e\phi \psi \quad (16-25)
$$

Note that for a Coulomb potential,

$$
\phi(\mathbf{r}) = -\frac{Ze}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} \quad (16-26)
$$

In what follows we discuss the interaction of an electron with a constant magnetic field. This is a rather rich subject, with many important physical applications.


<!-- Page 339 -->
250 Chapter 16 The Interaction of Charged Particles with the Electromagnetic Field

Since the magnetic field is constant, we may write

\begin{equation}
\psi(\mathbf{r}, t) = e^{-iEt/\hbar}\psi(\mathbf{r}) \tag{16-27}
\end{equation}

The Schrödinger equation becomes

\begin{equation}
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\nabla^2\psi - \frac{ie\hbar}{m_e}\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla\psi + \frac{e^2}{2m_e}\mathbf{A}^2\psi - e\phi\psi = E\psi \tag{16-28}
\end{equation}

16-3 THE CONSTANT MAGNETIC FIELD

For a constant, uniform magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, we may take$^1$

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{A} = -\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{B} \tag{16-29}
\end{equation}

It is simple to check that $\nabla \times \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B}$. Thus, in the Schrödinger equation above, the second term becomes

\begin{equation}
-\frac{ie\hbar}{m_e} \left(-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{B}\right) \cdot \nabla\psi = -\frac{ie\hbar}{2m_e} \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{r} \times \nabla\psi = \frac{e}{2m_e} \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{L}\psi \tag{16-30}
\end{equation}

This is a consequence of the relation

\begin{equation*}
-i\hbar \mathbf{r} \times \nabla\psi = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}_{op}\psi = \mathbf{L}\psi
\end{equation*}

The term quadratic in $\mathbf{A}$ takes the form

\begin{equation}
\frac{e^2}{2m_e} \left( -\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{B} \right)^2 \psi = \frac{e^2}{8m_e} (r^2 B^2 - (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{B})^2) \psi = \frac{e^2 B^2}{8m_e} (x^2 + y^2)\psi \tag{16-31}
\end{equation}

if the $z$-axis is defined by the direction of $\mathbf{B}$, so that $\mathbf{B} = (0, 0, B)$. This term looks like a two-dimensional harmonic oscillator potential.

Let us compare the magnitudes of the two terms. In making our estimate we choose $\langle L_z \rangle$ of order $\hbar$, and $\langle x^2 + y^2 \rangle$ to be of order $a_0^2$, where $a_0$ is the Bohr radius. This means that

\begin{align*}
\frac{e^2 B^2 a_0^2 / 8m_e}{eB\hbar / 2m_e} &= \frac{eB a_0^2}{4\hbar} = \frac{(1.6 \times 10^{-19} C)(0.5 \times 10^{-10} m)^2}{4(1.05 \times 10^{-34} J \cdot s)} B(\text{tesla}) \\
&= \frac{B(\text{tesla})}{10^6}
\end{align*}

For $B$ or the order of 1 tesla, the quadratic term is negligible. The term linear in $B$ is also small compared with typical atomic splittings. Comparison with the Coulomb energy yields

\begin{equation*}
\frac{eB\hbar / 2m_e}{m_e c^2 \alpha^2 / 2} = \frac{e\hbar}{(m_e c \alpha)^2} B = \frac{B(\text{tesla})}{2.3 \times 10^5}
\end{equation*}

The quadratic term can become important under certain conditions. One of them is when the magnetic field is very strong. Fields as large as $10^8$ T may exist on the surface of neutron stars, and such fields overwhelm the electric fields due to the electrostatic attraction between electrons and nuclei. In such an environment the structure of atoms is radically

---

$^1$This choice is not unique, since we may add the gradient of any function $\Lambda$ without changing $\mathbf{B}$. This choice is convenient for our purposes.


<!-- Page 340 -->
16-3 The Constant Magnetic Field \textbf{251}

altered. The other condition is when the $(x^2 + y^2)$ term in the interaction is of macroscopic size. This happens for motion of an electron in a synchrotron. Here both the radius of the orbit and $L$ are huge on an atomic scale.

If we wanted to take spin into account, we would only have to alter the term linear in $\mathbf{B}$ in the Schrödinger equation so that $\mathbf{L} \cdot \mathbf{B}$ is replaced by $(2\mathbf{S} + \mathbf{L}) \cdot \mathbf{B}$. In what follows, we ignore the spin.

The presence of $(x^2 + y^2)$ in the potential suggest the use of cylindrical coordinates. With

\begin{align}
x &= \rho \cos \phi \nonumber \\
y &= \rho \sin \phi \tag{16-32}
\end{align}

we follow the procedure outlined at the beginning of Supplement 7-B [\textbf{www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz}] to arrive at

\begin{align}
\frac{\partial}{\partial x} &= \cos \phi \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} - \frac{\sin \phi}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi} \nonumber \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial y} &= \sin \phi \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} + \frac{\cos \phi}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial \phi} \tag{16-33}
\end{align}

and hence

\begin{equation}
\nabla^2 = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2} + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \rho^2} + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\partial}{\partial \rho} + \frac{1}{\rho^2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \phi^2} \tag{16-34}
\end{equation}

If we now write

\begin{equation}
\psi(\mathbf{r}) = u_m(\rho) \: e^{im\phi} \: e^{ikz} \tag{16-35}
\end{equation}

We find that the differential equation satisfied by $u_m(\rho)$ is

\begin{equation}
\frac{d^2u_m}{d\rho^2} + \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{du_m}{d\rho} - \frac{m^2}{\rho^2} u_m - \frac{e^2B^2}{4\hbar^2} \rho^2 u_m + \left(\frac{2m_eE}{\hbar^2} - \frac{eB\hbar m}{\hbar^2} - k^2\right) u_m = 0 \tag{16-36}
\end{equation}

If we introduce the variable

\begin{equation}
x = \sqrt{\frac{eB}{2\hbar}} \rho \tag{16-37}
\end{equation}

we can rewrite the equation in the form

\begin{equation}
\frac{d^2u_m}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{x} \frac{du_m}{dx} - \frac{m^2}{x^2} u_m - x^2 u_m + \lambda u_m = 0 \tag{16-38}
\end{equation}

where

\begin{equation}
\lambda = \frac{4m_e}{eB\hbar} \left(E - \frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m_e}\right) - 2m \tag{16-39}
\end{equation}

It is fairly straightforward to determine that (a) the behavior of $u(x)$ at infinity, determined from

\begin{equation*}
\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} - x^2 u \approx 0
\end{equation*}

is $u(x) \sim e^{-x^2/2}$, and (b) the behavior of $u(x)$ near $x = 0$, determined from

\begin{equation*}
\frac{d^2u}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{x} \frac{du}{dx} - \frac{m^2}{x^2} u \approx 0
\end{equation*}


<!-- Page 341 -->
**252** Chapter 16 The Interaction of Charged Particles with the Electromagnetic Field

is $u(x) \sim x^{|m|}$. We thus write

\begin{equation}
u(x) = x^{|m|}e^{-x^2/2}G(x)
\end{equation}

and determine the differential equation obeyed by $G(x)$. A little algebra leads to

\begin{equation}
\frac{d^2G}{dx^2} + \left(\frac{2|m|+1}{x} - 2x\right)\frac{dG}{dx} + (\lambda - 2 - 2|m|)G = 0
\end{equation}

This can be brought into the same form as (8-27) if we change variables to

\begin{equation}
y = x^2
\end{equation}

The equation then takes the form

\begin{equation}
\frac{d^2G}{dy^2} + \left(\frac{|m|+1}{y} - 1\right)\frac{dG}{dy} + \frac{\lambda - 2 - 2|m|}{4y}G = 0
\end{equation}

We can now proceed as in Chapter 8. Comparison with (8-32) shows that we must have

\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{4}\lambda - \frac{1 + |m|}{2} = n_r
\end{equation}

as an eigenvalue condition, with $n_r = 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$. This implies that $E - \hbar^2k^2/2m_e$, the
energy with the kinetic energy of free motion in the $z$-direction subtracted out, is given by

\begin{equation}
E - \frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m_e} = \frac{eB\hbar}{2m_e}(2n_r + 1 + |m| + m)
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
G(y) = L_{n_r}^{|m|}(y)
\end{equation}

### Classical Limit

We limit our discussion to the classical limit. We first review classical theory. Recall that
we found the velocity in the form

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{p} + e\mathbf{A}}{m_e}
\end{equation}

With $\mathbf{A} = -\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{B}$ we find

\begin{align}
m_e\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} + e\mathbf{r} \times \left(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{B}\right) \notag \\
&= \mathbf{L} - \frac{e}{2}[\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{B}) - r^2\mathbf{B}]
\end{align}

We take the $z$-component of the equation to obtain

\begin{equation*}
m_e(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v})_z = L_z + \frac{eB}{2}(x^2 + y^2)
\end{equation*}

that is,

\begin{equation}
m_e\rho v = L_z + \frac{eB}{2}\rho^2
\end{equation}

The force on an electron is given by $\mathbf{F} = -e\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$, so that for circular motion we
have

\begin{equation}
m_e\frac{v^2}{\rho} = evB
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 342 -->
This, with (16-49) yields, after a little algebra,

\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{2} m_e v^2 = \frac{eB}{m_e} L_z \tag{16-51}
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
\rho = \sqrt{\frac{2 L_z}{e B}} \tag{16-52}
\end{equation}

We now return to the expression for the energy, (16-45). Because of the smallness of $\hbar$, the energy can only be of macroscopic size for reasonable $B$, if $(2n_r + 1 + |m| + m)$ is very large. We have two cases: (a) If $m < 0$, this implies that $n_r$ is very large. Now $n_r$ determines the degree of the polynomial $L_{n_r}^{|m|}(y)$---that is, the number of the zeros in the function$^2$---and if that is very large, the function cannot be large for some small range of $y$ where the classical orbit would be located. (b) If $m > 0$, the coefficient is $(2n_r + 1 + 2m)$, and this can be large, with $n_r$ small, provided that $m$ is large. The energy now is

\begin{equation}
E - \frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m_e} \cong \left(\frac{eB}{m_e}\right)\hbar m \tag{16-53}
\end{equation}

in agreement with the classical result. Note that

\begin{equation}
L_z = \hbar m \tag{16-54}
\end{equation}

is positive, as expected.

We can also show that the radius of the orbit, as determined by the peaking of the radial probability distribution, corresponds to the classical value. Let us take $n_r = 0$. In that case $L_{n_r}^{|m|}(y)$ is just a constant, and the square of the wave function is according to (16-40),

\begin{equation}
P(x) = x^{2|m|} e^{-x^2} \tag{16-55}
\end{equation}

This has a maximum where

\begin{equation*}
\frac{dP}{dx} = (2|m|x^{2|m|-1} - 2x^{2|m|+1}) \, e^{-x^2} = 0
\end{equation*}

that is, at

\begin{equation}
x = \sqrt{|m|} \tag{16-56}
\end{equation}

which yields

\begin{equation}
\rho = \left(\frac{2}{eB} \hbar m \right)^{1/2} \tag{16-57}
\end{equation}

This problem provides a beautiful illustration of the correspondence principle.

**16-4 LANDAU LEVELS**

The choice $\textbf{A} = (-yB/2, xB/2, 0)$ is not unique. The choice

\begin{equation}
\textbf{A} = (0, Bx, 0) \tag{16-58}
\end{equation}

---

$^2$See the discussion at the beginning of the section on the Degeneracy of the Spectrum in Chapter 8.


<!-- Page 343 -->
254

Chapter 16

The Interaction of Charged Particles with the Electromagnetic Field

leads to the same magnetic field. It differs by a simple gauge transformation from $\mathbf{A} = -\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{B}/2$:

\begin{equation}
\left( \frac{-yB}{2}, \frac{xB}{2}, 0 \right) = (0, Bx, 0) - \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \right) \left( \frac{yxB}{2} \right)
\tag{16-59}
\end{equation}

With this choice of vector potential, the Hamiltonian operator for an electron in a constant magnetic field takes the form

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{2m_e} (\mathbf{p} + e\mathbf{A})^2 &= \frac{1}{2m_e} (p_x^2 + (p_y + eBx)^2 + p_z^2) \\
&= \frac{1}{2m_e} (p_x^2 + p_y^2 + p_z^2 + 2eBxp_y + e^2B^2x^2)
\end{aligned}
\tag{16-60}
\end{equation}

It is clear that $[H, p_y] = 0$ and $[H, p_z] = 0$, so that we can construct functions that are simultaneous eigenfunctions of $p_y, p_z$ as well as $H$. For simplicity we choose the state to be an eigenfunction of $p_z$ with eigenvalue zero---that is, no motion outside of the $x$-$y$ plane. If we write the eigenvalue of $p_y$ as $\hbar k$, then the simultaneous eigenfunction takes the form

\begin{equation}
\psi(x, y) = e^{iky}v(x)
\tag{16-61}
\end{equation}

where $v(x)$ is a solution of the equation

\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{2m_e} \left( -\hbar^2 \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + e^2B^2\left(x + \frac{\hbar k}{eB}\right)^2 \right) v(x) = E v(x)
\tag{16-62}
\end{equation}

This is just the equation for a harmonic oscillator whose equilibrium point is shifted from $x = 0$ to $-x_0$ where $x_0 = \hbar k / eB$. We may thus write the solution as

\begin{equation}
\psi(x, y) = e^{ieBx_0y/\hbar} u(x - x_0)
\tag{16-63}
\end{equation}

where $u(x)$ is the eigensolution of the harmonic oscillator centered at $x = 0$. Note that a comparison with the usual potential $\frac{1}{2}m_e\omega^2x^2$ shows that the frequency is

\begin{equation}
\omega = \frac{eB}{m_e}
\tag{16-64}
\end{equation}

and the energy eigenvalues are

\begin{equation}
E = \hbar\omega\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right) \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots
\tag{16-65}
\end{equation}

The energy levels labeled by $n$ are called Landau levels.
If the electron is confined to a strip whose $x$-dimension is $L_1$ and $y$-dimension is $L_2$, then the boundary condition in the $y$-direction,

\begin{equation}
\psi(y) = \psi(y + L_2)
\tag{16-66}
\end{equation}

implies that

\begin{equation}
\frac{eBx_0}{\hbar} L_2 = 2\pi n* \qquad n* = 0, 1, 2, \dots
\tag{16-67}
\end{equation}

Since

\begin{equation}
0 \le x_0 \le L_1
\tag{16-68}
\end{equation}

we deduce that

\begin{equation}
0 \le n* \le \frac{eB}{2\pi\hbar} L_1 L_2
\tag{16-69}
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 344 -->
16-5 The Integral Quantum Hall Effect \textbf{255}

We can easily check that $\hbar /eB$ has the dimensions of an area. (A quick way is to see that $\upsilon eB$ appearing in the Lorentz force has the dimensions [$\text{MLT}^{-2}$]. Therefore $eB$ has the dimensions [$\text{MT}^{-1}$]. With $\hbar$ having dimensions of $\text{J}\cdot\text{s}$---that is, [$\text{ML}^2\text{T}^{-1}$], we get our result.) If we define a \textit{magnetic length} by
\begin{equation}
l_B^2 = \frac{\hbar}{eB}
\tag{16-70}
\end{equation}
(whose value is $l_B = \frac{256 \times 10^{-10}}{\sqrt{B(\text{tesla})}}\text{ m}$),

we can write
\begin{equation}
n^*_{\max} = \frac{L_1L_2}{2\pi l_B^2}
\tag{16-71}
\end{equation}
Since the area of the sample is $L_1, L_2$, the number of states per unit area of a full Landau level is therefore
\begin{equation}
n_B = \frac{1}{2\pi l_B^2}
\tag{16-72}
\end{equation}
The energy spacing of the Landau levels is
\begin{equation}
\hbar\omega = \frac{eB\hbar}{m_e} = \frac{\hbar^2}{m_e l_B^2}
\tag{16-73}
\end{equation}
The occupation of Landau levels is of great importance in the theoretical understanding of the \textit{Quantum Hall Effect}. We present a very much simplified discussion of this topic.

\subsection*{16-5 THE INTEGRAL QUANTUM HALL EFFECT}

Consider a two-dimensional sample as shown in Fig. 16-1. The $\textbf{B}$ field points in the $z$-direction and an electric field $\textbf{E}$ is applied in the $y$-direction. Electrons will flow in the negative $y$-direction, with a current density proportional to the electric field and the conductivity, so that
\begin{equation}
j_y = \sigma_0 E_y
\tag{16-74}
\end{equation}
The conductivity is given by $\sigma_0 = n_e e^2 \tau_0/m_e^*$. Here $n_e$ is the electron density, $m_e^*$ is the effective mass of the electron in the material, and $\tau_0$ is a quantity with the dimensions of time, which can be interpreted as the average time between collisions of the electron with imperfections in the lattice.$^3$ In the presence of the magnetic field the electrons experience a Lorentz force $\textbf{F} = -e\textbf{v} \times \textbf{B}$. Since the current is related to the velocity by $\textbf{j} = -n_ee\textbf{v}$, the extra force due to the magnetic field is
\[
\textbf{F} = \frac{\textbf{j} \times \textbf{B}}{n_e}
\]
This is equivalent to an additional electric field $\textbf{E}' = -\textbf{F}/e$, so that the current density is changed to
\begin{equation}
\textbf{j} = \sigma_0 \left(\textbf{E} - \frac{\textbf{j} \times \textbf{B}}{n_e e} \right)
\tag{16-75}
\end{equation}

\rule{\textwidth}{0.4pt}

$^3$For a brief discussion of conductivity, see Bernstein, Fishbane, and Gasiorowicz, \textit{loc. cit.}

The components of this are

\[
j_x = - \frac{\sigma_0 j_y B}{n_e e} = - \frac{e \tau_0}{m_e^*} j_y B \tag{16-76}
\]

and

\[
\begin{aligned}
j_y &= \sigma_0 E_y + \frac{\sigma_0 j_x B}{n_e e} = \sigma_0 E_y + \frac{e \tau_0}{m_e^*} j_x B \\
&= \sigma_0 E_y - \left( \frac{e \tau_0}{m_e^*} \right)^2 j_y B^2
\end{aligned} \tag{16-77}
\]

This leads to the following expressions for the current:

\[
j_y = \frac{\sigma_0 E_y}{1 + (e \tau_0 B / m_e^*)^2} \tag{16-78}
\]

and, after some manipulations,

\[
j_x = \frac{n_e e E_y}{B} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{1 + (e \tau_0 B / m_e^*)^2} \right) \tag{16-79}
\]

The density of electron---that is, the number of electrons per unit area, $n_e$---may be written in terms of the maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in a Landau level

\[
n_e = f n_B = f \frac{eB}{2\pi\hbar} \tag{16-80}
\]


<!-- Page 346 -->
16-6 An Additional Comment on Gauge Invariance \quad \textbf{257}

This lead to
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{j_y}{E_y} &= \frac{\sigma}{1 + (e\tau_0B/m_e^*)^2} \\
\frac{j_x}{E_y} &= f\frac{e^2}{2\pi\hbar} \left(1 - \frac{1}{1 + (e\tau_0B/m_e^*)^2}\right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{16-81}
\end{equation}

The density of electrons and the magnetic field $B$ are under the control of the experimen-
talist. If $n_e$ is fixed and $B$ is varied, then the ratios in (16-81) can be measured as a func-
tion of $B$. Equivalently, if $B$ is fixed and $n_e$ varied, the ratios can be measured as functions
of $n_e$. It was found by von Klitzing, Dorda, and Pepper in 1980 that the values of $B$ such
that $f$ takes on integer values $f = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ lead to (a) vanishing values of $j_y/E_y$, and
(b) values of $\lvert j_x/E_y \rvert = f(e^2/2\pi\hbar)$. A simple-minded explanation of the effect is that, when
the Landau levels are filled, an electron cannot undergo elastic scattering, since it cannot
recoil into another state of the same energy. It cannot be thermally excited into a higher
(empty) Landau level, since at low temperatures (0.1 K) and large magnetic fields ($B \approx
10$ T), $kT \ll eB\hbar/m_e^*$. Effectively $\tau_0 \to \infty$, and the observed result follows from (16-81).

This is an oversimplified discussion, since it does not take into account a very large
number of effects that occur in the non-ideal case. For example, some electrons are
trapped at imperfections in the crystal lattice, Landau levels are not sharp because of ther-
mal and impurity effects, and electron--electron interactions have been completely ne-
glected. Nevertheless, when all of these complications are taken into account, it is still
true that at critical values of $B$, $j_x/E_y$ is an integral multiple of $e^2/2\pi\hbar$, to an accuracy of
better than one part in 10 million.\textsuperscript{4}

\subsection*{16-6 AN ADDITIONAL COMMENT ON GAUGE INVARIANCE}

The relations between the electric and magnetic fields and the vector and scalar potentials
appear to suggest that when the fields vanish, so do the potentials. This is not as simple a
statement as appears on the face of it. Let us consider a constant magnetic field pointing in
the $z$-direction

\[
\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{k}B
\]

confined to a cylindrical region $0 \leq \rho \leq a$. We may use Stokes' theorem

\[
\oint d\boldsymbol{\ell} \cdot \mathbf{A} = \int_{\text{surface}} d\mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{B} = \pi \rho^2 B
\]

to see that $\mathbf{A}$ in cylindrical coordinates only has a component in the $\phi$-direction, and that
for $\rho \leq a$,

\begin{equation}
A_\phi = \frac{1}{2} B\rho \tag{16-82}
\end{equation}

If we take our circular path about the field outside the radius $a$, we get

\[
2\pi \rho A_\phi = \pi a^2 B
\]

\noindent\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}
\textsuperscript{4}The precise \textit{quantization} actually follows from gauge invariance, as has been pointed out by R. Laughlin and
B. Halperin. A presentation of this argument may be found in C. Kittel, \textit{Introduction to Solid State Physics}, 6th
Ed., John Wiley, New York, 1986.


<!-- Page 347 -->
**258** Chapter 16 The Interaction of Charged Particles with the Electromagnetic Field

so that for $\rho \ge a$,

\begin{equation}
A_{\phi} = \frac{B \pi a^2}{2 \pi \rho} = \frac{\Phi}{2 \pi \rho}
\tag{16-83}
\end{equation}

where $\Phi$ is the uniform magnetic flux contained in the cylinder $\rho \le a$. We see that in the outer region the vector potential *does not vanish* even though the magnetic field does. In the region in which the magnetic filed vanishes the vector potential may be written as the gradient of a function $g(\phi)$,

\begin{equation}
A_{\phi} = \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{d g(\phi)}{d \phi}
\tag{16-84}
\end{equation}

When we set this equal to $\frac{\Phi}{2 \pi \rho}$, we get

\begin{equation}
g = \left( \frac{\Phi}{2 \pi} \right) \phi
\tag{16-85}
\end{equation}

where $\phi$ is the polar angle. In classical electromagnetic theory we can make a gauge transformation that sets $A_{\phi} = 0$—we just add to **A** the gradient of $-g$. In quantum mechanics this has some additional consequences. As noted in the material leading up to eq. (16-19), the Schrödinger wave function for an electron acquires an additional phase factor, which is

\begin{equation}
e^{i \Lambda} = e^{i e g / \hbar} = e^{i (e \Phi / 2 \pi \hbar) \phi}
\tag{16-86}
\end{equation}

The phase factor has no consequences for $|\psi(\mathbf{r}, t)|^2$ but there are circumstances in which it is measurable. This was first pointed out by Y. Aharanov and D. Bohm, and is discussed in some detail in Supplement 16-A [**www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz**].

\section*{The Aharanov--Bohm Effect}

Let us return to the description of an electron of charge $-\text{e}$ and mass $\text{m}_e$, in a time-independent magnetic field. The system is described by the Hamiltonian

\begin{equation}
\text{H} = \frac{1}{2\text{m}_e} ( -\text{i}\hbar \ \bm{\nabla} + \text{e}\text{A}(\text{r}) )^2 - \text{e}\phi(\text{r})
\tag{16A-1}
\end{equation}

and the time-independent Schr\"{o}dinger equation reads

\begin{equation}
\text{H}\psi(\text{r}) = \text{E}\psi(\text{r})
\tag{16A-2}
\end{equation}

In the absence of a vector potential the Hamiltonian reads

\begin{equation}
\text{H}_0 = \frac{1}{2\text{m}_e} ( -\text{i}\hbar \ \bm{\nabla} )^2 - \text{e}\phi(\text{r})
\tag{16A-3}
\end{equation}

and the Schr\"{o}dinger equation reads

\begin{equation}
\text{H}_0\psi_0(\text{r}) = \text{E}\psi_0(\text{r})
\tag{16A-4}
\end{equation}

We can show that formally the solution of (16A-4) and (16A-2) are related by a simple phase factor. Let us write a general expression

\begin{equation}
\psi(\text{r}) = \text{e}^{\text{ie}\Lambda(\text{r})} \psi_0(\text{r})
\tag{16A-5}
\end{equation}

It follows that

\begin{equation}
( -\text{i}\hbar \ \bm{\nabla} + \text{e}\text{A} ) \ \psi = \text{e}\hbar \ \bm{\nabla}\Lambda \text{e}^{\text{ie}\Lambda} \psi_0 + \text{e}^{\text{ie}\Lambda} ( -\text{i}\hbar \ \bm{\nabla} + \text{e}\text{A} ) \ \psi_0
\tag{16A-6}
\end{equation}

We now observe that if we choose $\Lambda$ such that

\begin{equation}
\text{e}\hbar \ \bm{\nabla}\Lambda + \text{e}\text{A} = 0
\tag{16A-7}
\end{equation}

then

\begin{equation}
( -\text{i}\hbar \ \bm{\nabla} + \text{e}\text{A} ) \ \psi = \text{e}^{\text{ie}\Lambda} ( -\text{i}\hbar \ \bm{\nabla} ) \ \psi_0
\tag{16A-8}
\end{equation}

When this is repeated, we obtain

\begin{equation}
\text{H}\psi = \text{e}^{\text{ie}\Lambda}\text{H}_0\psi_0 = \text{e}^{\text{ie}\Lambda} \text{E}\psi_0 = \text{E}\psi
\tag{16A-9}
\end{equation}

What we have just shown is that we can relate a solution of the Schrodinger equation with a vector potential $\text{A}(\text{r})$ to one of the Schrodinger equation without a vector potential by performing the gauge transformation shown in Eq. (16A-5). This depended, however, on our ability for find a gauge function $\Lambda(\text{r})$ that satisfies Eq. (16A-7). This can only happen if

\begin{equation*}
\text{B}(\text{r}) = \bm{\nabla} \times \text{A}(\text{r}) = -\hbar \bm{\nabla} \times \bm{\nabla}\Lambda(\text{r}) = 0
\end{equation*}

You may wonder why we bother to go through this, since if B $= 0$, we did not have to write out the Schrodinger equation in the form (16A-1). The point is that in quantum mechanics it is the potentials that matter, and there are circumstances where their presence creates physical

effects even when the magnetic field vanishes. We can write out the dependence on the vector potential by noting that Eq. (16A-7) can be solved by a line integral,

$$\Lambda(\mathbf{r}) = -\frac{1}{\hbar} \int_{\mathrm{P}}^\mathbf{r} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}' \cdot \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}')$$

which starts at some fixed point P and goes to $\mathbf{r}$. In terms of this (16A-5) takes the form

$$\psi(\mathbf{r}) = \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}(e/\hbar)\int_\mathrm{P}^\mathbf{r} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}' \cdot \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}')} \psi_0(\mathbf{r})$$ \hfill (16A-10)

Is the line integral in the phase is independent of the path taken between P and $\mathbf{r}$? Let us consider two paths as shown in Fig. 16A-1. The difference between the line integrals is

$$\int_2 \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{A} - \int_1 \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{A} = \oint_{\text{counterclockwise}} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{A}$$ \hfill (16A-11)

By Stokes' theorem we have

$$\oint \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{A} = \iint_{\text{encl. surface}} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{A} = \iint_S \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{B} = \Phi$$ \hfill (16A-12)

This shows that for all paths that do not enclose any magnetic flux, the integral in the phase factor is the same, so that the phase factor does not depend on the path taken. The important point is that there may be situations when there is a local magnetic field, and paths that go around the flux tube are not equivalent.

In 1959 Y. Aharanov and D. Bohm pointed out a previously overlooked$^1$ aspect of the quantum mechanics of a charged particle in the presence of electromagnetic fields—namely, that even in a field free region, in which $\mathbf{B} = 0$, the presence in a field elsewhere can have physical consequences because $\mathbf{A} \neq 0$.

Consider, for example, a two-slit diffraction experiment carried out with electrons, as shown in Fig. 16A-2. Suppose that there is a solenoid perpendicular to the plane in which the electrons move, located as in Fig. 16A-2(a) away from the slits. The interference pattern at the screen depends on the difference in phase between the wave functions for the

pattern emerges from the relative phases of $\psi_{1}$ and $\psi_{s2}$ in

\[
\psi = \psi_{1} + \psi_{2} = \text{R}_{1}e^{i\text{S}_{1}} + \text{R}_{2}e^{i\text{S}_{2}} = e^{i\text{S}_{1}}(\text{R}_{1} + e^{i(\text{S}_{2}-\text{S}_{1})} \text{R}_{2})

In the presence of a solenoid, (16A-13) is replaced by

\[
\begin{aligned}

&= e^{-\frac{ie}{\hbar} \int\limits_{1} \text{d}\ell' \cdot \text{A}(\text{r}')} e^{i\text{S}_{1}}(\text{R}_{1} + \text{R}_{2} e^{i(\text{S}_{2}-\text{S}_{1}) + ie\Phi/\hbar})
\end{aligned}
\tag{16A-14}
\]

If the solenoid is placed as in Fig. 16A-2(a), then no flux is enclosed by the paths
of the electrons and there is no change in the interference pattern. If the flux is placed
between the slits, as in Fig. 16A-2(b), then there is an additional contribution to the
phase difference between $\psi_{1}$ and $\psi_{2}$, so that the optical path difference is changed by a
constant that depends on the enclosed flux. This has the effect of shifting the peak inter
ference pattern from the previous center, by an amount that depends on the enclosed
flux. The first experimental confirmation of the effect is due to R. G. Chambers in
1960. The definitive experiments were done by A. Tonomura and collaborators in 1980.

The A-B paper generated a certain amount of controversy, because many people be
lieved that since only electric and magnetic fields were “physical” nothing could depend
on vector potentials. As was pointed out by M. Peshkin and others, the existence of the
A-B effect is intimately tied to the quantization of angular momentum, and its absence
would raise serious questions about quantum mechanics.

B inside the solenoid points in the positive z-direction. The vector potential in a conve

\[
\text{A} = -\frac{1}{2} \text{r} \times \text{B}
\]

magnetic flux is trapped inside the ring. The wave function of the superconductor is single-valued, and this implies that the phase factor that appears in (16A-10), when taken around a path that is inside the superconducting ring and encircles the flux region, must be unity. This implies that

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}e\Phi/\hbar} = 1 \tag{16A-22}
\end{equation}

Thus the flux inside the ring is quantized, with

\begin{equation}
\frac{\mathrm{e}\Phi}{\hbar} = 2\pi \mathrm{n} \tag{16A-23}
\end{equation}

This is almost right. The only modification that must be made is that the superconductor consists of a condensate of “correlated electron pairs,” so that the appropriate charge that appears in eq. (16A-23) is $2\mathrm{e}$, and the flux quantization reads

\begin{equation}
\Phi = \frac{2\pi\hbar}{2\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{n} \tag{16A-24}
\end{equation}

where $\mathrm{n}$ is an integer. The effect has been measured and the prediction (16A-24) was confirmed.

\vspace{1cm}

\begin{center}
    \huge A Little About Bessel Functions
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5cm}

The solution of the equation

\[
\frac{d^2u}{dz^2} + \frac{1}{z} \frac{du}{dz} + \left(1 - \frac{n^2}{z^2}\right) u = 0
\]

with n integral, are known as Bessel functions, for the regular solutions

\[
J_n(z) = \left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^n \sum_{l=0}^\infty \frac{(iz/2)^{2l}}{l!(n + l)!}
\]

and Neumann functions for the irregular solutions

\[
N_n(z) = \frac{2}{\pi} J_n(z) \log \frac{\gamma z}{2} - \frac{1}{\pi} \left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^n \sum_{l=0}^\infty \frac{(iz/2)^{2l}}{l!(n + l)!} a_{nl} - \frac{1}{\pi} \left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{-n} \sum_{l=0}^{n-1} \frac{(n - l - 1)!}{l!} \left(\frac{z}{2}\right)^{2l}
\]

\[
(\log \gamma = 0.5772 \dots) \quad \quad a_{nl} = \left( \sum_{m=1}^l \frac{1}{m} + \sum_{m=1}^{l+n} \frac{1}{m} \right)
\]

They have the asymptotic behavior

\[
J_n(z) \sim \left(\frac{2}{\pi z}\right)^{1/2} \cos\left(z - \frac{n\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) \left[1 + 0\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)\right]
\]

\[
N_n(z) \sim \left(\frac{2}{\pi z}\right)^{1/2} \sin\left(z - \frac{n\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) \left[1 + 0\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)\right]
\]

A detailed discussion of their properties may be found in any book on the special functions of mathematical physics.

\section*{Chapter 17}
\vspace{1cm}
\begin{center}
\Huge \textbf{Radiative Decays}
\end{center}
\vspace{1cm}
\subsection*{17-1 TRANSITION RATE}

In Chapter 16 we discussed the Hamiltonian that describes the interaction of charged particles with an electromagnetic field, and studied in some detail the interaction with a constant, uniform magnetic field. In this chapter we discuss radiative transitions, with emphasis on what are usually called \textit{electric dipole} transitions. Our starting point is eq. (16-17), with the choice of Coulomb gauge specified by

\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0 \tag{17-1}
\end{equation}

This implies that in the operator

\begin{equation*}
\frac{1}{2m_e}(\mathbf{p} + e\mathbf{A})^2 = \frac{1}{2m_e}(-i\hbar\boldsymbol{\nabla} + e\mathbf{A})^2
\end{equation*}

We may write the cross term in the expansion of this as

\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{2m_e}(-2ie\hbar\mathbf{A}\cdot\boldsymbol{\nabla}) = \frac{e}{m_e}\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{p} \tag{17-2}
\end{equation}

We shall be interested in the emission and absorption of \textit{single photons}, and we will see later that this implies that we can neglect the term $e^2 A^2 / 2m_e$ in the Hamiltonian.

We will use time-independent perturbation theory. Writing

\begin{equation}
H = H_0 + \lambda V(t) \tag{17-3}
\end{equation}

we will take for $H_0$ the Hamiltonian for the atom (e.g., the hydrogen atom), and take

\begin{equation}
\lambda V(t) = \frac{e}{m_e} \mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{p} \tag{17-4}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \mathbf{A}_0(\mathbf{r}) e^{-i\omega t} + \mathbf{A}_0^{\dagger}(\mathbf{r}) e^{i\omega t} \tag{17-5}
\end{equation}

The perturbation is harmonic in time, and we can take over a great deal of material from Chapter 15. In particular, the first term will correspond to an increase in the energy of the system described by $H_0$---that is, the \textit{absorption} of a photon---while the second term will represent the \textit{emission} of a photon.

Away from the source of the electromagnetic field, we find from (16-12) that

\begin{equation}
-\nabla^2 \mathbf{A}_0(\mathbf{r}) - \frac{\omega^2}{c^2} \mathbf{A}_0(\mathbf{r}) = 0 \tag{17-6}
\end{equation}

whose solution is

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{A}_0(\mathbf{r}) = \mathbf{A}_0 e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} \tag{17-7}
\end{equation}

\vspace{1cm}
\noindent \textbf{260}



<!-- Page 356 -->
17-1 Transition Rate 261

with $\mathbf{k}^2 = \omega^2/c^2$. We chose the sign of the exponent so that the space-time dependence is $e^{\pm i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-\omega t)}$. This may be used without loss of generality, since the direction of $\mathbf{k}$ is not specified. With this solution, the electric and magnetic fields are

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{E} &= -\frac{\partial \mathbf{A}}{\partial t} = i\omega\mathbf{A}_0e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-\omega t)} - i\omega\mathbf{A}_0^+e^{-i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-\omega t)}\\
\mathbf{B} &= \nabla \times \mathbf{A} = -i\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0e^{i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-\omega t)} + i\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0^+e^{-i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}-\omega t)}
\end{aligned}
\tag{17-8}
\end{equation}

Note that the equation $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0$ implies that

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{A}_0 = \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{A}_0^+ = 0 \tag{17-9}
\end{equation}

The energy density of the electromagnetic field is

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
U &= \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\mathbf{E}^2 + \frac{1}{2\mu_0}\mathbf{B}^2\\
&= \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}[\omega^2(\mathbf{A}_0 \cdot \mathbf{A}_0^+ + \mathbf{A}_0^+ \cdot \mathbf{A}_0)]\\
&\quad+ \frac{1}{2\mu_0}[(\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0) \cdot (\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0^+) + (\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0^+) \cdot (\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0)]\\
&\quad+ \text{oscillating terms}
\end{aligned}
\tag{17-10}
\end{equation}

If we average over time, the oscillating terms drop out. If we use (17-9), the vector identity

\[
(\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0) \cdot (\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0^+) + (\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0^+) \cdot (\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{A}_0) = k^2(\mathbf{A}_0 \cdot \mathbf{A}_0^+ + \mathbf{A}_0^+ \cdot \mathbf{A}_0)
\]

and

\[
\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}k^2 = c^2k^2 = \omega^2
\]

we end up with

\begin{equation}
U = \varepsilon_0\omega^2(\mathbf{A}_0 \cdot \mathbf{A}_0^+ + \mathbf{A}_0^+ \cdot \mathbf{A}_0) \tag{17-11}
\end{equation}

We may treat the electromagnetic field *semiclassically*. What this means is that we do *not* treat $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A}^+$ as operators, but we nevertheless ascribe to the electromagnetic field energy the property that it is carried by photons of energy $\hbar\omega$. In this case, (17-11) may be rewritten as

\begin{equation}
U = 2\varepsilon_0\omega^2|\mathbf{A}_0|^2 \tag{17-12}
\end{equation}

If the radiation is enclosed in a volume $V$, then the total energy of the electromagnetic field is

\begin{equation}
\int_V d^3r U = 2\varepsilon_0\omega^2|\mathbf{A}_0|^2 V \tag{17-13}
\end{equation}

Let us now assume that this energy is carried by $N$ photons, each of energy $\hbar\omega$. We may then set the right-hand side of (17-13) equal to $N\hbar\omega$. This then gives us the magnitude of $\mathbf{A}_0$.

The direction of $\mathbf{A}_0$ is specified by the polarization of the electric field. We denote it by the unit vector $\mathbf{\epsilon}$. It must satisfy

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{\epsilon} &= 1\\
\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{\epsilon} &= 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{17-14}
\end{equation}

Actually there are *two* directions of polarization that are perpendicular to $\mathbf{k}$. In a semiclassical treatment, the magnitude of the vector potential comes from expressing (17-13) in


<!-- Page 357 -->
262 Chapter 17 Radiative Decays

terms of photons. The net result is that for $N$ photons of angular frequency $\omega$ the vector
potential has the form


\begin{equation}
\mathbf{A}_{0} = \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \sqrt{\frac{N \hbar}{2 \varepsilon_{0} \omega V}} \tag{17-15}
\end{equation}


This needs modification because there are two polarization states, which we label by $\lambda$,
with $\lambda = 1$, 2. If we put in the suppressed notation, which indicates that the number of
photons also depends on $\mathbf{k}$ and on $\lambda$, we write


\begin{equation}
\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 \varepsilon_{0} \omega V}} \sum_{\lambda=1}^{2} \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} [A_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k})e^{+i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r} - \omega t)} + A_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathbf{k})e^{-i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r} - \omega t)}] \tag{17-16}
\end{equation}


In the semiclassical approximation we have, as indicated above,


\begin{equation}
A_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k}) = A_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathbf{k}) = \sqrt{N_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k})} \tag{17-17}
\end{equation}


If we treat photons quantum mechanically, as outlined in Supplement 18-A [www.wiley.com/
college/gasiorowicz], the $A$ and $A^{+}$ are operators, like the harmonic oscillator lowering and
raising operators. These act on $N$ photon states as follows:


\begin{align}
A_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k})\,|N_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k})\rangle &= \sqrt{N_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k})} \,|N_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k}) - 1\rangle \\
A_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathbf{k})\,|N_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k})\rangle &= \sqrt{N_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k}) + 1} \,|N_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k}) + 1\rangle \tag{17-18}
\end{align}


We see that for $N_{\lambda}(\mathbf{k}) \gg 1$ the semiclassical approximation will give the same result as
the proper quantum treatment of photons.

Let us now consider a special situation. We start from an excited state of a hydrogen-
like atom, $|\phi_{n}\rangle$, with no photons present. There is a transition that leads to a lower energy
state of the atom $|\phi_{m}\rangle$, with the emission of a single photon. This corresponds to taking the
photon states in (17-18) with $N_{\lambda} = 0$. The vector potential operative here is now


\begin{equation}
\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2 \varepsilon_{0} \omega V}} \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} e^{-i(\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r} - \omega t)} \tag{17-19}
\end{equation}


The time dependence goes into the appearance of the energy-conservation delta function
[see (15-14) on p. 240]. We are therefore left with the need to evaluate the absolute square
of the matrix element of the rhs in (17-4), and this must be multiplied by $2\pi/\hbar$ to get the
transition rate. We therefore need to calculate


\begin{equation}
\frac{2\pi}{\hbar} \left| \left\langle \phi_{m} \left| \frac{e}{m_{e}} \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2\varepsilon_{0}\omega V}} e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{\text{op}} \right| \phi_{n} \right\rangle \right|^{2} = \frac{\pi e^{2}}{m_{e}^{2} \varepsilon_{0} \omega V} |\langle \phi_{m} | e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{\text{op}} | \phi_{n} \rangle|^{2} \tag{17-20}
\end{equation}


**17-2 CALCULATION OF THE MATRIX ELEMENT**

Our task is to calculate $\langle \phi_{m} | e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} \, \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{\text{op}} | \phi_{n} \rangle$. We begin by estimating the magnitude of
the matrix element. For a typical atomic state,


\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p} \approx |p| \approx Zm_{e}c\alpha \tag{17-21}
\end{equation}


This is not enough, since there is an oscillating factor $e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$ appears, and that can change
the estimate considerably. With


\begin{equation*}
r \approx \frac{\hbar}{m_{e}Z\alpha c}
\end{equation*}



<!-- Page 358 -->
17-3 Angular Integration and Selection Rules \textbf{263}

and
\[
|k| = \frac{\hbar\omega}{\hbar c} \approx \frac{m_e(Z\alpha c)^2}{2\hbar c} \approx \frac{m_ec(Z\alpha)^2}{2\hbar}
\]
we get $kr = Z\alpha/2$. This means that for $Z\alpha \ll 1$ we can set the exponential factor equal to
unity. It simplifies matters that in the expansion
\[
e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-i)^n}{n!} (\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r})^n
\]
the successive terms are estimated to decrease as $Z\alpha$.

The leading term may be rewritten as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\langle \phi_m | \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{op} | \phi_n \right\rangle &= \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \left\langle \phi_m \Bigg| m_e \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt} \Bigg| \phi_n \right\rangle \\
&= m_e \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \left\langle \phi_m \Bigg| \frac{i}{\hbar} [H_0, \mathbf{r}] \Bigg| \phi_n \right\rangle \\
&= i m_e \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \left\{ \frac{E_m^{(0)} - E_n^{(0)}}{\hbar} \langle \phi_m | \mathbf{r} | \phi_n \rangle \right\} \\
&= -im_e\omega \, \langle \phi_m | \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{r} | \phi_n \rangle
\end{aligned}
\]
\hfill (17-22)

In the final analysis, we need to calculate the matrix elements of the operator $\mathbf{r}$. This
arises from the approximation in which we replaced the oscillating factor by unity. The
approximation is called the \textit{electric dipole approximation}. A justification for this name
comes from the fact that in this approximation, with (17-8),
\[
\frac{e}{m_e} \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) \cdot \mathbf{p} = e \mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t) \cdot \mathbf{r}
\]
and this, in fact, is the potential energy of a dipole, with moment $\mathbf{d} = -e\mathbf{r}$, in an electric
field $\mathbf{E}$.

For hydrogenlike atoms, the matrix element in (17-22) involves an initial state $|\phi_n\rangle$,
which we shall characterize by the quantum numbers ($n_i$, $l_i$, $m_i$) and a final state $|\phi_m\rangle$ with
quantum numbers ($n_f$, $l_f$, $m_f$). We will therefore want to calculate
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle \phi_m | \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{r} | \phi_n \rangle &= \int\limits_0^{\infty} r^2 \, dr \int d\Omega R_{n_f l_f}^{*}(r) Y_{l_f m_f}^{*}(\theta, \varphi) \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{r} R_{n_i l_i}(r) Y_{l_i m_i}(\theta, \varphi) \\
&= \int\limits_0^{\infty} r^3 \, dr \, R_{n_f l_f}^{*}(r) R_{n_i l_i}(r) \, \times \! \int d\Omega Y_{l_f m_f}^{*}(\theta, \varphi) \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{\hat{r}} Y_{l_i m_i}(\theta, \varphi)
\end{aligned}
\]
\hfill (17-23)

The radial integral will be discussed for a special case in a later section. At this point we
concentrate on the angular integral.

\textbf{17-3 ANGULAR INTEGRATION AND SELECTION RULES}

The angular integral involves the quantity
\[
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{\hat{r}} = \varepsilon_x^{(\lambda)} \sin\theta \cos\varphi + \varepsilon_y^{(\lambda)} \sin\theta \sin\varphi + \varepsilon_z^{(\lambda)} \cos\theta
\]
\hfill (17-24)



<!-- Page 359 -->
**264** Chapter 17 Radiative Decays

In what follows we leave off the $\lambda$ superscript for simplicity. It will reappear at the end. A
look at the table of spherical harmonics shows that

$$\cos \theta = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{3}}Y_{10}(\theta, \varphi)$$

$$\sin \theta e^{\pm i\varphi} = \mp \sqrt{\frac{8\pi}{3}}Y_{1,\pm1}(\theta, \varphi) \eqno(17-25)$$

so that

$$\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\left(\epsilon_z Y_{10} + \frac{-\epsilon_x + i\epsilon_y}{\sqrt{2}}Y_{1,1} + \frac{\epsilon_x + i\epsilon_y}{\sqrt{2}}Y_{1,-1}\right) \eqno(17-26)$$

The angular integration in (17-23) therefore involves

$$\int d\Omega Y_{l_f m_f}^*(\theta, \varphi) Y_{1,m}(\theta, \varphi) Y_{l_i m_i}(\theta, \varphi) \eqno(17-27)$$

Let us first consider the azimuthal integration. It involves

$$\int_0^{2\pi} d\varphi e^{-im_f \varphi} e^{im \varphi} e^{im_i \varphi} = 2\pi \delta_{m=m_f - m_i} \eqno(17-28)$$

The Kronecker delta gives us the first *selection rule*. It requires that in dipole transitions
we must have

$$m_f - m_i = m = 1, 0, -1 \eqno(17-29)$$

We saw this selection rule earlier when we discussed the transitions in the Zeeman effect.
Actually we can say more: If the photon momentum direction $\mathbf{k}$ is chosen to define the
$z$-axis, then the *transversality condition* in (17-14) implies that the $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ must lie in the $x$-$y$
plane. This means that $m$ above can only be equal to $\pm 1$, and our selection rule states that

$$m_f - m_i = \pm 1 \eqno(17-30)$$

As a special case, consider the final state to be the ground state, with $l_f = m_f = 0$. In that
case, $m = m_i$. For example if $m_i = 1$, then $m = -1$, and hence the polarization for the ra-
diation is $(\epsilon_x + i\epsilon_y)/\sqrt{2}$. The implication is that if the atom in the initial state is polarized
along the $z$-axis with $m_i = 1$, then in a decay to a state with zero angular momentum, *an-
gular momentum conservation*, specifically that of the $z$-component, requires that the out-
going photon carry off the initial angular momentum. Thus the photon must have its spin
aligned along the positive $z$-axis, its direction of motion. The component of spin of a par-
ticle along its direction of motion is called the *helicity*. In the special case under discus-
sion, the helicity of the photon must be positive. This is equivalent to the statement that
the photon has a left-circular polarization, which is what the term $(\epsilon_x + i\epsilon_y)/\sqrt{2}$ implies.

The $\theta$ integration gives rise to another selection rule. Again, in the special case that
$l_f = 0$, the final wave (angular) function $Y_{00} = 1/\sqrt{4\pi}$ leads to the integral

$$\int d\Omega \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} Y_{1,m}(\theta, \varphi) Y_{l_i m_i}(\theta, \varphi) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} \delta_{1,l_i}\delta_{m,-m_i} \eqno(17-31)$$

which implies that the initial state *must have* $l_i = 1$. In hydrogen, the dominant transition
to the ground state will be $np \to 1s$.

More generally, when neither the initial or final $l$ vanish, we still get a selection rule.
We do not have the machinery at our disposal to work this out, but the result is simply a


<!-- Page 360 -->
17-3 Angular Integration and Selection Rules 265

consequence of the rules of addition of angular momentum and of angular momentum
conservation. The initial angular momentum is $l_i$. In the final state the angular momen
tum is the sum of that of the atom $l_f$ and, *in the dipole approximation*, the angular mo
mentum of the photon reflected in the wave function $Y_{1,m}$. Our rules of addition of
angular momentum, stated in Chapter 10, tell us that the total angular momentum in the
final state is one of $l_f + 1$, $l_f$, $|l_f - 1|$. This must be equal to $l_i$. We can thus rewrite the *se
lection rule for the orbital angular momentum* as

$$l_f = l_i + 1, l_i, |l_i - 1|$$

This is the general form of the *electric dipole selection rule*

$$\Delta l = \pm 1, 0 \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (17\text{-}32)$$

Note that if the initial and final states both have $l = 0$, then the integral has the form
$\int d\Omega Y_{1m}(\theta, \varphi) = 0$. Thus, *there are no zero-zero transitions*. There is a further constraint
that comes from parity conservation. Since $\mathbf{r}$ is *odd* under reflections ($x \to -x$ and so on),
there is an additional selection rule that states

*The atomic state must change parity*$\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (17\text{-}33)$

Since the parity of a spherical harmonic $Y_{lm}$ is $(-1)^l$, this implies that the $l$-value of the
state must actually change. For example, $3p \to 2p$ transitions, allowed by the rule (17-32),
as stated, cannot actually take place. Thus (17-32) should really be replaced by

$$\Delta l = \pm 1\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (17\text{-}32')$$

To the extent that the only coupling of the electromagnetic field to the atoms is
through the perturbation

$$\lambda V(t) = \frac{e}{m_e} \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) \cdot \mathbf{p}$$

there is no spin dependence in it, and thus if the initial state is an “up” state, then the final
state will also be an “up” state. In other words, the spin cannot flip over in a transition.
This is equivalent to a selection rule

$$\Delta S = 0 \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (17\text{-}34)$$

as mentioned earlier in connection with the spectrum of helium.

The selection rules stated above are not absolute. The conservation laws of angular
momentum and parity (for electromagnetic processes) are absolute, but (17-32') is only
approximately true. Transitions between states that involve changes of $l$ larger than one
cannot take place through the electric dipole mechanism, but they can occur as long as
there is a nonvanishing matrix element.

$$\langle \phi_f | e^{-i\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}} \mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{op} | \phi_i \rangle$$

For $\Delta l = 2$, the first power of $\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}$ in the expansion of the exponential will give a nonvan
ishing contribution. We may write

$$\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p} = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} + \mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{k}) + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{k})$$
$$= \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} + \mathbf{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{k}) + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{\epsilon}) \cdot (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p}) \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad (17\text{-}35)$$

The first of these terms is called an *electric quadrupole* term. The second is clearly related
to an **L $\cdot$ B term**, and it is called a *magnetic dipole* term. For these transitions, whose ma
trix elements we estimated in the material following (17-21) to be $Z\alpha$ times smaller than


<!-- Page 361 -->
**266** Chapter 17 Radiative Decays

the electric dipole terms, we will have $\Delta l = 2$ and $\Delta l = 0$, respectively. Since the opera-
tors in (17-35) are even, there will be *no parity change* in the atomic states taking part in
these transitions. These matrix elements are smaller than the leading ones, but when elec-
tric dipole transitions are forbidden, then these are the ones that matter. For example, tran-
sitions $3d \to 1s$, forbidden for dipole transitions, can go via the electric quadrupole
mechanism. Actually, it turns out that a two-step dipole transition $3d \to 2p$, $2p \to 1s$ is
much more probable than a direct quadrupole transition, even though in the two-step
process two photons are emitted in succession.

The spin selection rule $\Delta S = 0$ is also not sacred. In addition to the coupling in (17-4)
there is the coupling discussed in connection with the anomalous Zeeman effect,

\begin{equation}
\lambda \mathcal{V}(t) = \frac{e g}{2 m_e} \mathbf{S} \cdot \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}, t)
\end{equation}

The matrix elements for the $\Delta S \neq 0$ transition-inducing process can be estimated. We
compare it with the electric dipole matrix element

\begin{equation}
\frac{\displaystyle\frac{e g}{2 m_e} \hbar \, |\mathbf{k} \times \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}|}{\displaystyle\frac{2e}{m_e} |\mathbf{p} \cdot \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}|} \approx \frac{g}{4} \frac{|\mathbf{k}|}{|\mathbf{p}|} \approx \frac{\hbar \omega}{|\mathbf{p}| c} \approx \frac{m_e c^2 (Z\alpha)^2}{m_e c^2 (Z\alpha)} = Z\alpha
\end{equation}

We see that it is suppressed, just like the magnetic dipole matrix element, which it
strongly resembles.

As an example where the coupling (17-36) plays an important role, we consider a
process important in low-energy nuclear physics, the *photodisintegration of the deuteron*

\[
\gamma + d \to p + n
\]

The deuteron is a weakly bound state of a proton and a neutron. The lowest bound state in
any sensible potential will be a state of orbital angular momentum zero. Since the neutron
and the proton both have spin $1/2$, the deuteron can be a singlet state or a triplet state. Experi-
ments show that the total angular momentum is $J = 1$, so that deuteron is a $^3S_1$ state. An elec-
tric dipole transition must lead to a final $^3P$ state, since $\Delta l = 1$ and the spin does not change.
In general, particles will be likely to be in a relative angular momentum $L$ state only if

\begin{equation}
|\mathbf{p}| \, a \geq \hbar L
\end{equation}

where $|\mathbf{p}|$ is the magnitude of the relative momentum and $a$ represents the range of the
forces that involve the two particles. For the energies of the magnitude of the deuteron
binding energy this strongly supports the $L = 0$ assignment. Let us consider the interac-
tion analogous to (17-36):

\begin{equation}
-\frac{e}{2M} (g_p \mathbf{S}_p + g_n \mathbf{S}_n) \cdot \mathbf{B}
\end{equation}

where $M$ is the nucleon mass ($M_p \cong M_n$) and $g_p$ and $g_n$ are the gyromagnetic ratios for the
proton and neutron, respectively. This interaction can lead to a transition between the $^3S_1$
bound state and the unbound $^1S_0$ $n$-$p$ state. The interaction (17-39) may be rewritten in the
form

\begin{equation}
-\frac{e}{2M} \left[ \frac{g_p + g_n}{2} (\mathbf{S}_p + \mathbf{S}_n) + \frac{g_p - g_n}{2} (\mathbf{S}_p - \mathbf{S}_n) \right] \cdot \mathbf{B}
\end{equation}

The initial spin state is a total $S = 1$ state, and we know from our discussion of the addi-
tion of two spins in Chapter 10 that this state is symmetric in the $n$ and $p$ spinors. The final
state is an $S = 0$ state, antisymmetric in the $n$ and $p$ spinors. Thus the first term, consisting


<!-- Page 362 -->
17-4 The $2p \rightarrow 1s$ Transition $\quad \mathbf{267}$

of the sum of the spin operators, is symmetric, and it cannot therefore act on a symmetric
state and lead to an antisymmetric one. Thus ony the second term contributes. The coeffi-
cient in front is actually quite large since $g_p = 5.56$ and $g_n = -3.81$.

There is one selection rule that is sacred, and that is the one forbidding zero-zero
transitions (referring to $\textit{total}$ angular momentum $j = 0$) in one-photon processes. A gen-
eral way of arguing the absoluteness of this selection rule is the following: The matrix ele-
ment, a scalar quantity, must involve the photon polarization linearly, and must therefore
be of the form $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \boldsymbol{\cdot} \mathbf{V}$, where $\mathbf{V}$ is some vector that enters into the problem. If the initial and
final states are $j = 0$ states—that is, have no directionality associated with them—then the
only vector is $\mathbf{k}$, the photon momentum. However, $\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \boldsymbol{\cdot} \mathbf{k} = 0$, so that there is no way of
constructing a matrix element. It must therefore not exist.$^{1}$

### 17-4 THE $2p \rightarrow 1s$ TRANSITION

Let us now specialize to the transition $2p \rightarrow 1s$ in (17-23). We need to evaluate the radial
integral

\begin{align*}
\int\limits_0^{\infty} dr\; r^3\, R_{10}^* (r)\, R_{21}(r)
& = \int\limits_0^{\infty} dr\; r^3 \left[\, 2\left(\frac{Z}{a_0}\right)^{\!3/2} e^{-Zr/a_0}\right]
\!\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{24}} \left(\frac{Z}{a_0}\right)^{\!5/2} r\; e^{-Zr/2a_0}\right] \\
& = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \left(\frac{Z}{a_0}\right)^{\!4} \int\limits_0^{\infty} dr\; r^4\, e^{-3Zr/2a_0}
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \left(\frac{Z}{a_0}\right)^{\!4} \left(\frac{2a_0}{3Z}\right)^{\!5} \int\limits_0^{\infty} dx\; x^4\, e^{-x} \tag{17-41}\\
& = \frac{24}{\sqrt{6}} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{\!5} Z^{-1} a_0
\end{align*}

The angular integral is

\begin{align*}
d\Omega Y_{0,0}^* \, \boldsymbol{\epsilon \cdot \hat{r}} \, Y_{1,m}
& = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}} \int d\Omega \; \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{3}}
\left( \varepsilon_z Y_{1,0} + \frac{-\varepsilon_x + i\varepsilon_y}{\sqrt{2}} Y_{1,1} + \frac{\varepsilon_x + i\varepsilon_y}{\sqrt{2}} Y_{1,-1} \right) Y_{1,m} \\
& = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \left( \varepsilon_z \, \delta_{m,0} + \frac{-\varepsilon_x + i\varepsilon_y}{\sqrt{2}} \, \delta_{m,-1} + \frac{\varepsilon_x + i\varepsilon_y}{\sqrt{2}} \, \delta_{m,1} \right)
\tag{17-42}
\end{align*}

The absolute square of the product of (17-41) and (17-42) is

\[
96 \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{\!10} \left(\frac{a_0}{Z}\right)^{\!2}
\times \frac{1}{3} \left[ \delta_{m0}\varepsilon_z^2 + \frac{1}{2}(\delta_{m,1} + \delta_{m,-1})(\varepsilon_x^2 + \varepsilon_y^2) \right]
\tag{17-43}
\]

To get the rate, we must multiply by $2\pi/\hbar$ and the phase space factor. Combining equa-
tion (17-20), (17-43), and (15-29) we get

\[
d\Gamma = \frac{\pi e^2}{m_e^2 \varepsilon_0 \omega V} m_e^2 \omega^2
\left[\, 96\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{\!10} \!\left(\frac{a_0}{Z}\right)^{\!2} \right]
\frac{1}{3} \left[\, \delta_{m0}\varepsilon_z^2 + \frac{1}{2}\, (\delta_{m,1} + \delta_{m,-1}) (\varepsilon_x^2 + \varepsilon_y^2) \right]
\frac{V}{(2\pi)^3} \frac{\omega^2}{\hbar c^3} \, d\Omega_{\mathbf{k}}
\]

The fact that the factors $V$ cancel is always a good check on the calculation. The result is

\[
d\Gamma = \frac{\alpha}{2\pi} \, \frac{\omega^3}{c^2} \left(\frac{a_0}{Z}\right)^{\!2}
\frac{2^{15}}{3^{10}}
\left[\, \delta_{m0}\varepsilon_z^2 + \frac{1}{2}\, (\delta_{m,1} + \delta_{m,-1}) (\varepsilon_x^2 + \varepsilon_y^2) \right]
d\Omega_{\mathbf{k}}
\tag{17-44}
\]

---

$^1$The relation $\boldsymbol{\epsilon \cdot \mathbf{k}} = 0$ is independent of the choice of gauge, and is a statement about the transversality of the
electromagnetic field.


<!-- Page 363 -->
**268** Chapter 17 Radiative Decays

For the $2p \rightarrow 1s$ transition, the angular frequency of the photon emitted is

$$
\omega = \frac{1}{\hbar} \left[ \frac{1}{2}m_ec^2(Z\alpha)^2 \left( 1 - \frac{1}{4} \right) \right] = \frac{3}{8}\frac{m_ec^2}{\hbar}(Z\alpha)^2 \quad (17\text{-}45)
$$

The differential rate needs to be integrated over the photon directions. This is not trivial, since the polarization vector $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ is constrained to be perpendicular to the photon direction $\mathbf{\hat{k}}$. The result is simplified if the initial $l = 1$ state of the excited atom is _unaligned_—that is, if all three $m$ states ($m = 1$, $0$, $-1$) are equally populated. In that case the rate, _averaged_ over the three initial $m$ states, is

$$
d\Gamma = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{m=-1}^1 d\Gamma_m \quad (17\text{-}46)
$$

Now

$$
\sum_{m=-1}^1 \left[ \delta_{m0}\epsilon_z^2 + \frac{1}{2}(\delta_{m1} + \delta_{m,-1})(\epsilon_x^2 + \epsilon_y^2) \right] = \epsilon_z^2 + \epsilon_x^2 + \epsilon_y^2 = 1 \quad (17\text{-}47)
$$

so that for this case, the integrand becomes independent of the photon direction. The result should also be multiplied by 2. As noted before, there are two polarization states for the photon, denoted by the (suppressed) label $\lambda$. Since we are detecting both polarization states, we sum over $\lambda$. In the case under consideration nothing depends on $\lambda$, so that we merely double our result. More generally we work with

$$
\sum_{\lambda=1}^2 |\langle \phi_m | e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{r} | \phi_n \rangle|^2 \quad (17\text{-}48)
$$

If we insert the factor of 2, integrate over $d\Omega$ (which here gives $4\pi$), and use (17-45), we end up with

$$
\Gamma(2p \rightarrow 1s) = \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^8 \alpha^5 \frac{m_ec^2}{\hbar} Z^4 = 0.62 \times 10^9 Z^4 \text{s}^{-1} \quad (17\text{-}49)
$$

This result differs by a factor of about 25 from our initial rough estimate, which shows that detailed calculations are necessary for obtaining the numerical coefficients. Nevertheless, dimensional considerations and a proper counting of powers of $\alpha$ do give us an order of magnitude guidance to the size of physical quantities in atomic physics.
It is worthwhile to notice that we can obtain the intensity of the radiation by multiplying the rate by the photon energy. We obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dI(\omega)}{d\Omega_k} &= \hbar\omega \frac{\pi e^2}{m_e^2\epsilon_0\omega V} m_e^2\omega^2 \sum_{\lambda=1}^2 |\langle \boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{r} \rangle|^2 \frac{V}{(2\pi)^3} \frac{\omega^2}{c^3} \\
&= \frac{1}{24} \frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{\omega^4}{c^3} \sum_{\lambda=1}^2 |\langle \boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{(\lambda)} \cdot \mathbf{r} \rangle|^2 \quad (17\text{-}50)
\end{aligned}
$$

This, however, is just the _classical_ formula for the intensity of light emitted by an oscillating dipole, of dipole moment

$$
\mathbf{d} = e \langle \phi_m | \mathbf{r} | \phi_n \rangle e^{-i\omega t} \quad (17\text{-}51)
$$

This is yet another illustration of the correspondence principle. In this calculation we paid no attention to spin; this is relegated to Supplement 17-A **[www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz]**.

The reason for summing over all the initial states is that when the atom is excited, all the p-levels are equally occupied, since their energy difference is so tiny compared to the $\mathrm{2p}-\mathrm{1s}$ energy difference. We also sum over all the final states if we perform an experiment that does not discriminate between them, as is the case for a spectroscopic measurement. In our calculation of the $\mathrm{2p} \rightarrow \mathrm{1s}$ transition rate, we averaged over the initial m-states. There we were concerned with the problem of asking: “If we have $\mathrm{N}$ atoms in the $\mathrm{2p}$ states, how many will decay per second?” The averaging came about because of the fact that under most circumstances, when $\mathrm{N}$ atoms are excited, about $\mathrm{N}/3$ go into each one of the $\mathrm{m}=1,0,-1$ states. Here, the fact that there are more levels in the $\mathrm{P}_{3/2}$ state than there are in the $\mathrm{P}_{1/2}$ state is relevant. There will be altogether six levels, (four with $\mathrm{j}=3/2$ and two with $\mathrm{j}=1/2$), and there will be on the average $\mathrm{N}/6$ atoms in each of the states. The fact that there are more atoms in the $\mathrm{j}=3/2$ subset of levels just means that more atoms decay, and that therefore the intensity will be larger.

\chapter{18}
\title{Selected Topics on Radiation}

In our discussion of radiative transitions, which involved the emission or absorption of a single photon, it was possible to treat the electromagnetic field semiclassically. We were able to treat the vector potential $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)$ as an external field, though its magnitude was adjusted so that the total energy associated with the electromagnetic field corresponded to that carried by a single photon, as seen in Eq. (17-16). In this chapter we will be dealing with \textit{lasers}, and this means that we will be dealing with multiple-photon states. To do this properly we must treat the electromagnetic field quantum mechanically. A simplified version of this is outlined in Supplement 18-A. The result is that we treat the electric field as an \textit{operator} in the form

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{V}} \sum_{\mathbf{k}, \lambda} \sqrt{\frac{\hbar \omega}{2 \varepsilon_0}} \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_\lambda(\mathbf{k}) [ -i A_\lambda(\mathbf{k}) e^{-i(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \omega t)} + i A_\lambda^{+}(\mathbf{k}) e^{-i(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \omega t)} ] \tag{18-1}
\end{equation}

Here $A_\lambda(\mathbf{k})$ and $A_\lambda^{+}(\mathbf{k})$ are annihilation and creation operators for a photon with wave number $\mathbf{k}$ and polarization $\lambda$. They act exactly as the energy lowering and raising operators for the simple harmonic oscillator, as discussed in Chapter 6. In particular, the electric field operator acting on a state containing $N$ identical photons (say, all with the attributes $(\mathbf{k}, \lambda)$) will be enhanced compared with the one-photon case by a factor $\sqrt{N(\mathbf{k}, \lambda) + 1}$, and the square of the matrix element will contain a factor $N(\mathbf{k}, \lambda) + 1$. This means that when a system emits a photon of a certain kind, and $N$ photons of that kind are present, then the emission rate is proportional to $N + 1$. The part involving the factor 1 in this is described as \textit{spontaneous emission}, while the factor proportional to $N$ is described as \textit{induced emission}. We saw this explicitly in Supplement 1-A \textbf{[www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz]}. Induced emission plays the central role in the operation of the \textit{laser}.

\section*{18-1 LASERS}

Induced emission finds its most dramatic technological application in the production of coherent, monochromatic, highly directional electromagnetic radiation by means of \textit{light amplification through stimulated emission} in a device called the \textit{laser}.\footnote{The phenomenon holds for radiation of all frequencies and was indeed first studied in the microwave region. The device was called the Maser.} The basic components of a laser are the following:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item[1.] A lasing medium in which there are at least two energy levels, separated by an energy gap, such that the atoms in the upper level can make a transition that is stimulated by the presence of photons of the right frequency.
    \item[2.] Some mechanism for repopulating the upper level for repeated operation.
    \item[3.] A suitable cavity in which the stimulating photons can be contained and that also contains the lasing medium.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent \rule{0.5\textwidth}{0.4pt}

\noindent $\mathbf{270}$


<!-- Page 368 -->
18-1 Lasers **271**

**Conditions for the Operation of a Laser**

Consider a material in which we focus on two energy levels with energies $E_1$ and $E_0$
and $E_1 > E_0$. We will label the number of photons purely by their frequency, suppress
ing the direction of $\mathbf{k}$ and the polarization $\lambda$, since we are talking about identical pho
tons. The number of photons $N(\nu)$ will change with time. The number will increase,
because of stimulated as well as spontaneous emission. If the number of emitting atoms
in the upper level is $N_1$, then the rate of emission involves the spontaneous rate (single
photon emission) multiplied by $(N(\nu) + 1)$ and the transition rate, denoted by $A_{10}$. The
decrease is due to stimulated absorption, proportional to the number of absorbing
atoms, $N_0$, $A_{10}$, and $N(\nu)$. There is a further loss of photons due to leakage, which is
proportional to the number of photons $N(\nu)$. The leakage losses are described by the
last term in the equation below, and the cavity must be designed to make $\tau_0$ as large as
possible. We write

$$\frac{dN(\nu)}{dt} = N_1 (N(\nu) + 1)A_{10} - N_0N(\nu)A_{10} - \frac{N(\nu)}{\tau_0}$$
$$= N(\nu) \left\{ (N_1 - N_0)A_{10} - \frac{1}{\tau_0} \right\} + N_1A_{10} \quad (18-2)$$

(in writing the above we have neglected the fact that different levels may have different
degeneracies—for the purpose of our discussion this is not relevant) We see from this
equation that the number of photons will decrease with time unless

$$N_1 - N_0 > 0 \quad (18-3)$$

In thermal equilibrium we have

$$\frac{N_1}{N_0} = \frac{e^{-E_1/kT}}{e^{-E_0/kT}} = e^{-(E_1-E_0)/kT} = e^{-h\nu/kT} \quad (18-4)$$

which is always smaller than 1. Thus a laser must operate in a nonequilibrium mode, and
we must create an excess population of atoms in the upper level—that is, a *population in*
*version*. On way of doing this is described below.

**Optical Pumping**

A way of setting up a population inversion is to use a material in which the process in
volves transitions between three levels. Figure 18-1 shows a three-level system. The lev
els have energies $E_2 > E_1 > E_0$. The goal is to create a population inversion in level 1
relative to level 0. The state with energy $E_2$ must have the property that it is possible to in
crease its occupation number by some mechanism, and it must decay readily to state $E_1$
but not to $E_0$. The *pumping* of atoms into this excited state is accomplished by a variety of
