means, one of which is by subjecting the material to a powerful source of incoherent light, as is done in a *ruby laser*. In that material, the level $E_1$ is *metastable*: Selection rules slow down spontaneous transitions to the ground level, so that there is time for a large build-up of level 1 atoms by the decay of level 2 atoms.² There are of course many types of lasers and many pumping mechanisms. In this way one may create lasers in different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. By selecting materials in which the laser transition terminates on a set of closely spaced vibrational molecular levels, one may actually construct *tuneable* lasers.

**The Cavity**

The production of a collimated, narrow beam of photons requires a cylindrical structure for the cavity, with only slightly transparent mirrors at the ends. The mirrors are there to keep the photons inside the cavity to build up the number of photons $n(\nu_{10})$. The losses depend on the value of $\tau_0$.

We can estimate $\tau_0$, the "lifetime of photons in the cavity," as follows: Assume that the radiation only travels back and forth in the cylindrical cavity of length $L$. If $n^*$ is the refractive index of the medium, then the traversal time is $n^*L/c$. If the reflection coefficient of the mirror is $r$ $(\approx 0.99)$, then after $k$ traversals, the intensity of the light is reduced to $r^k$, so that, with $r = 1 - \varepsilon$,

\[ I_k / I_0 = (1 - \varepsilon)^k \approx e^{-k\varepsilon} \]

The intensity is reduced to $1/e$ of its original value after $k = 1/\varepsilon = 1/(1 - r)$ traversals. Thus the lifetime of the radiation in the cavity is

\[ \tau_0 \approx kn^*L/c = n^*L/c(1 - r) \]

The reflection coefficient can be brought closer to unity if the cavity is terminated with Brewster angle windows (which almost perfectly contain one state of polarization of the radiation), beyond which identical spherical mirrors, separated by a distance equal to their common radius of curvature, are placed (Fig. 18-2). Note that the linewidth of the radiation is

\[ \Delta\nu = 1/\tau_0 = c(1 - r)n^*L \]

which is very small compared with $c/2n^*L$, the frequency separation of two adjacent modes in a cavity of dimension $L$. Thus a nearly monochromatic beam is produced.

18-2 The Cooling of Atoms \hfill \textbf{273}

\textbf{18-2 THE COOLING OF ATOMS}

In this section we describe one application of lasers that is directly related to the study of
atoms—namely, their use to slow down atoms and in this way to reduce the \textit{Doppler}
\textit{broadening} of spectral lines.

Spectral lines can be broadened in several ways; atoms are generally not observed in
isolation. In a gas of atoms, there will generally be collisions, and the time between colli
sions $\tau_c$, if shorter than the mean life of the state under consideration, determines the
width of the spectral line, because $\tau_c$ is effectively the lifetime of the state, and $\hbar / \tau_c$ is then
larger than the natural width of the line. Collision broadening can be reduced by reducing
the density (equivalently, the pressure) of the gas of atoms under consideration. There is
also \textit{Doppler broadening}. When an atom is moving with speed $v$, then the frequency of
the radiation emitted by the atom is shifted by $\Delta \omega = (v/c)\omega$. If for $v$ we take $v_{\text{rms}} =$
$\sqrt{3kT/M_{\text{atom}}}$, the root-mean-square velocity of atoms in a gas at temperature $T$, then for
hydrogen, for example, $\Delta \omega / \omega \approx 0.3 \times 10^{-6} \sqrt{T}$. This is much larger than the natural
value of $\Delta \omega / \omega$, which for the $2p \to 1s$ line is $\approx 3 \times 10^{-8}$. Thus to overcome the Doppler
broadening, the atoms need to be \textit{cooled}. This is done by placing the atom in a laser beam.
Consider an atom moving in the positive $z$-direction with a velocity $v$. Let the energy dif
ference between the two levels for which a transition occurs be $\hbar \omega_0$, and let the frequency
of the (monochromatic) laser beam be $\omega$. We shall take $\omega$ a little different from $\omega_0$, and
take the \textit{detuning parameter} $\delta = \omega - \omega_0 < 0$. If the laser beam propagates along the
$z$-axis in the positive $z$-direction, then the atom “sees” a red-shifted beam, since the
origin of the beam appears to be moving away. Thus, the frequency as seen by the atom is
$\omega(1 - v/c)$. This means that the amount of detuning of the laser beam away from the reso
nant frequency is $\omega(1 - v/c) - \omega_0 = \delta - \omega v/c$. For $\delta < 0$, the magnitude of this is larger
than the magnitude of $\delta$, and the probability of absorption of the photons is decreased,
since the frequency of the light absorbed is farther out on the resonance curve. On the
other hand, with another laser beam propagating in the negative $z$-direction, the detuning
is $\omega(1 + v/c) - \omega_0 = \delta + \omega v/c$, so that the frequency of the light absorbed is closer to the
peak of the resonance (with $\omega v/c = |\delta|$ one would be at resonance). Thus the probability
of absorbing a photon is larger. This means that the atom experiences a net force in the
negative $z$-direction. The atom re-emits the photon, because it decays, but the emission
has no preferred direction associated with it, and on the average, it is spherically symmet
ric.$^3$ Thus there is a net loss of momentum for the atom along the $z$-direction. If there are
three pairs of lasers, aligned along the $x$-, $y$-, and $z$-axes and pairwise of equal intensity,
then all of the degrees of freedom are covered.

To make this more quantitative, we calculate the radiation pressure force exerted on
the atom by the beam. We assume that there are only two levels that are relevant in the
atom. This is a good approximation when the frequency of the oscillating electric field is
close to the frequency associated with the energy of excitation of the state above the ground
state. The rate at which momentum of magnitude $\hbar\omega/c$ is absorbed was calculated to be

\begin{align}
\Gamma &= \frac{2\pi}{\hbar} |\langle 1|er \cdot E|0 \rangle |^2 \ \delta(E_1 - E_0 - \hbar\omega) \nonumber \\
&= \frac{2\pi}{\hbar^2} |\langle 1|er \cdot E|0 \rangle |^2 \ \delta(\omega_0 - \omega) \tag{18-5}
\end{align}

\hrulefill

\footnotesize{$^3$We assume that the intensity of the laser beam is not very large, so that the excitation and the subsequent decay
are events that are well separated. Later in this chapter we shall see situations in which the system oscillates
rapidly between the ground state and the excited state. In that case, the emission is coherent with the excitation,
and directional information is not lost.}


<!-- Page 371 -->
where the dipole moment operator $e\mathbf{r}$ gives rise to the transition. We now take into account that the delta function needs to be modified because of the finite linewidth of the excited state, so that

\begin{equation}
\pi\delta(\omega_{0}-\omega) \rightarrow \frac{\Gamma/2}{(\omega_{0}-\omega)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}
\tag{18-6}
\end{equation}

where $\Gamma$ is the spontaneous decay rate. This means that the radiation pressure is

\begin{equation}
F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{\hbar\omega}{c} \times (\text{rate}) = \frac{\hbar\omega}{c} \frac{2}{\hbar^2} |\langle 1 | e\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{E}|0 \rangle|^2 \frac{\Gamma/2}{(\omega_0 - \omega)^2 + (\Gamma/2)^2}
\tag{18-7}
\end{equation}

We introduce the dimensionless quantity

\begin{equation}
I = \frac{|\langle 1 | e\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{E}|0 \rangle|^2}{(\hbar\Gamma/2)^2}
\tag{18-8}
\end{equation}

in terms of which

\begin{equation}
F = \frac{\hbar\omega}{c} I\Gamma \frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{(\omega_0-\omega)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}
\tag{18-9}
\end{equation}

For a weak field—that is, for $I$ small—the force is very small. For a very large field—that is, for large $I$—the induced decays overwhelm the spontaneous ones, and under those circumstances the atom oscillates rapidly between the ground state and the excited state.\footnote{See Section 18-3.} In particular, the emitted photons are coherent with the absorbed photons, so that the atom does not absorb any net momentum. It turns out that the optimum laser intensity is such that $I \approx 1$.

For an atom moving in the same direction as the beam, there is the additional Doppler shift detuning, so that

\begin{equation}
F = \frac{\hbar\omega}{c} I\Gamma \frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{(\omega_0-\omega-\omega v/c)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2}
\tag{18-10}
\end{equation}

If now a standing wave beam is considered, or, equivalently we ad a laser beam with the same frequency $\omega$ traveling in the negative $z$-direction, we get a force in the opposite direction, with the frequency blue-shifted to $\omega(1+v/c)$. Thus the net force on the beam is

\begin{equation*}
F_{\text{net}} = \frac{\hbar\omega}{c} I\Gamma \left( \frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{(\omega_0-\omega-\omega v/c)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2} - \frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{(\omega_0-\omega+\omega v/c)^2+(\Gamma/2)^2} \right)
\end{equation*}

To the lowest order in $v/c$, one gets

\begin{equation}
F_{\text{net}} = \frac{\hbar\omega I\Gamma}{c} \frac{(\Gamma/2)^2}{\delta^2+(\Gamma/2)^2} \frac{4\omega\delta}{\delta^2+(\Gamma/2)^2} v
\tag{18-11}
\end{equation}

Since $\delta < 0$—that is, the laser frequency is chosen to be a little below the resonance peak $\omega_0$—the force is in a direction opposite to that of $v$; that is, **it is a frictional force**, of the form $F_{\text{net}} = -\beta v$. The force depends on the amount of detuning, and it is largest when $dF/d\delta = 0$—that is, when $|\delta| = \omega_0-\omega = \Gamma/2\sqrt{3}$. The atomic motion in all three dimensions must be slowed down, and for this purpose three pairs of lasers are used, to create an environment commonly called **optical molasses**.

The maximum frictional force for $I \approx 1$ is therefore

\begin{equation*}
F \approx \sqrt{\frac{27}{4}} \frac{\hbar\omega_0^2}{c^2} v
\end{equation*}

\noindent\rule{4cm}{0.4pt}

\footnotesize{$^4$See Section 18-3.}


<!-- Page 372 -->
18-3 The Two-Level System 275

The atoms are also subject to a random force due to the random encounters with the pho
tons that make up the laser beam. They thus behave like particles in the fluid undergoing
Brownian motion. The details of the cooling process are beyond the scope of our discus
sion, but the prediction of the semiclassical argument just presented is that the atoms will
be cooled down to a temperature given by

\[
T = \frac{\hbar \omega}{k}
\]

where $k$ is Boltzmann's constant. This is generally in the range of $2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ K}$. A deeper
examination of the details of the process, which takes into account the degeneracy of the
excited levels and the polarization of the photons, shows that one should expect to be able
to cool atoms to a temperature of order $4 \times 10^{-5}\text{ K}$, which agrees with what has been
found experimentally.$^5$ In fact, recent improvements in the technology of laser cooling of
atoms have yielded atomic temperatures of $4 \times 10^{-7}\text{ K}$. When atoms are cooled to such
low temperatures, measurements of the natural linewidth become possible, and this has
had a large impact on the testing of quantum electrodynamics predictions.

### 18-3 THE TWO-LEVEL SYSTEM

Consider an atom in an external time-dependent electric field, which induces transitions
between two levels that we label $|a\rangle$ and $|b\rangle$. Their energies can be expressed in terms of
angular frequencies $\omega_a$ and $\omega_b$ so that $E_a = \hbar \omega_a$, $E_b = \hbar \omega_b$ with $E_a > E_b$.

The operator $H_0$ has the property that

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
H_0|a\rangle &= E_a|a\rangle \\
H_0|b\rangle &= E_b|b\rangle
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Since $|a\rangle$ and $|b\rangle$ form the complete set of states, we may use them to give a matrix repre
sentation of $H_0$. The matrix is diagonal in the basis that uses the energy eigenstates, so that

\begin{equation}
H_0 = \begin{pmatrix} \hbar \omega_a & 0 \\ 0 & \hbar \omega_b \end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}

The system is perturbed by an external oscillating electric field. We write

\begin{equation}
H_1 = eE_0x \cos \omega t
\end{equation}

with the choice of polarization such that $E$ points in the $x$-direction. Because of parity
conservation, $\langle a|x|a\rangle = \langle b|x|b\rangle = 0$, so that $H_1$ only has off-diagonal elements. Let us intro
duce the notation

\begin{equation}
W = eE_0\langle a|x|b\rangle
\end{equation}

Note that $W$ has the dimensions of an energy. This leads to

\begin{equation}
H_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & W \cos \omega t \\ W^* \cos \omega t & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\end{equation}

We shall use the *interaction picture* described in Supplement 15-B [www.wiley.com/college/
gasiorowicz]. Briefly, the procedure is to solve the equation satisfied by

\begin{equation}
|\psi_I(t)\rangle = e^{iH_0t/\hbar}|\psi(t)\rangle
\end{equation}

\hrulefill

$^5$This is discussed in nontechnical detail by C. N. Cohen-Tannoudji and W. D. Phillips in *Phys. Today*, 43(10),
33 (1990). This article also contains many references.


<!-- Page 373 -->
**276** Chapter 18 Selected Topics on Radiation

The equation has the form

\begin{equation}
\frac{d}{dt}|\psi_{I}(t)\rangle = -\frac{i}{\hbar}V(t)|\psi_{I}(t)\rangle \tag{18-18}
\end{equation}

with

\begin{equation}
V(t) = e^{iH_0t/\hbar} H_{1} e^{-iH_0t/\hbar} \tag{18-19}
\end{equation}

To obtain $V(t)$ in (18-19) we need to calculate $e^{iH_0t/\hbar}$. With $H_0$ diagonal, this is very simple and we have

$$
e^{iH_0t/\hbar} = \begin{pmatrix}
e^{i\omega_a t} & 0 \\
0 & e^{i\omega_b t}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

The calculation of $V(t) = e^{iH_0t/\hbar} H_{1} e^{-iH_0t/\hbar}$ is just a matter of multiplying three $2 \times 2$ matrices. The result is

\begin{equation}
V(t) = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & W e^{i(\omega_a-\omega_b)t} \cos\omega t \\
W^{*} e^{-i(\omega_a-\omega_b)t} \cos\omega t & 0
\end{pmatrix} \tag{18-20}
\end{equation}

The expression can be simplified somewhat. We can write

$$
e^{i(\omega_a-\omega_b)t} \cos\omega t = \frac{1}{2}(e^{i(\omega_a-\omega_b + \omega)t} + e^{i(\omega_a-\omega_b - \omega)t})
$$

Experimentally the $\omega$ is *tuned* to the energy difference between the two levels. This means that $\omega_a - \omega_b - \omega \equiv \Delta$ is small. The first term above oscillates very rapidly, and contributes nothing when averaged over time. As in our discussion of *paramagnetic resonance* we drop these terms. Applying this approximation, called the *rotating wave approximation*, we get

\begin{equation}
V(t) = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & (W/2)e^{i\Delta t} \\
(W^*/2)e^{-i\Delta t} & 0
\end{pmatrix} \tag{18-21}
\end{equation}

Let us now write out (18-18) in detail. With $|\psi_I(t)\rangle$ represented by the column vector

\begin{equation}
|\psi_{I}(t)\rangle \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} a(t) \\ b(t) \end{pmatrix} \tag{18-22}
\end{equation}

our equation reads

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
i\hbar \frac{da(t)}{dt} & = \frac{W}{2} e^{i\Delta t} b(t) \\
i\hbar \frac{db(t)}{dt} & = \frac{W^*}{2} e^{-i\Delta t} a(t)
\end{aligned} \tag{18-23}
\end{equation}

We differentiate the first of these, and using the second equation, we get, after some minor rearrangements, the equation

$$
\frac{d^{2}a(t)}{dt^{2}} - i\Delta \frac{da(t)}{dt} + \frac{|W|^{2}}{4\hbar^{2}} a(t) = 0
$$

If we substitute $a(t) = e^{i\Omega t}$ into the above, we find that

$$
\Omega^{2} - \Delta\Omega - \frac{|W|^{2}}{4\hbar^{2}} = 0
$$


<!-- Page 374 -->
18-3 The Two-Level System 277

The roots of this are
\begin{equation}
\Omega = \frac{\Delta}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{\Delta^2}{4} + \frac{|W|^2}{4\hbar^2}} \equiv \omega_{\pm}
\tag{18-24}
\end{equation}

We now get our solutions as follows: Choose
\begin{equation}
a(t) = a_+ e^{i\omega_+ t} + a_- e^{i\omega_- t}
\tag{18-25}
\end{equation}

Then the equation for $b(t)$ is obtained by differentiating $a(t)$. A little algebra leads to the result
\begin{equation}
b(t) = \frac{2\hbar\omega_+}{|W|} a_+ e^{-i\omega_- t} - \frac{2\hbar\omega_-}{|W|} a_- e^{-i\omega_+ t}
\tag{18-26}
\end{equation}

Let us suppose that the system is initially in the \textit{upper} state, so that $a(0) = 1$ and $b(0) = 0$.
This is satisfied if
\begin{align*}
a_+ + a_- &= 1 \\
\omega_+ a_+ + \omega_- a_- &= 0
\end{align*}
or, equivalently
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
a_+ &= \frac{\omega_-}{\omega_- - \omega_+} = -\frac{\omega_-}{2R} \\
a_- &= -\frac{\omega_+}{\omega_- - \omega_+} = \frac{\omega_+}{2R}
\end{aligned}
\tag{18-27}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
R = \sqrt{\frac{\Delta^2}{4} + \frac{|W|^2}{4\hbar^2}}
\tag{18-28}
\end{equation}

This results in
\begin{equation}
b(t) = \frac{2\hbar\omega_+ \omega_-}{a2|W|R} (e^{-i\omega_- t} - e^{-i\omega_+ t})
\tag{18-29}
\end{equation}

We may use this to calculate the probability that at a time $t$ the system is in the lower state.
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
P(t) = |b(t)|^2 &= \frac{4\hbar^2 (\omega_+ \omega_-)^2}{4 |W|^2 R^2} |e^{-i\omega_- t} - e^{-i\omega_+ t}|^2 \\
&= \frac{\hbar^2 \left(\dfrac{|W|^2}{4\hbar^2}\right)}{|W|^2 \left(\dfrac{\Delta^2}{4} + \dfrac{|W|^2}{4\hbar^2}\right)} 4 \sin^2 \sqrt{\frac{\Delta^2}{4} + \frac{|W|^2}{4\hbar^2}} t \\
&= \frac{|W|^2}{|W|^2 + \hbar^2 \Delta^2} \sin^2 \sqrt{\frac{\Delta^2}{4} + \frac{|W|^2}{4\hbar^2}} t
\end{aligned}
\tag{18-30}
\end{equation}

With perfect \textit{tuning}, the frequency of the eternal field matches the energy difference between the levels, so that then $\Delta = 0$. In that case
\begin{equation}
P(t) = \sin^2 \frac{|W|}{2\hbar} t \equiv \sin^2 r t
\tag{18-31}
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 375 -->
278\quad Chapter 18\quad Selected Topics on Radiation

The system returns to its original state after a time $T = 2\pi/r$. Thus the angular frequency
for the \textit{flopping} is given by $2\pi/T = r$. This frequency is known as the \textit{Rabi frequency}.

In our discussion we have treated the external electric field classically. It appeared in
the form
\[
W = e E_0 \langle b | x | a \rangle
\]
If we treat the electromagnetic field quantum mechanically, then $\mathbf{E}_0$ is an operator, and the
above quantity is to be replaced by
\[
W_N = e \langle N + 1 | \mathbf{E}_0 | N \rangle \langle b | x | a \rangle = \sqrt{N + 1} W \tag{18-32}
\]
as discussed in Supplement 18-A [\textbf{www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz}]. In the above we have
explicitly assumed that we have $N$ photons in the upper state, and $N + 1$ photons in the
lower state. This changes the \textit{Rabi frequency} by a factor of $\sqrt{N + 1}$ to $r\sqrt{N + 1}$. If the
initial state has $N + 1$ photons and the final state $N$ photons, then it is the \textit{lowering} opera
tor that plays a role, and the frequency is $r\sqrt{N}$.

The study of single atoms in a cavity in which there is only one mode of an oscillat
ing electric field present has been made possible through the invention and construction of
radio-frequency traps by H. Dehmelt and collaborators. The oscillations predicted above
have been experimentally established.

\section*{18-4\quad THE THREE-LEVEL SYSTEM}

The three-level system (Fig. 18-3) has many interesting features. The three levels, $A, B, C$
with energies $\hbar \omega_a > \hbar \omega_b > \hbar \omega_c$ is placed in a pair of electric fields. One of them is char
acterized by a frequency $\omega_1$ close to the difference $\omega_a - \omega_b$, the other by a frequency $\omega_2$
close to the difference $\omega_a - \omega_c$. The perturbing Hamiltonian is thus
\[
H_1 = e E_1 x \cos \omega_1 t + e E_2 x \cos \omega_2 t \tag{18-33}
\]
If the state vector (in the interaction picture) is represented by
\[
|\psi_I(t)\rangle \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} a(t) \\ b(t) \\ c(t) \end{pmatrix} \tag{18-34}
\]

so that the probability of exciting an atom in the $|B\rangle$ state to the $|A\rangle$ state is very small, leading to

18-5 Observation of Quantum Jumps \hspace{1em} \textbf{279}

then our task is to calculate the amplitudes for the occupation of these three states, $a(t), \dots$
The details of the calculation in the simplifying limit of perfect tuning, so that

\begin{align}
\omega_1 &= \omega_a - \omega_b \nonumber \\
\omega_2 &= \omega_a - \omega_c \label{eq:18-35} \tag{18-35}
\end{align}

are relegated to Supplement 18-B [www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz]. We find that different
initial conditions allow for interesting phenomena. The calculation shows that:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item[\textbf{1.}] If the states $|b\rangle$ and $|c\rangle$ lie together, and the field strengths are chosen such that
    \begin{equation}
    eE_1\langle b|x|a\rangle = eE_2\langle c|x|a\rangle \tag{18-36}
    \end{equation}
    then, with $a(0) = 0, b(0) = -c(0) = 1/\sqrt{2}$ we find that $a(t) = 0$ for \textit{all times}. This
    means that the state $A$ is never excited. It is therefore called a \textit{dark state}.

    \item[\textbf{2.}] If we consider a situation in which $E_1 \gg E_2$, one can show that with the initial
    conditions $a(0) = b(0) = 0$, the state $A$ is very unlikely to be excited by a $C \rightarrow A$
    induced transition. This means that for light of the frequency $\omega_a - \omega_c$ the proba-
    bility of a photon absorption is very small, and this in turn means that we get \textit{elec-
    tomagnetically induced transparency} at that frequency.

    \item[\textbf{3.}] We do not discuss this in Supplement 18-B [www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz], but it
    is possible to arrange the phases of the external fields such that we can get \textit{lasing}
    without creating a population inversion.
\end{enumerate}

Basically the idea is that the probability of transitions from $A$ to $B$ and $C$ is the sum of the
probabilities $P(A \rightarrow B)$ and $P(A \rightarrow C)$. On the other hand, the probability of transitions
that populate $A$ is proportional to $|b(t) + c(t)|^2$ and it is possible to arrange that the two
amplitudes interfere. This means that photons are \textit{not} absorbed by the states $B$ and $C$ (Fig.
18-3).\textsuperscript{6}

\section*{18-5 OBSERVATION OF QUANTUM JUMPS}

The invention of the traps in which single ions could be studied allows for a variety of
new techniques to study atoms. One ingenious idea was first proposed by H. Dehmelt and
observed by several experimental groups in the past decade. The principle of the experi-
ment is the following: Consider a three-level system, consisting of the ground state $|0\rangle$
and two excited states $|1\rangle$ and $|2\rangle$. Transitions between the states $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$ are allowed,
while those between $|2\rangle$ and the ground state are forbidden (but not absolutely forbidden),
so that the state $|2\rangle$ is metastable. A strong light source (laser) tuned to the angular fre-
quency $\omega_{10} = (E_1 - E_0)/\hbar$ is now directed at the atom, as is a weak light source tuned to
the frequency $\omega_{20} = (E_2 - E_0)/\hbar$. The number of transitions between the ground state and
the allowed excited state is very large. Effectively the strong laser field excites the elec-
tron to the state $|1\rangle$ at a very rapid rate, and the electron decays to the ground state also at
a very rapid rate. Thus a continuous signal of light emitted by the atom is observed. This
is just a manifestation of the Rabi oscillations discussed in Section 18-4. Very occasion-
ally the electron is excited by the weak laser to the state $|2\rangle$. Since the electron now finds
itself in a metastable state, the time until it decays to the ground state may be as long as
seconds. \textit{During that time there is no fluorescence}---that is, the atom is dark. When the

\end{figure}

**Figure 18-4** A typical trace of fluorescence from showing the quantum jumps. The atom is definitely known to be in the shelf level during the low fluorescence periods. (From W. Nagourney, J. Sandberg, and H. Dehmelt, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* **56**, 2797 (1986), by permission.)

electron finally does decay to the ground state, it is immediately excited by the strong laser field to the allowed excited state, and rapidly decays, giving rise to a resumption of the fluorescent radiation. Effectively the fluorescence monitors the quantum jumps between the ground state and the metastable state (Fig. 18-4).

Let $A_{10}$ and $A_{20}$ be the spontaneous transition rates for $|1\rangle \rightarrow |0\rangle$ and $|2\rangle \rightarrow |0\rangle$, respectively. The conditions on the transitions imply that $A_{10} \gg A_{20}$. If the energy densities of the laser beams are $U_1$ and $U_2$, respectively, then the rate equations for the probability that the atom is in the excited state $|1\rangle$ (assuming no degeneracies so that all the $g_i$ are $1$), is

$$\frac{dP_1}{dt} = -P_1 A_{10}(1 + N_1 U_1) + P_0 A_{10} N_1 U_1$$ \hfill (18-37)

Here $N_1$ is the number of photons with frequency $\omega_{10}$ present. The equation describes the loss of probability due to spontaneous and stimulated emission, and its buildup due to stimulated absorption from the ground state, the latter proportional to the probability $P_0$ that the electron is in the ground state. Similarly the rate equation for the probability that the atom is in the metastable state $|2\rangle$.

$$\frac{dP_2}{dt} = -P_2 A_{20}(1 + N_2 U_2) + P_0 A_{20} N_2 U_2$$ \hfill (18-38)

where $N_2$ is the number of photons with frequency $\omega_{20}$ that are present.

The probabilities add up to 1, so that $P_0 + P_1 + P_2 = 1$. If the laser coupling the ground state to the excited state $|1\rangle$ is intense, so that $U_1$ is very large, then equation (18-37) implies that $P_1 = P_0$ after a very short time. Under these circumstances, we may ask for the probability that the metastable state is excited. If we call this $P_+ (= P_2)$, and write the probability that it is *not* excited as $P_- (= 1 - P_+ = P_0 + P_1 = 2P_0)$, we have

$$\frac{dP_+}{dt} = -\Gamma_- P_+ + \Gamma_+ P_-$$ \hfill (18-39)



<!-- Page 378 -->
18-5 Observation of Quantum Jumps  281

with $\Gamma_{+} = \frac{1}{2} A_{20} N_2 U_2$ and $\Gamma_{-} = A_{20} (1 + N_2 U_2)$. Since $P_{+} + P_{-} = 1$, the equation for $P_{-}$
follows automatically. We may view these equations as representing a two-level system
in which the upward transition rate is $\Gamma_{+}$ and the downward transition rate is $\Gamma_{-}$

Experimentally interesting quantities are the probabilities that in the time interval
from $t$ to $t + T$ no transitions have occurred, and that at the end of the interval the electron
ends either in the excited state, $P_{0+}$ or in the ground state $P_{0-}$. A little reflection shows
that once the experiment starts and the laser beam intensities are independent of time,
these probabilities only depend on the length of the time interval $T$. We can write rate
equations for these probabilities, and these are

\begin{align}
\frac{dP_{0+}}{dT} &= -\Gamma_{-} P_{0+} \tag{18-40}
\\
\frac{dP_{0-}}{dT} &= -\Gamma_{+} P_{0-} \tag{18-41}
\end{align}

The “initial conditions” for these equations require that we know $P_{0\pm}(T = 0)$. Suppose
that the intensity of fluorescence turns off at some time $t$. We choose that time to de-
note $T = 0$, so that $P_{0+}(T = 0) = 1$. The solution to the equation with this initial con-
dition is

\begin{equation}
P_{0+}(T) = e^{-\Gamma_{-} T} \tag{18-42}
\end{equation}

This is the probability that the signal is still “off” after a time $T$. Similarly one can show
that if the fluorescence has just turned on, then the probability that it is still on after a time
interval $T$ is

\begin{equation}
P_{0-}(T) = e^{-\Gamma_{+} T} \tag{18-43}
\end{equation}

A statistical analysis of the distribution of on and off times as shown in Fig. 18-5 can be
used to measure $A_2$. For very long lived states, \textit{direct} measurements of $A_2$ are very diffi-
cult, since the rate at which photons are emitted is very small, and they can be emitted in
all directions, so counting them is a very slow process.

It is interesting to note that quantum mechanics usually involves the study of a
large ensemble of identical systems. In this case, one is studying a single atom and the
ensemble is replaced by rebuilding over and over again that single member of the en-
semble with identical initial conditions. This is generally not possible when radiation

\section*{8-6 THE MÖSSBAUER EFFECT}

An atom (or any other quantum system) can act as a very accurate clock, since its transitions are signaled by radiation of a very well-defined frequency. If the only limitation were the natural linewidth, great accuracy could be obtained.

Unfortunately, as stated in our discussion of the cooling of atoms, the motion of atoms leads to the broadening of lines by the Doppler effect. One might think that the use of a liquid or solid source would eliminate this effect, but then broadening caused by the effect of neighboring atoms is just as harmful. Let us consider nuclear transitions. A nucleus such as $_{77}\text{Ir}^{191}$ emits a $\gamma$-ray of energy of the order of $100\text{ keV}$, with a lifetime of $10^{-10}\text{ s}$. This corresponds to

\begin{equation}
\frac{\Delta \omega}{\omega} = \frac{\Delta E}{E} = \frac{\hbar/\tau}{E} \simeq \frac{10^{-34}/10^{-10}}{10^5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \simeq 0.6 \times 10^{-10} \tag{18-44}
\end{equation}

There will, unfortunately, be a recoil shift of the line. The $\gamma$-ray carries off momentum $\hbar \omega / c$, and the nucleus, to conserve momentum, must recoil with the same momentum. This gives rise to a recoil energy

\begin{equation}
\Delta E = \frac{P_{\text{recoil}}^2}{2M} = \frac{1}{2M} \left( \frac{\hbar \omega}{c} \right)^2 \tag{18-45}
\end{equation}

and thus a decrease in the energy radiated. The fractional change in frequency is

\begin{equation}
\frac{\Delta E}{\hbar \omega} \simeq \frac{\hbar \omega}{2Mc^2} \simeq \frac{10^{-1}(\text{MeV})}{2 \times 940 \times 191(\text{MeV})} \simeq 3 \times 10^{-7} \tag{18-46}
\end{equation}

The observation of radiation of this energy cannot be carried out with the conventional, extremely accurate spectroscopic methods, but must utilize a detector that is extremely “well tuned” to the radiation. This is best done by using the same material (e.g., $_{77}\text{Ir}^{191}$) as an absorber. The absorption will be very much enhanced at the “resonant” frequency at which the radiation is emitted, but here, too, there will be a recoil shift. The overall shift is thus $\Delta \omega / \omega \simeq 6 \times 10^{-7}$. Thus, the “fine tuning” does not work, since the line is shifted by far more than the width, which is of the order of $10^{-10}\text{ } \omega$. One could try to compensate for the recoil by moving the emitter with the recoil velocity. This is given by

\begin{equation}
\frac{v}{c} = \frac{P_{\text{recoil}}}{Mc} = \frac{\hbar \omega / c}{Mc} = 2\frac{\hbar \omega}{2Mc^2} \simeq 6 \times 10^{-7} \tag{18-47}
\end{equation}

that is, $v = 1.8 \times 10^2\text{ m/s}$. This presents technical difficulties, but it has been achieved with an ultracentrifuge.

A major breakthrough came with the discovery by Mössbauer in 1958 that under certain conditions there is a high probability of recoilless emission. The emission is not recoilless, of course; however, the recoil is not taken up by the nucleus, but instead by a large part of the crystal that the nucleus is imbedded in. Since the mass of the nucleus is $10^{22}$ times smaller than that of the crystal, the recoil energy is completely negligible. To get some intuition about what is happening, let us consider the nucleus as moving in a



<!-- Page 380 -->
18-6 The Mössbauer Effect 283

harmonic oscillator well, with characteristic frequency $\omega_0$. The energy levels of the oscillator are

\begin{equation}
E_n = \hbar\omega_0 \left(n_x + n_y + n_z + \frac{3}{2}\right)
\tag{18-48}
\end{equation}

The harmonic well is just an approximate description of the crystalline forces that are responsible for the properties of the lattice. If the forces that tie the nucleus to its neighbors are strong—if the “springs” are stiff—then $\omega_0$ is large; if the “springs” are soft, then $\omega_0$ is small. In terms of level spacing, a “stiff spring” has widely separated levels—that is, a low density of states—whereas a “soft spring” has a high density of states. Let us now consider the matrix element for a transition from a nuclear state described by $\Psi_i(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \dots \mathbf{r}_N)$ to a nuclear state described by $\Psi_f(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, \dots \mathbf{r}_N)$, and we take the interaction to be

\begin{equation}
-\frac{e}{M} \sum_{\text{protons}} \mathbf{p}_k \cdot \mathbf{A}_k(\mathbf{r}_k, t)
\tag{18-49}
\end{equation}

The matrix element then is proportional to

\begin{equation}
-\frac{e}{M} \int \dots \int d^3\mathbf{r}_1, \dots, d^3\mathbf{r}_N \Psi_f^* (\mathbf{r}_1, \dots, \mathbf{r}_N) \sum_k \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p}_k \, e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_k} \Psi_i (\mathbf{r}_1, \dots, \mathbf{r}_N)
\tag{18-50}
\end{equation}

If we introduce the center-of-mass coordinate $\mathbf{R} = (1/N) \sum_i \mathbf{r}_i$ then (a) the interaction term takes the form

\begin{equation}
-\frac{e}{M} \, e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} \sum_{\text{protons}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p}_k \, e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\rho}_k}
\tag{18-51}
\end{equation}

where $\boldsymbol{\rho}_i = \mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{R}$, and (b) the nuclear wave function decomposes into a product describing the internal motion and the motion of the nuclear center of mass in the harmonic potential

\begin{equation}
\Psi (\mathbf{r}_1, \dots, \mathbf{r}_N) = \psi_{n_x n_y n_z} (\mathbf{R}) \, \phi(\boldsymbol{\rho}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{\rho}_{N-1})
\tag{18-52}
\end{equation}

Thus the matrix element (18-50) becomes

\begin{align}
&-\frac{e}{M} \int d^3\mathbf{R} \psi_{n_f}^* (\mathbf{R}) \; e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} \, \psi_{n_i} (\mathbf{R}) \nonumber \\
&\qquad \times \int d^3\boldsymbol{\rho}_1, \dots, d^3\boldsymbol{\rho}_{N-1} \phi_f^* (\boldsymbol{\rho}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{\rho}_{N-1}) \sum_{\text{protons}} \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \cdot \mathbf{p}_k \, e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\rho}_k} \phi_i (\boldsymbol{\rho}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{\rho}_{N-1})
\tag{18-53}
\end{align}

We may write this in the form

\begin{equation}
M = M_{\text{internal}} \int d^3\mathbf{R} \psi_{n_f}^* (\mathbf{R}) \; e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} \, \psi_{0} (\mathbf{R})
\tag{18-54}
\end{equation}

where we have set $n_i = 0$, since the initial state is in the ground state of the lattice. The probability that the radiative transition leaves the nucleus in the lattice ground

\begin{align}
P_0(k) &= \frac{ |M_{\text{int}}|^2 \, \left| \displaystyle \int d^3\mathbf{R} \psi_0^* (\mathbf{R}) \; e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} \, \psi_0 (\mathbf{R}) \right|^2}{ |M_{\text{int}}|^2 \displaystyle \sum_{n_f} \, \left| \int d^3\mathbf{R} \psi_{n_f}^* (\mathbf{R}) \; e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} \, \psi_0 (\mathbf{R}) \right|^2} \nonumber \\
&= \left| \int d^3\mathbf{R} \psi_0^* (\mathbf{R}) \; e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} \, \psi_0 (\mathbf{R}) \right|^2
\tag{18-55}
\end{align}


<!-- Page 381 -->
284
Chapter 18 Selected Topics on Radiation

In the last step we replaced the sum in the denominator by unity, using completeness.$^7$ To
calculate this, we use the normalized ground-state wave function of the oscillator. We
found in Chapter 6 that the one-dimensional ground-state wave function is
\[
\psi_0(x) = \left( \frac{m\omega_0}{\pi\hbar} \right)^{1/4} e^{-m\omega_0 x^2/2\hbar}
\]

Hence, for three dimensions we have
\[
\psi_0(R) = \psi_0(x)\ \psi_0(y)\ \psi_0(z) = \left( \frac{m\omega_0}{\pi\hbar} \right)^{3/4} e^{-m\omega_0 \mathbf{R}^2/2\hbar} \tag{18-56}
\]

We thus calculate
\[
\left| \left( \frac{M_N\omega_0}{\pi\hbar} \right)^{3/2} \int d^3\mathbf{R} e^{-M_N\omega_0 \mathbf{R}^2/\hbar} e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} \right|^2
\]

where $M_N$ is the mass of the nucleus. We get
\begin{align}
P_0 &= \left( \frac{M_N\omega_0}{\pi\hbar} \right)^{3} \left| \int d^3\mathbf{R} e^{-M_N\omega_0/\hbar[\mathbf{R} + i\mathbf{k}(\hbar/2M_N\omega_0)]^2} e^{-k^2\hbar/4M_N\omega_0} \right|^2 \nonumber \\
&= e^{-\hbar^2 k^2/2M_N\hbar\omega_0} \tag{18-57} \\
&= e^{-\text{recoil energy/level spacing}} \nonumber
\end{align}

since $P_{\text{recoil}} = \hbar k$ and $\hbar\omega_0$ is the level spacing in the lattice. Thus, if the level spacing is
large—that is, we have a stiff spring—recoilless emission becomes more probable. The
model of the lattice that was used here, that of each nucleus moving in its own harmonic
potential, is the Einstein model of a lattice, and the frequency $\omega_0$ is the so-called \textit{Debye}
\textit{frequency}, so that we should really replace $\omega_0$ by $\omega_D$, which is related to the Debye tem
perature $T_D$ by
\[
\hbar\omega_D = k T_D \tag{18-58}
\]
A more accurate treatment of the lattice using the Debye model for its description merely
changes the exponent by a factor of 3/2.

It is not quite correct to say that the whole crystal recoils; instead, in a time $\tau$ equal
to the lifetime of the transition (1.4 $\times$ 10$^{-7}$ s for Fe$^{57}$), only a region of the crystal of
magnitude
\[
L = v_s\tau
\]
where $v_s$ is the velocity of propagation of a lattice disturbance, (i.e., the velocity of sound)
absorbs the recoil. Now a reasonable estimate of $v_s$ is given by
\[
v_s \simeq \frac{a\omega_D}{2\pi}
\]

\noindent\rule{14cm}{0.4pt}
$^7$The formal proof is quickest. We have
\[
\sum_{n_f} |\langle n_f | e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} | 0\rangle|^2 = \sum_{n_f} \langle 0 | e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} | n_f\rangle \langle n_f | e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} | 0\rangle
\]
Using
\[
1 = \sum |n_f\rangle\langle n_f|
\]
one gets
\[
\langle 0 | e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{R}} | 0\rangle = 1
\]


<!-- Page 382 -->
18-6 The Mössbauer Effect \textbf{285}

where $a$ is the lattice spacing. Thus

\[
\frac{L}{a} \simeq \frac{\omega_D \tau}{2\pi}
\]

and with $\omega_D \simeq 10^{13}\text{ s}^{-1}$, the number of nuclei absorbing the recoil, $\sim (L/a)^3$ is still enormous.

The preceding estimates, combined with the uncertainty relation, may be used to show that it is not possible to determine whether it is a single nucleus that "really" recoils. To measure the recoil energy $\hbar^2k^2/2M_N$ takes a time of the order of

\[
\Delta t \gg \frac{\hbar}{(\hbar^2k^2/2M_N)}
\]

The condition for the Mössbauer effect to occur is that

\[
\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2M_N} < \hbar\omega_D
\]

Hence

\[
\Delta t \gg \frac{1}{\omega_D}
\]

During that time the disturbance will have traveled a distance

\[
d \simeq v_s\, \Delta t \sim \frac{a\omega_D}{2\pi} \Delta t \gg \frac{a}{2\pi}
\]

that is, over a distance covering many nuclei.

The question arises of how did we manage to get away from the problem of recoil and momentum conservation by talking about the energy states of the nucleus in the crystal lattice? Where does it say that the crystal absorbed the momentum? The quantum mechanical answer is that, if we want to talk about momentum, we should work in a momentum representation. This, however, is complicated, since it is difficult to describe the crystal forces in that representation. What one must do is to decompose the crystal motion (the crystal is just a lot of oscillators with nearest neighbor "springs") into normal modes and quantize these. The quanta of the lattice motion, analogs of photons, are the \textit{phonons}. Recoilless emission then means a transition in which phonons are not emitted. The resulting formula is very similar to (18-57). Under these circumstances, the recoil broadening is infinitesimal compared to the natural linewidth. There is still Doppler broadening because of the thermal motion, but this can be handled by cooling the emitter and absorber.

Recoilless emitters provide us with a superb clock, and research utilizing the Mössbauer effect has been done in many fields, such as solid-state physics and chemistry. We will mention just one application, the terrestrial measurement of the gravitational red shift. It follows from the equivalence principle that a photon will have its frequency shifted by

\[
\frac{\Delta \omega}{\omega} = \frac{gx}{c^2} \tag{18-59}
\]

if it falls through a height $x$. This can be compensated by a recoil of velocity $v$.

\[
v^2 = 2gx \tag{18-60}
\]


<!-- Page 383 -->
**286**\quad Chapter 18 \quad Selected Topics on Radiation

(If the photon and the absorber were to fall freely together there would be resonant
absorption.) If the absorber or the source is allowed to oscillate rapidly—one uses a
transducer—and the absorption curve is correlated with the oscillations, it is possible to
check the gravitational shift. Since the velocity, for a separation $x = 20$ m, is of the order
of $\sim$20 m/s, the experiment is feasible, and was carried out by several groups. Within the
errors, the effect is confirmed. For example, for $\text{Fe}^{57}$ the predicted shift is $\Delta\omega/\omega = 4.92 \times
10^{-15}$, and the experimental shift found by Pound and Rebka is $(5.13 \pm 0.51) \times 10^{-15}$. A
similar experiment in which the energy shift of the $\gamma$-ray emitted by $\text{Fe}^{57}$ accelerated on a
rapidly rotating turntable was measured again yielded results in agreement with the equiv
alence principle.

{\huge Quantizing the Electromagnetic \\ Field Without Frills}

Our goal is to express the electromagnetic field in terms of photons. In terms of the vector
potential $A(\mathbf{r}, t)$ we write
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}, t) &= \nabla \times \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) \\
\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{r}, t) &= -\frac{\partial \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)}{\partial t} \tag{18A-1}
\end{align*}

As elsewhere in the book, we work in the gauge $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) = 0$; we have also made the
choice $\phi(\mathbf{r}) = 0$, possible in the absence of charges.

The energy carried by the electromagnetic field is
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{H} = \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} \int \mathrm{d}^3\mathrm{r} (\mathbf{E}^2(\mathbf{r}, t) + \mathrm{c}^2\mathbf{B}^2(\mathbf{r}, t)) \tag{18A-2}
\end{equation*}

Let us now expand $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t)$ in a Fourier series in a cubical box of volume $\mathrm{V} = \mathrm{L}^3$. We write
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{V}}} \sum_{\mathbf{k},\lambda} \mathrm{f}(\mathbf{k}) \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_\lambda(\mathbf{k}) [\mathrm{A}_\lambda^{+}(\mathbf{k}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \omega\mathrm{t})} + \mathrm{A}_\lambda(\mathbf{k}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \omega\mathrm{t})}] \tag{18A-3}
\end{equation*}

This will obey the wave equation provided that
\begin{equation*}
\omega^2 = \mathrm{k}^2\mathrm{c}^2 \tag{18A-4}
\end{equation*}

The gauge-fixing condition implies that
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)}(\mathbf{k}) = 0 \tag{18A-5}
\end{equation*}

This means that the polarization vectors $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{(\lambda)}(\mathbf{k})$ ($\lambda = 1, 2,$) are perpendicular to the direc
tion of propagation of the wave $\mathbf{k}$; that is, the polarization is transverse.

Let us now calculate the energy in terms of the $\mathrm{A}_\lambda(\mathbf{k})$ and $\mathrm{A}_\lambda^{+}(\mathbf{k})$. We get for the first
term involving the electric field,

\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{\mathrm{V}} \int \mathrm{d}^3\mathrm{r} \sum_{\mathbf{k},\lambda} \sum_{\mathbf{q},\lambda'} \mathrm{f}(\mathbf{k}) \, \mathrm{f}(\mathbf{q}) \, \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_\lambda(\mathbf{k}) \, \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{\lambda'}(\mathbf{q}) &[- \mathrm{i}\omega \mathrm{A}_\lambda^{+}(\mathbf{k}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \omega\mathrm{t})} + \mathrm{i}\omega \mathrm{A}_\lambda(\mathbf{k}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \omega\mathrm{t})}] \\
\times &[- \mathrm{i}\omega' \mathrm{A}_{\lambda'}^{+}(\mathbf{q}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}(\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \omega'\mathrm{t})} + \mathrm{i}\omega' \mathrm{A}_{\lambda'}(\mathbf{q}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{r} - \omega'\mathrm{t})}] \tag{18A-6}
\end{align*}

We use the notation $\omega' = |\mathbf{q}|\mathrm{c}$. The values of $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are determined by the fact that we
are expanding in a box, and we choose periodic boundary conditions. Thus in any direc
tion we require that
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{ikx}} = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{ik}(\mathrm{x} + \mathrm{L})} \tag{18A-7}
\end{equation*}

so that $\text{k}_{1}\text{L} = 2\pi\text{n}_{1}$, and so on. Thus the summations are over integers $\text{n}_{1}, \text{n}_{2}, \text{n}_{3} = 1, 2, 3, \dots$. We do not need to sum over negative integers, since these are contained in the $\text{A}^{+}$ terms. Now

\begin{equation}

The integration over all the spatial coordinates again yields

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{\text{V}}\int \text{d}^{3}\text{r}\text{e}^{\text{i}(\text{k}+\text{q})\text{r}} &= 0 \\
\frac{1}{\text{V}}\int \text{d}^{3}\text{r}\text{e}^{\text{i}(\text{k}-\text{q})\text{r}} &= \delta_{\text{kq}}

The vector identity

\begin{equation}
(\text{k} \times \varepsilon_{\lambda}(\text{k})) \bullet (\text{k} \times \varepsilon_{\lambda'}(\text{k})) = \text{k}^{2}\varepsilon_{\lambda}(\text{k}) \bullet \varepsilon_{\lambda'}(\text{k}) - (\text{k} \bullet \varepsilon_{\lambda}(\text{k}))(\text{k} \bullet \varepsilon_{\eta'}(\text{k}))\label{eq:18A-12b}\tag{18A-12}
\end{equation}

with the help of the transversality condition and $\varepsilon_{\lambda}(\text{k}) \bullet \varepsilon_{\lambda'}(\text{k}) = \delta_{\lambda\lambda'}$ yields $\text{k}^{2}\delta_{\lambda\lambda'}$. This means that the part of $\text{H}$ involving $\text{B}$, when multiplied by $\text{c}^{2}$, yields the same factor as the $\text{E}^{2}$ term. We thus get

\begin{equation}
\text{H} = \varepsilon_{0}\sum_{\text{k},\lambda}\text{f}^{2}(\text{k})\omega^{2}\{ \text{A}_{\lambda}(\text{k})\text{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\text{k}) + \text{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\text{k})\text{A}_{\lambda}(\text{k}) \}\label{eq:18A-13}\tag{18A-13}
\end{equation}

The form looks very much like the sum of terms in the simple harmonic oscillator. In fact, had we chosen $\text{f}(\text{k})$ such that

\begin{equation*}
\varepsilon_{0}\text{f}^{2}(\text{k})\omega^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\hbar\omega
\end{equation*}

that is,

\begin{equation*}
\text{f}(\text{k}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2\varepsilon_{0}\omega}}
\end{equation*}

we would have obtained

\begin{equation}
\text{H} = \sum_{\text{k},\lambda}\frac{1}{2}\hbar\omega \{\text{A}_{\lambda}(\text{k})\text{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\text{k}) + \text{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\text{k})\text{A}_{\lambda}(\text{k})\}\label{eq:18A-14}\tag{18A-14}
\end{equation}



<!-- Page 386 -->
Quantizing the Electromagnetic Field Without Frills 

W-85

Let us now assume that the ${\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k})}$ and $\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{k})$ are operators that obey the same commutation relations as the operators A and $\mathrm{A}^{+}$ for the simple harmonic oscillator problem; that is

\[\{ \mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k}), \mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{q}) \} = \delta_{\lambda \lambda'} \delta_{\mathrm{k} \mathrm{q}}\] 

(18A-15)

Then we get

\[\mathrm{H} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}\lambda} \hbar\omega \left( (\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{k})\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k}) + \frac{1}{2}) \right)\] 

(18A-16)

Actually the second term $\Sigma_{\mathrm{k},\lambda} \hbar\omega / 2$ is infinite. We sweep this problem under the rug by observing that all energy measurements are measurements of energy differences. We thus concentrate on

\[\mathrm{H} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}\lambda} \hbar\omega \mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{k})\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k})\] 

(18A-17)

We may now go through the same steps that we did with the harmonic oscillator. For each value of k and $\lambda$ we have creation and annihilation operators, and for each value of k and $\lambda$ we have states of zero, one, two, . . . photons. The zero photon state, the vacuum state, is $|0\rangle$, defined by

\[\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k})|0\rangle = 0\] 

(18A-18)

A state with n photons of momentum $\hbar\mathrm{k}$ and energy $\hbar\omega$ is given by

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{n}!}} (\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{k}))^{\mathrm{n}} |0\rangle\] 

(18A-19)

What we have done is to decompose the electromagnetic field into modes, each of which represents photons. Thus

\[\mathrm{E}(\mathrm{r},\mathrm{t}) = \frac{\partial \mathrm{A}(\mathrm{r},\mathrm{t})}{\partial \mathrm{t}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{V}}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}\lambda} \sqrt{\frac{\hbar\omega}{2\varepsilon_0}} \varepsilon_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k}) \left[ -\mathrm{i}\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{k}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}(\mathrm{k} \cdot \mathrm{r} - \omega \mathrm{t})} + \mathrm{i}\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\mathrm{k} \cdot \mathrm{r} - \omega \mathrm{t})} \right]\] 

(18A-20)

will annihilate or create a single photon.

As a check we can calculate the momentum carried by the electromagnetic field. We need to calculate

\[\mathrm{P} = \varepsilon_0 \int \mathrm{d}^3\mathrm{r} (\mathrm{E}(\mathrm{r},\mathrm{t}) \times \mathrm{B}(\mathrm{r},\mathrm{t}))\] 

(18A-21)

Using the expressions obtained above, we find, after a page of algebra, that

\[\mathrm{P} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}\lambda} \hbar\mathrm{k}(\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{k})\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k}) + 1) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}\lambda} \hbar\mathrm{k}\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{k})\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k})\] 

(18A-22)

The last step follows from the fact that $\Sigma_k \mathrm{k} = 0$ by symmetry. We may thus interpret the product $\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}^{+}(\mathrm{k})\mathrm{A}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k}) \equiv \mathrm{N}_{\lambda}(\mathrm{k})$ as the operator representing the number of photons of momentum k and polarization $\lambda$.

Supplement 18-B

Details of the Three-Level System

The three-level system has many interesting features, so that we discuss it in some detail.
The system of three levels, A, B, C with energies $\hbar\omega_a > \hbar\omega_b > \hbar\omega_c$ is placed in a set of
electric fields. One of them is characterized by a frequency $\omega_1$ close to the difference $\omega_a$
$- \omega_b$, and the other by a frequency $\omega_2$, close to the difference $\omega_a - \omega_c$. The perturbing
Hamiltonian is

\begin{equation}
H_1 = eE_1x \cos \omega_1 t + eE_2x \cos \omega_2 t \tag{18B-1}
\end{equation}

In matrix form, the only nonvanishing elements are taken to be $\langle a|x|b \rangle$ and $\langle a|x|c \rangle$, which
can be taken to be real. We introduce the notation

\begin{align}
W_{1ab} &= eE_1\langle a|x|b \rangle \notag \\
W_{2ab} &= eE_2\langle a|x|b \rangle \notag \\
W_{1ac} &= eE_1\langle a|x|c \rangle \tag{18B-2} \\
&......... \notag
\end{align}

and so on. With this notation the matrix representation of H$_1$ has the form

\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & W_{1ab} \cos \omega_1 t + W_{2ab} \cos \omega_2 t & W_{1ac} \cos \omega_1 t + W_{2ac} \cos \omega_2 t \\
W_{1ab} \cos \omega_1 t + W_{2ab} \cos \omega_2 t & 0 & 0 \\
W_{1ac} \cos \omega_1 t + W_{2ac} \cos \omega_2 t & 0 & 0 
\end{pmatrix} \tag{18B-3}
\end{equation}

We next need to calculate $e^{iH_0t/\hbar}H_1e^{-iH_0t/\hbar}$. To get this we pre-multiply the matrix for H$_1$

\begin{equation}
e^{iH_0t/\hbar} = \begin{pmatrix}
e^{i\omega_a t} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & e^{i\omega_b t} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & e^{i\omega_c t}
\end{pmatrix} \tag{18B-4}
\end{equation}

and post-multiply it by the hermitian conjugate matrix. Some algebra yields the matrix

\begin{equation}
V(t) = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & X & Y \\
X^* & 0 & 0 \\
Y^* & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix} \tag{18B-5}
\end{equation}

with

\begin{align}
X &= (W_{1ab} \cos \omega_1 t + W_{2ab} \cos \omega_2 t) \, e^{i(\omega_a - \omega_b)t} \notag \\
Y &= (W_{1ac} \cos \omega_1 t + W_{2ac} \cos \omega_2 t) \, e^{i(\omega_a - \omega_c)t} \tag{18B-6}
\end{align}

W-86


<!-- Page 388 -->
Details of the Three-Level System \quad W-87

We now again apply the rotating wave approximation, with $\omega_{\text{a}} - \omega_{\text{b}} - \omega_1 = \delta_1$, and $\omega_{\text{a}} - \omega_{\text{c}} - \omega_2 = \delta_2$ being the only terms that we keep in this approximation. This means that in X and Y we decompose the cosines, and only keep the terms below:

\begin{align*}
\text{X} &= \frac{1}{2} \text{W}_{1\text{ab}} \text{e}^{\text{i}\delta_1 \text{t}} \\
\text{Y} &= \frac{1}{2} \text{W}_{2\text{ac}} \text{e}^{\text{i}\delta_2 \text{t}} \tag{18B-7}
\end{align*}

Let us take the state vector as represented by the column vector

\begin{equation*}
|\psi_1(t)\rangle \rightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \text{a(t)} \\ \text{b(t)} \\ \text{c(t)} \end{pmatrix} \tag{18B-8}
\end{equation*}

The set of equations to be solved is

\begin{align*}
\text{i}\hbar \frac{\text{da(t)}}{\text{dt}} &= \frac{1}{2} \text{W}_{1\text{ab}} \text{e}^{\text{i}\delta_1 \text{t}} \text{ b(t)} + \frac{1}{2} \text{W}_{2\text{ac}} \text{e}^{\text{i}\delta_2 \text{t}} \text{ c(t)} \\
\text{i}\hbar \frac{\text{db(t)}}{\text{dt}} &= \frac{1}{2} \text{W}_{1\text{ab}} \text{e}^{-\text{i}\delta_1 \text{t}} \text{ a(t)} \tag{18B-9} \\
\text{i}\hbar \frac{\text{dc(t)}}{\text{dt}} &= \frac{1}{2} \text{W}_{2\text{ac}} \text{e}^{-\text{i}\delta_2 \text{t}} \text{ a(t)}
\end{align*}

Let us write

\begin{align*}
\text{B(t)} &= \text{e}^{\text{i}\delta_1 \text{t}} \text{b(t)} \\
\text{C(t)} &= \text{e}^{\text{i}\delta_2 \text{t}} \text{c(t)} \tag{18B-10}
\end{align*}

In terms of these, the equations become

\begin{align*}
\text{i}\hbar \frac{\text{da(t)}}{\text{dt}} &= \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2} \text{ B(t)} + \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2} \text{ C(t)} \\
\text{i}\hbar \frac{\text{dB(t)}}{\text{dt}} &+ \hbar \delta_1 \text{B(t)} = \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2} \text{ A(t)} \tag{18B-11} \\
\text{i}\hbar \frac{\text{dC(t)}}{\text{dt}} &+ \hbar \delta_2 \text{C(t)} = \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2} \text{ A(t)}
\end{align*}

Let us now assume the time dependence $\text{e}^{\text{i}\Omega \text{t}}$ in all the terms. We then get from the various equations

\begin{align*}
-\hbar \Omega \text{a(0)} &= \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2} \text{ B(0)} + \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2} \text{ C(0)} \\
-\hbar (\Omega - \delta_1) \text{ B(0)} &= \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2} \text{ a(0)} \tag{18B-12} \\
-\hbar (\Omega - \delta_2) \text{ C(0)} &= \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2} \text{ a(0)}
\end{align*}

This leads to a cubic equation for $\Omega$, as might have been expected. The equation reduces to

\begin{equation*}
\Omega(\Omega - \delta_1)(\Omega - \delta_2) = \left(\frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2\hbar}\right)^2 (\Omega - \delta_2) + \left(\frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2\hbar}\right)^2 (\Omega - \delta_1) \tag{18B-13}
\end{equation*}


<!-- Page 389 -->
W-88 Supplement 18-B Details of the Three-Level System

We can greatly simplify matters by assuming perfect tuning so that $\delta_1 = \delta_2 = 0$. In that
case the equation has simple roots: $\Omega = 0, \Omega = \text{r}, \Omega = -\text{r}$, where
\begin{equation}
\text{r} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2\hbar}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2\hbar}\right)^2}
\tag{18B-14}
\end{equation}
Thus we have
\begin{align}
\text{a(t)} &= \text{a}_0 + \text{a}_+\text{e}^{\text{irt}} + \text{a}_-\text{e}^{-\text{irt}} \nonumber \\
\text{b(t)} &= \text{b}_0 + \text{b}_+\text{e}^{\text{irt}} + \text{b}_-\text{e}^{-\text{irt}} \tag{18B-15} \\
\text{c(t)} &= \text{c}_0 + \text{c}_+\text{e}^{\text{irt}} + \text{c}_-\text{e}^{-\text{irt}} \nonumber 
\end{align}
The nine parameters will be determined by the equations (18B-12).
We now write the solutions in terms of the eigenstates corresponding to the different
eigenvalues
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a(t)} \\
\text{b(t)} \\
\text{c(t)}
\end{pmatrix} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_0 \\
\text{b}_0 \\
\text{c}_0
\end{pmatrix} + 
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_+ \\
\text{b}_+ \\
\text{c}_+
\end{pmatrix} \text{e}^{\text{irt}} + 
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_- \\
\text{b}_- \\
\text{c}_-
\end{pmatrix} \text{e}^{-\text{irt}}
\tag{18B-16}
\end{equation}
To find the normalized eigenstates we proceed as follows:
$\Omega = 0$: We have $\text{a}_0 = 0$, and $\text{W}_{1\text{ab}} \text{b}_0 + \text{W}_{2\text{ac}} \text{c}_0 = 0$. The normalized solutions is
therefore
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_0 \\
\text{b}_0 \\
\text{c}_0
\end{pmatrix} = 
\begin{pmatrix}
0 \\
\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}/2\hbar\text{r} \\
-\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}/2\hbar\text{r}
\end{pmatrix}
\tag{18B-17}
\end{equation}
This is normalized to unity since it $\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}^2 + \text{W}_{1\text{ab}}^2 = 4\hbar^2 \text{r}^2$.
For $\Omega = \text{r}$, we must satisfy
\begin{align}
-\hbar \text{r} \text{a}_+ &= \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2} \text{b}_+ + \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2} \text{c}_+ \nonumber \\
-\hbar \text{r} \text{b}_+ &= \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2} \text{a}_+ \tag{18B-18} \\
-\hbar \text{r} \text{c}_+ &= \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2} \text{a}_+ \nonumber
\end{align}
The first equation is automatically satisfied if the other two are, which is to be expected,
since $\text{a}_+$ is to be determined by normalization. A little algebra shows that
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_+ \\
\text{b}_+ \\
\text{c}_+
\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\
-\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}/2\hbar\text{r} \\
-\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}/2\hbar\text{r}
\end{pmatrix}
\tag{18B-19}
\end{equation}
The case for $\Omega = -\text{r}$ is easily solved by just changing the sign of r. We get
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_- \\
\text{b}_- \\
\text{c}_-
\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\
\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}/2\hbar\text{r} \\
\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}/2\hbar\text{r}
\end{pmatrix}
\tag{18B-20}
\end{equation}
It is easy to check that the three eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal.
The general solution is
\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a(t)} \\
\text{b(t)} \\
\text{c(t)}
\end{pmatrix} = \alpha_0
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_0 \\
\text{b}_0 \\
\text{c}_0
\end{pmatrix} + \alpha_+
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_+ \\
\text{b}_+ \\
\text{c}_+
\end{pmatrix} \text{e}^{\text{irt}} + \alpha_-
\begin{pmatrix}
\text{a}_- \\
\text{b}_- \\
\text{c}_-
\end{pmatrix} \text{e}^{-\text{irt}}
\tag{18B-21}
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 390 -->
Details of the Three-Level System \quad W-89

and the coefficients ($\alpha_0$, $\alpha_+ \alpha_-$) are determined by the initial conditions. At time $\text{t} = 0$ we have

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\text{a}(0) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \, \alpha_+ + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \, \alpha_- \\
\text{b}(0) &= \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2\hbar\text{r}} \, \alpha_0 - \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2\sqrt{2}\hbar\text{r}} \, \alpha_+ + \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2\sqrt{2}\hbar\text{r}} \, \alpha_- \\
\text{c}(0) &= \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{2\hbar\text{r}} \, \alpha_0 - \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2\sqrt{2}\hbar\text{r}} \, \alpha_+ + \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2\sqrt{2}\hbar\text{r}} \, \alpha_-
\end{aligned} \tag{18B-22}
\end{equation*}

Dark States

Consider a configuration in which the $|\text{b}\rangle$ and the $|\text{c}\rangle$ states lie close together (Fig. 18-3a) and

\begin{equation*}
\text{W}_{1\text{ab}} = \text{W}_{2\text{ac}} \tag{18B-23}
\end{equation*}

We now take our initial state to be

\begin{equation*}
|\psi_1(0)\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|\text{b}\rangle - |\text{c}\rangle) \tag{18B-24}
\end{equation*}

This implies that $\text{a}(0) = 0$; $\text{b}(0) = -\text{c}(0) = 1/\sqrt{2}$. We now solve for ($\alpha_0, \alpha_+, \alpha_-$), and get

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_0 &= \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}} + \text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{2\sqrt{2}\hbar\text{r}} = \frac{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{\sqrt{2}\hbar\text{r}} \\
\alpha_+ &= -\alpha_- = \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}} - \text{W}_{1\text{ab}}}{4\hbar\text{r}} = 0
\end{aligned} \tag{18B-25}
\end{equation*}

This implies that $\text{a}(\text{t}) = 0$ for all times. Thus the state $|\text{a}\rangle$ is never excited, and is therefore called a dark state. The reason it is inaccessible is that the amplitudes for exciting from the $|\text{b}\rangle$ and $|\text{c}\rangle$ states interfere destructively.

Electromagnetically Induced Transparency

Consider, next, a situation in which the $|\text{a}\rangle$ and $|\text{b}\rangle$ states are strongly coupled by an electromagnetic field, while $|\text{a}\rangle$ and $|\text{c}\rangle$ are weakly coupled. What this implies is that

\begin{equation*}
|\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}| \gg |\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}| \tag{18B-26}
\end{equation*}

One can show that under these circumstances the state $|\text{a}\rangle$ is very unlikely to be excited, and this means that photons cannot be absorbed by a $|\text{c}\rangle \rightarrow |\text{a}\rangle$ transition.

We take for our initial condition $\text{a}(0) = \text{b}(0) = 0$. This implies that

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_- &= -\alpha_+ \\
\alpha_+ &= \frac{\text{W}_{2\text{ac}}}{\sqrt{2}\text{ W}_{1\text{ab}}} \, \alpha_0
\end{aligned} \tag{18B-27}
\end{equation*}

Furthermore, since $\text{a}(0) = \text{b}(0) = 0$, we must necessarily have $|\text{c}(0)| = 1$. Since

\begin{equation*}
\text{c}(0) = \frac{2\hbar\text{r}}{\text{W}_{1\text{ab}}} \, \alpha_0
\end{equation*}


<!-- Page 391 -->
W-90 Supplement 18-B Details of the Three-Level System

we may choose for convenience

\begin{equation}
\alpha_0 = \frac{\text{W}_{\text{lab}}}{2\hbar r} \tag{18B-28}
\end{equation}

Now, at a later time t, we get

\begin{equation}
\text{a(t)} = \frac{\alpha_+}{\sqrt{2}} (\text{e}^{\text{irt}} - \text{e}^{-\text{irt}}) = \text{i} \frac{\text{W}_{\text{2ac}}}{2\hbar r} \sin{\text{rt}} \tag{18B-29}
\end{equation}

Thus the probability of finding the system in the state $|\text{a}\rangle$ at a later time is

\begin{equation}
\text{P}_\text{a}(\text{t}) = |\text{a(t)}|^2 = \frac{\text{W}^2_{\text{2ac}}}{\text{W}^2_{\text{2ac}} + \text{W}^2_{\text{lab}}} \sin^2{\text{rt}} \tag{18B-30}
\end{equation}

Because of the condition (18B-26) the probability of exciting the state $|\text{a}\rangle$ is very small. This, however, implies that photons cannot be absorbed through the mechanism of exciting state $|\text{a}\rangle$, so the material becomes transparent at the frequency corresponding to this energy difference.

\chapter{19}
\section*{Collision Theory}

\textbf{A}tomic and molecular structure was largely explored through spectroscopy. When it
comes to trying to understand nuclear forces and the laws that govern the interactions
of elementary particles, the only technique available is that of scattering a variety of
particles by a variety of targets. In some sense, spectroscopy is also a form of
“scattering.” The atom in the ground state is excited by some projectile (it may be
electrons in a discharge tube or collisions with other target particles, as in heating up of
the gas), and then an outgoing photon is observed, with the atom going into the ground
state again, or possibly another excited state. We do not usually describe these processes
as “collision processes” because the atom has very well-defined energy levels, in which
it stays for times that are enormously long compared to collision times,$^1$ so that it is
possible to separate the “decay” from the excitation process. In particular, the
characteristics of the decay are not sensitive to the particular mode of excitation. In nuclei
and also in elementary particles, there exist levels, but frequently the lifetime is not
sufficiently long to warrant a separation into excitation and decay, especially since
accompanying the “resonant” scattering there is also nonresonant “background”
scattering, and the disentangling of the two is sometimes complicated. In this chapter
we will therefore discuss the process as a whole.

\subsection*{19-1 \quad COLLISION CROSS SECTION}

The ideal way to talk about scattering is to formulate equations that describe exactly what
happens: An incident particle, described by a wave packet, approaches the target. The
wave packet must be spatially large, so that it does not spread appreciably during the ex
periment, and it must be large compared with the target particle, but small compared with
the dimensions of the laboratory; that is, it must not simultaneously overlap the target and
detector. The lateral dimensions are, in fact, determined by the beam size in the accelera
tor. There follows an interaction with the target, and finally we see two wave packets: One
continues in the forward direction, describing the unscattered part of the beam, and the
other flies off at some angle and describes the scattered particles. The number of particles
scattered into a given solid angle per unit time and unit incident flux is defined to be the
\textit{differential scattering cross section}. We will not follow this approach directly, but will
instead use some of the material developed in Supplement 8-B [\textbf{www.wiley.com/college/}
\textbf{gasiorowicz}] obtain the differential cross section. We will, however, keep the wave-packet
treatment in mind as we interpret our formal results.

\rule{10cm}{0.4pt}

$^1$Recall that the lifetime of a $2p$ hydrogen state is $1.6 \times 10^{-9}$ s, which is large compared to the characteristic
time $a_0/\alpha c \simeq 2 \times 10^{-17}$ s.

\hfill \textbf{287}



<!-- Page 393 -->
**288** 	Chapter 19 	Collision Theory

In our discussion of the continuum solutions of the Schr\"odinger equation in Supplement
8-B {www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz} we concluded that: (a) A solution of the Schr\"odinger
equation in the absence of a potential is the plane wave form $e^{i\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{r}}$, which describes a flux

\[
\textbf{j} = \frac{\hbar}{2im}(\psi^* \nabla \psi - \psi \nabla \psi^*) = \frac{\hbar \textbf{k}}{m} \tag{19-1}
\]

If we choose $\textbf{k}$ to define the z-axis, then the large $r$ behavior of this solution may be writ
ten in the form of an incoming + an outgoing spherical wave

\[
e^{i\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{r}} \Rightarrow \frac{i}{2k} \sum_{l=0}^\infty (2l + 1)i^l \left[ \frac{e^{-i(kr - l\pi/2)}}{r} - \frac{e^{i(kr - l\pi/2)}}{r} \right] P_l(\cos \theta) \tag{19-2}
\]

(b) The conservation of particles forces us to the conclusion that the presence of a radial
potential can only alter this to a function, whose asymptotic form is

\[
\psi(\textbf{r}) \Rightarrow \frac{i}{2k} \sum_{l=0}^\infty (2l + 1)i^l \left[ \frac{e^{-i(kr - l\pi/2)}}{r} - S_l(k)\frac{e^{i(kr - l\pi/2)}}{r} \right] P_l(\cos \theta) \tag{19-3}
\]

subject to$^2$

\[
|S_l(k)| = 1 \tag{19-4}
\]

The asymptotic form (19-3) may be rewritten, with the help of (19-2), as

\[
\psi(\textbf{r}) \Rightarrow e^{i\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{r}} + \left[ \sum_{l=0}^\infty (2l + 1) \frac{S_l(k) - 1}{2ik} P_l(\cos \theta) \right] \frac{e^{ikr}}{r} \tag{19-5}
\]

corresponding to a plane wave + an outgoing spherical wave. Note that we are working
with the effective one-particle Schr\"odinger equation, so that $m$ is the reduced mass and $\theta$
is the center of mass angle between the direction of $\textbf{k}$ (the z-axis) and the asymptotic point
$\textbf{r}$, where presumably the counter will be set up. When the target is much more massive
than the projectile, there is no distinction between the laboratory angle and the center-of
mass angle. Note also that we could, of course, have set up a solution that has the asymp
totic form of a plane wave + an incoming spherical wave, since it is the first term in
(19-3) that could be modified by a coefficient satisfying (19-4). However, the solution that
describes the scattering is the one involving the outgoing wave. Let us calculate the flux
for the asymptotic solution (19-5).

\[
\textbf{j} = \frac{\hbar}{2im} \left\{ \left[ e^{i\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{r}} + f(\theta)\frac{e^{ikr}}{r} \right]^* \nabla \left[ e^{i\textbf{k}\cdot\textbf{r}} + f(\theta)\frac{e^{ikr}}{r} \right] - \text{complex conjugate} \right\} \tag{19-6}
\]

where we have defined

\[
f(\theta) = \sum_{l=0}^\infty (2l + 1)f_l(k) P_l(\cos \theta) \tag{19-7}
\]

with

\[
f_l(k) = [S_l(k) - 1]/2ik \tag{19-8}
\]

---
$^2$See the discussion following (8B-3). $S_l(k)$ is the standard notation for $e^{2i\delta_l(k)}$ defined in (8B-6). See Supplement
8-B {www.wiley.com/college/gasiorowicz}.


<!-- Page 394 -->
19-1 Collision Cross Section 289

Calculating the gradient gives
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{j} &= \frac{\hbar}{2im} \Bigg\{ \left[ e^{-i\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}} + f^*(\theta) \frac{e^{-ikr}}{r} \right] \Bigg[ i\mathbf{k} \, e^{i\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r}} + \hat{i}_\theta \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial f(\theta)}{\partial \theta} \frac{e^{ikr}}{r} \\ 
&\quad+ \hat{i}_r f(\theta) \left( ik \frac{e^{ikr}}{r} - \frac{e^{ikr}}{r^2} \right) \Bigg] - \text{complex conjugate} \Bigg\} \\ 
&= \frac{\hbar}{2im} \Bigg\{ i\mathbf{k} + i\mathbf{k} f^*(\theta) \frac{e^{-ikr(1 - \cos \theta)}}{r} + i\mathbf{k} \hat{i}_r f(\theta) \frac{e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)}}{r} + i\mathbf{k} \hat{i}_r |f(\theta)|^2 \frac{1}{r^2} \\ 
&\quad- \hat{i}_r f(\theta) \frac{e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)}}{r^2} + \hat{i}_\theta \frac{\partial f(\theta)}{\partial \theta} \frac{e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)}}{r^2} - \text{complex conjugate} \Bigg\}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

We have used $\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{r} = kr \cos \theta$, in the exponential factors. $\hat{i}_r$ is the unit vector in the $\mathbf{r}$ direction.

In carrying out this calculation we have left out the $1/r^3$ terms, since these are dominated by the $1/r^2$ terms for large $r$. We will be interested in the flux at a detector, which is located at a distance $r$ from the origin, where the potential that gives rise to the scattering is localized, and thus in large $r$. Thus the flux is

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{j} &= \frac{\hbar \mathbf{k}}{m} + \frac{\hbar k}{m} \hat{i}_r |f(\theta)|^2 \frac{1}{r^2} \\ 
&\quad+ \frac{\hbar \mathbf{k}}{2m} \frac{1}{r} \left[ f^*(\theta) \, e^{-ikr(1 - \cos \theta)} + f(\theta) \, e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)} \right] \\ 
&\quad+ \frac{\hbar k \, \hat{i}_r}{2m} \frac{1}{r} \left[ f^*(\theta) \, e^{-ikr(1 - \cos \theta)} + f(\theta) \, e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)} \right] \\ 
&\quad- \frac{\hbar \, \hat{i}_r}{2im \, r^2} \Bigg[ f(\theta) \, e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)} - f^*(\theta) \, e^{-ikr(1 - \cos \theta)} \Bigg] \\ 
&\quad+ \frac{\hbar \, \hat{i}_\theta}{2im \, r^2} \Bigg[ \frac{\partial f(\theta)}{\partial \theta} \, e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)} - \frac{\partial f^*(\theta)}{\partial \theta} \, e^{-ikr(1 - \cos \theta)} \Bigg]
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

This rather involved expression simplifies considerably when we consider that $\theta \neq 0$, since one never does a scattering experiment directly in the forward direction,$^3$ and that in a measurement one always integrates the flux over a small but finite solid angle. Thus in the last four terms of this expression we should replace $e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)}$ by
\begin{equation}
\int \sin \theta \, d\theta \, d\phi \, g(\theta, \phi) \, e^{ikr(1 - \cos \theta)}
\end{equation}

where $g(\theta, \phi)$ is some sort of smooth, localized acceptance function for the counter. Now, as $r \to \infty$, we have an integral over a product of a smooth function and an extremely rapidly varying one, and this vanishes faster than any power of $1/r$. This is what is known in the mathematical literature as the Riemann-Lesbegue lemma, and it is illustrated in Problem 7. Thus, only the first two terms remain, so that

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{j} = \frac{\hbar \mathbf{k}}{m} + \frac{\hbar k}{m} \hat{i}_r \frac{|f(\theta)|^2}{r^2}
\end{equation}

$^3$How could one tell scattered from unscattered particles?


<!-- Page 395 -->
**290** Chapter 19 Collision Theory

In the absence of a potential, only the first term is there; it represents the incident flux. In a
wave-packet treatment, $\hbar\mathbf{k}/m$ would be multiplied by a function that defines the lateral di
mensions of the beam. Thus, if we ask for the radial flux, $\hat{\mathbf{r}} \cdot \mathbf{j}$, then that term gives a con
tribution $\hbar\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}}/m = \hbar k \cos \theta / m$, but only within a finite region of the $z$-axis (see Fig.
19-1). Since the counter is put outside of that region, this first term does not contribute to
the radial flux in the asymptotic region, so that only the second term in (19-11) con
tributes, and

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{j} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \frac{\hbar k}{m} \cdot \frac{|f(\theta)|^2}{r^2} \tag{19-12}
\end{equation}

Thus the number of particles crossing the area that subtends a solid angle $d\Omega$ at the origin
(the target) is

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{j} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{r}} \, dA = \frac{\hbar k}{m} \cdot \frac{|f(\theta)|^2}{r^2} r^2 d\Omega \tag{19-13}
\end{equation}

Notice that the factor of $r^2$ drops out. This justifies the dropping of the $1/r^3$ terms in
(19-9), since these would contribute terms of order $1/kr$ to the number of particles. The
differential cross section is this number, divided by the incident flux, $\hbar k/m$; that is,

\begin{equation}
d\sigma = |f(\theta)|^2 \, d\Omega \tag{19-14}
\end{equation}

If the potential has spin dependence, there may be an azimuthal dependence, so that more
generally,

\begin{equation}
\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} = |f(\theta, \phi)|^2 \tag{19-15}
\end{equation}

The total cross section is given by

\begin{equation}
\sigma_{\text{tot}}(k) = \int d\Omega \, \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega} \tag{19-16}
\end{equation}

If we now use $f(\theta)$ as expressed in terms of $S_l(k)$, and express the latter in terms of the
phase shift $S_l(k) = e^{2i\delta_l(k)}$, so that

\begin{equation}
f(\theta) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{l=0}^\infty (2l + 1) \, e^{i\delta_l(k)} \sin \delta_l(k) \, P_l(\cos \theta) \tag{19-17}
\end{equation}

then

\begin{align*}
\sigma_{\text{tot}} = & \int d\Omega \left[ \frac{1}{k} \sum_l (2l + 1) e^{i\delta_l(k)} \sin \delta_l(k) P_l(\cos\theta) \right] \\
& \left[ \frac{1}{k} \sum_{l'} (2l' + 1) e^{-i\delta_{l'}(k)} \sin \delta_{l'}(k) P_{l'}(\cos\theta) \right]
\end{align*}

and using

\begin{equation}
\int d\Omega P_l(\cos\theta) P_{l'}(\cos\theta) = \frac{4\pi}{2l + 1} \delta_{ll'}
\tag{19-18}
\end{equation}

we get

\begin{equation}
\sigma_{\text{tot}} = \frac{4\pi}{k^2} \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (2l + 1) \sin^2 \delta_l(k)
\tag{19-19}
\end{equation}

It is an interesting fact that

\begin{align}
\text{Im}\, f(0) &= \frac{1}{k} \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (2l + 1) \text{Im}[e^{i\delta_l(k)} \sin \delta_l(k)] P_l(1) \nonumber \\
&= \frac{1}{k} \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (2l + 1) \sin^2 \delta_l(k) = \frac{k}{4\pi} \sigma_{\text{tot}}
\tag{19-20}
\end{align}

This relation is known as the *optical theorem* and it is true even when inelastic processes can occur, as they do in nuclear and particle physics scattering processes. It is a very useful relation and in wave language it follows from the fact that the total cross section represents the removal of flux from the incident beam. Such a removal can only occur as a result of destructive interference, and the latter can only occur between the incident wave and the elastically scattered wave in the forward direction. This explains why $f(0)$ appears linearly.
This hand-waving argument does not explain why it is the imaginary part that is involved, but this can be shown to be generally true.$^4$

**Elastic and Inelastic Scattering**

The requirement that $|S_l(k)| = 1$ followed from conservation of flux. Actually, in many scattering experiments there is *absorption* of the incident beam; the target may merely get excited, or change its state, or another particle may emerge. Under these circumstances our discussion is unchanged except that

\begin{equation}
S_l(k) = \eta_l(k) e^{2i\delta_l(k)}
\tag{19-21}
\end{equation}

is to be used, with

\begin{equation}
0 \le \eta_l(k) \le 1
\tag{19-22}
\end{equation}

because we are dealing with absorption. The partial wave scattering amplitude is now

\begin{equation}
f_l(k) = \frac{S_l(k) - 1}{2ik} = \frac{\eta_l(k) e^{2i\delta_l(k)} - 1}{2ik} = \frac{\eta_l \sin 2\delta_l}{2k} + i \frac{1 - \eta_l \cos 2\delta_l}{2k}
\tag{19-23}
\end{equation}

---
$^4$See L. I. Schiff, *Progr. Theor. Phys.* (Kyoto), **11**, 288 (1954).


<!-- Page 397 -->
**292** Chapter 19 Collision Theory

and the total *elastic* cross section is

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_{el} &= 4\pi \sum_{l} (2l + 1)|f_l(k)|^2 \\
&= 4\pi \sum_{l} (2l + 1)\frac{1 - \eta_l^2 - 2\eta_l \cos 2\delta_l}{4k^2}
\end{aligned}
\tag{19-24}
\end{equation}

There is also a cross section for the *inelastic* processes. Since we do not specify what the inelastic processes consist of, we can only talk about the *total inelastic cross section*, which describes the loss of flux. If we look at a particular term in (19-3), the inward radial flux carried by

$$ \frac{i}{2k} \frac{e^{-ikr}}{r} P_l(\cos \theta) $$

is

$$ \left(\frac{\hbar k}{m}\right) \left[\frac{4\pi}{(2k)^2}\right] $$

(Recall that $Y_{l0} = P_l(\cos \theta)/\sqrt{4\pi}$). The outward radial flux is $(\hbar k/m)(|S_l(k)|^2 \ 4\pi/4k^2)$, so that the net flux lost is $(\hbar k/m)(\pi/k^2)[1 - \eta_l^2(k)]$ for each $l$-value. Hence, dividing by the incident flux, we get

\begin{equation}
\sigma_{inel} = \frac{\pi}{k^2} \sum_l (2l + 1)[1 - \eta_l^2(k)] \tag{19-25}
\end{equation}

Thus the total cross section is

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\sigma_{tot} &= \sigma_{el} + \sigma_{inel} \\
&= \frac{\pi}{k^2} \sum_{l} (2l + 1)(1 + \eta_l^2 - 2\eta_l \cos 2\delta_l + 1 - \eta_l^2) \\
&= \frac{2\pi}{k^2} \sum_{l} (2l + 1)(1 - \eta_l \cos 2\delta_l)
\end{aligned}
\tag{19-26}
\end{equation}

It also follows from (19-23) that

\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\text{Im } f(0) &= \sum_{l} (2l + 1) \text{ Im } f_l(k) \\
&= \sum_{l} (2l + 1) \frac{1 - \eta_l \cos 2\delta_l}{2k} = \frac{k}{4\pi} \sigma_{tot}
\end{aligned}
\tag{19-27}
\end{equation}

so that the optical theorem is indeed satisfied.
If $\eta_l(k) = 1$, we have no absorption, and the inelastic cross section vanishes. When $\eta_l(k) = 0$ we have total absorption. Nevertheless there is still elastic scattering in that partial wave. This becomes evident in *scattering by a black disc*. The black disc is described as follows: (a) it has a well-defined edge; and (b) it is totally absorbing. Since we will consider scattering for short wavelength—that is, large $k$-values—condition (a) specifies that we only consider partial waves $l \leq L$, where

\begin{equation}
L = ka \tag{19-28}
\end{equation}


<!-- Page 398 -->
19-1 Collision Cross Section 293

\begin{figure}[h!]
\centering
%% INSERT IMAGE HERE
