\end{flushright}


<!-- Page 440 -->
The Creation of GHZ States\hspace{\fill}W-97

This is a GHZ state. To make this look more like the GHZ state described in the text of the chapter, all we have to do is rotate the polarization detector $\text{D}_3$ so that $|\text{H}\rangle_3 \rightarrow |\text{V}\rangle_3$ and $|\text{V}\rangle_3 \rightarrow -|\text{H}\rangle_3$. The paper quoted above describes all the tests made to show that the state is indeed what it is expected to be. The experimental test showing that measurements on the GHZ state agree with the quantum mechanical predictions were carried out by the same authors, and the results can be found in Nature 403, 515 (2000). To translate the algebra into the algebra of spin 1/2 states, we note that right- and left-circular polarization states are given by

\[ |\text{R}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( |\text{H}\rangle - \text{i} |\text{V}\rangle \right) \]
\[ |\text{L}\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left( |\text{H}\rangle + \text{i} |\text{V}\rangle \right) \]

The translation can now be carried out if we make the association

\[ |\text{R}\rangle \rightarrow \chi_+ = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}; \qquad |\text{L}\rangle \rightarrow \chi_- = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \]

then

\[ |\text{H}\rangle \rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}; \qquad |\text{L}\rangle \rightarrow \frac{\text{i}}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \]

which correspond to the eigenspinors of $\sigma_x$.


<!-- Page 441 -->
\LARGE{Supplement \huge{20-C}}\n\n\vspace{2em}\n\huge{The Density Operator}\n\n\vspace{1em}\n\normalsize\nIn all of our discussions we have dealt with the time development of physical systems, whose initial states were of the form\n\begin{equation}\n|\psi\rangle = \sum_n C_n |u_n\rangle \tag{20C-1}\n\end{equation}\n\nOften such initial states are not the ones that are provided by the method of preparing the states. It may be that instead of a single ensemble consisting of identical states $|\psi\rangle$ we may be presented with a number of different ensembles on which measurements are to be performed. We may have a set of ensembles of the form\n\begin{equation}\n|\psi^{(i)}\rangle = \sum_n C_n^{(i)} |u_n\rangle \tag{20C-2}\n\end{equation}\n\nand all we know is that the probability of finding an ensemble characterized by (i) is $\text{p}_\text{i}$, with\n\begin{equation}\n\sum_i \text{p}_\text{i} = 1 \tag{20C-3}\n\end{equation}\n\nFor example, we may have a beam of hydrogen atoms in an excited state, with fixed energy and orbital angular momentum l, but completely unpolarized, so that all m-values $-1 \le \text{m} \le \text{l}$ are equally probable. In that case $\text{p}_\text{m} = 1 / (2\text{l} + 1)$, independent of m. It is not correct to say that the beam is described by the wave function\n\begin{equation}\n|\psi\rangle = \sum_\text{m} C_\text{m} |Y_{lm}\rangle \tag{20C-4}\n\end{equation}\n\nwith $|C_\text{m}|^2 = 1 / (2\text{m} + 1)$, since the physical situation represents $2\text{m} + 1$ independent beams, so that there is no phase relationship between different m-values.\n\nThe density operator formalism allows us to deal with both of these cases.\n\n\vspace{1em}\n\large{Pure State}\n\normalsize\nConsider a pure state first. Define the density operator $\rho$ by\n\begin{equation}\n\rho = |\psi\rangle\langle\psi| \tag{20C-5}\n\end{equation}\n\nWe can write this in the form\n\begin{equation}\n\rho = \sum_{\text{m,n}} C_\text{n} C^*_\text{m} |\text{u}_\text{n}\rangle\langle \text{u}_\text{m}| \tag{20C-6}\n\end{equation}\n\n\vspace{1em}\n\small\nW-98


<!-- Page 443 -->
W-100 \quad Supplement 20-C \quad The Density Operator

where $\rho_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the density operator in the $v$-basis. Thus
\[
\rho_{\mathrm{D}} = \mathrm{U}^+ \, \rho \mathrm{U}
\]
It follows from the unitarity of U that the properties of $\rho$ also apply to $\rho_{\mathrm{D}}$.

Since $\rho = \rho^+$, it follows that $\rho$ may be diagonalized by a unitary transformation. This means that it is possible to choose a basis $|v_n\rangle$ such that $\rho$ is diagonal. Since $\rho^2 = \rho$, this means that the eigenvalues can only be 1 and 0, and since $\mathrm{Tr} \rho = 1$, only one eigenvalue can be 1, and all the others must be zero. Thus only one of the $\mathrm{D}_k$ can be nonvanishing. This means that in a suitably chosen basis, a pure state is a state that is an eigenstate of a maximally commuting set of observables, whose eigenfunctions are the set $|v_n\rangle$.

\section*{Mixed State}

For a mixed state we define the density operator by
\begin{equation}
\rho = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} |\psi^{(\mathrm{i})}\rangle \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} \langle \psi^{(\mathrm{i})}| \tag{20C-11}
\end{equation}
In the $|\mathrm{u}_n\rangle$ basis, this takes the form
\[
\rho = \sum_{\mathrm{i}\mathrm{m},\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}^{(\mathrm{i})} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{m}}^{(\mathrm{i})*} \, \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} |\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{n}}\rangle \langle \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{m}}|
\]
so that
\begin{equation}
\rho_{\mathrm{k}\mathrm{l}} = \langle \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{k}} | \rho | \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{l}}\rangle = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} \, \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{k}}^{(\mathrm{i})} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{l}}^{(\mathrm{i})*} \tag{20C-12}
\end{equation}
Note that $\rho_{\mathrm{k}\mathrm{l}} = \rho_{\mathrm{l}\mathrm{k}}^*$ so that $\rho$ is hermitian. Since
\[
\sum_{\mathrm{n}} |\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}^{(\mathrm{i})}|^2 = 1
\]
it follows that
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Tr} \, \rho = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \rho_{\mathrm{k}\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} = 1 \tag{20C-13}
\end{equation}
as before. Also
\begin{align}
\langle \mathrm{A} \rangle &= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} \, \langle \psi^{(\mathrm{i})} | \mathrm{A} | \psi^{(\mathrm{i})}\rangle \notag \\
&= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{m}\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} \, \langle \psi^{(\mathrm{i})} | \mathrm{u}_n\rangle \langle \mathrm{u}_n| \mathrm{A} |\mathrm{u}_m\rangle \langle \mathrm{u}_m | \psi^{(\mathrm{i})} \rangle \notag \\
&= \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{m}\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} \, \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{m}}^{(\mathrm{i})} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{n}}^{(\mathrm{i})*} \, \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}} \tag{20C-14} \\
&= \sum_{\mathrm{m}\mathrm{n}} \rho_{\mathrm{m}\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}} = \mathrm{Tr} \, (\rho \mathrm{A}) \notag
\end{align}
as for pure state. On the other hand, it is no longer true that $\rho^2 = \rho$. In fact,
\[
\rho^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}} |\psi^{(\mathrm{i})}\rangle \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}} \langle \psi^{(\mathrm{i})} | \psi^{(\mathrm{j})}\rangle \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{j}} \langle \psi^{(\mathrm{j})}| = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} |\psi^{(\mathrm{i})}\rangle \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{i}}^2 \langle \psi^{(\mathrm{i})}|
\]


<!-- Page 444 -->
The Density Operator W-101

and, since $\sum\limits_{\text{i}} \text{p}_{\text{i}} = 1$,

\begin{equation}
\text{Tr}\, \rho^2 = \sum_{\text{i}} \text{p}_{\text{i}}^2 < 1
\tag{20C-15}
\end{equation}

for a mixed state.

It follows from the Schr\"odinger equation

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{dt}} | \psi^{(i)} \rangle = -\frac{\text{i}}{\hbar} \text{H} | \psi^{(i)} \rangle
\end{equation*}

and (since $\text{H} = \text{H}^+$)

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{dt}} \langle \psi^{(i)} | = \frac{\text{i}}{\hbar} \langle \psi^{(i)} | \text{H}
\end{equation*}

that

\begin{equation}
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{dt}} \rho = -\frac{\text{i}}{\hbar} \text{H} \rho + \frac{\text{i}}{\hbar} \rho \text{H} = -\frac{\text{i}}{\hbar} [\text{H}, \rho]
\tag{20C-16}
\end{equation}

Note that the sign is opposite to the expression for the time rate of change of a general operator, which reads

\begin{equation*}
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{dt}} \text{A} = \frac{\text{i}}{\hbar} [\text{H}, \text{A}]
\end{equation*}

The simplest application of the formalism is in the description of a beam of electrons or any other particles of spin $1/2$. Here $\rho$ is a $2 \times 2$ hermitian matrix. The most general form of such a matrix is

\begin{equation}
\rho = \frac{1}{2} (\text{a1} + \text{b} \bullet \boldsymbol{\sigma})
\tag{20C-17}
\end{equation}

with a and b real. The condition $\text{tr} \rho = 1$ implies that $\text{a} = 1$. We can calculate $\rho^2$ as follows:

\begin{align}
\rho^2 = \frac{1}{4} (1 + \text{b} \bullet \boldsymbol{\sigma})(1 + \text{b} \bullet \boldsymbol{\sigma}) &= \frac{1}{4} (1 + \text{b}^2 + 2 \text{b} \bullet \boldsymbol{\sigma}) \nonumber \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1 + \text{b}^2}{2} + \text{b} \bullet \boldsymbol{\sigma} \right)
\tag{20C-18}
\end{align}

The density matrix $\rho$ will describe a pure state only if $\rho^2 = \rho$---that is, if $\text{b}^2 = 1$. For a mixed state, it follows from (20C-15) that $\text{b}^2 < 1$.

Let us now obtain a physical interpretation for b. Consider a mixture of spin $1/2$ beams. Each of the beams will have electrons aligned along either the z- or x- or y-axis. The fraction of particles that are in an eigenstate of $\sigma_{\text{z}}$ with eigenvalue $+1$ will be denoted by $\text{f}_3^{(+)}$. The fractions that are in an eigenstate of $\sigma_{\text{z}}$ with eigenvalue $-1$ will be denoted by $\text{f}_3^{(-)}$ and so on, so that

\begin{equation}
\text{f}_3^{(+)} + \text{f}_3^{(-)} + \text{f}_1^{(+)} + \text{f}_1^{(-)} + \text{f}_2^{(+)} + \text{f}_2^{(-)} = 1
\tag{20C-19}
\end{equation}

The eigenstates, with eigenvalues $\pm 1$ of $\sigma_{\text{z}}$, $\sigma_{\text{x}}$, and $\sigma_{\text{y}}$, are

\begin{equation*}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \quad \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \quad \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ \text{i}/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \quad \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ -\text{i}/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix}
\end{equation*}


<!-- Page 445 -->
W-102 Supplement 20-C The Density Operator

Thus the density matrix has the form

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\rho &= \text{f}_3^{(+)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \text{f}_3^{(-)} \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} + \text{f}_1^{(+)} \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \\
&\quad + \text{f}_1^{(-)} \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & -1/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} + \text{f}_2^{(+)} \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ \text{i}/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & -\text{i}/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \\
&\quad + \text{f}_2^{(-)} \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} \\ -\text{i}/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & \text{i}/\sqrt{2} \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}

A little algebra, with the use of (20C-19), shows that this can be written in the form

\begin{equation}
\rho = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \boldsymbol{\sigma} \boldsymbol{\cdot} \mathbf{P}
\tag{20C-20}
\end{equation}

where $\text{P}_i = \text{f}_i^{(+)} - \text{f}_i^{(-)}$. The fraction of particles in a mixture that is aligned in the $+z$-direction minus the fraction that is aligned in the $-z$-direction is called the polarization in the z-direction, and we denote it by $\text{P}_3$. Similarly for the other directions. Thus by comparing (20C-20) with (20C-18), we can interpret $\mathbf{b}$ as the net polarization vector $\mathbf{P}$ of the beam. In the case of beams of atoms of angular momentum $\text{l}$, the most general $\rho$ is a $(2\text{l} + 1) \times (2\text{l} + 1)$ hermitian matrix, and the interpretation of the elements is more complicated. Further discussion of the density matrix is beyond the scope of this book.

\section*{References$^1$}

\subsection*{I. Books on Various Topics in Modern Physics$^2$}

\begin{itemize}
\item[] J. Bernstein, P. M. Fishbane, and S. Gasiorowicz, \textit{Modern Physics}, Prentice Hall, Upper Saddle River, N.J., (2000).
\item[] J. Brehm and W. J. Mullin, \textit{Introduction to the Structure of Matter}, John Wiley, New York, 1989.
\item[] R. Eisberg and R. Resnick, \textit{Quantum Physics of Atoms, Molecules, Solids, Nuclei and Particles} (2nd edition), John Wiley, New York, 1985.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{II. Textbooks and Monographs}

\begin{itemize}
\item[] G. Baym, \textit{Lectures on Quantum Mechanics}, W. A. Benjamin, New York, 1969.
\end{itemize}
This is a very appealing book, with just the right mixture of formalism, intuitive arguments, and applications. It should be considered an advanced book, accessible to the student who has covered the material in this book.
\begin{itemize}
\item[] H. A. Bethe and R. W. Jackiw, \textit{Intermediate Quantum Mechanics} (2nd edition), W. A. Benjamin, New York, 1968.
\end{itemize}
This book contains detailed discussions of calculational methods applicable to the theory of atomic structure, multiplet splittings, the photoelectric effect, and atomic collisions. Much of the material is not to be found in any other textbook. The book is thus an advanced text, as well as an exhaustive reference book.
\begin{itemize}
\item[] H. A. Bethe and E. E. Salpeter, \textit{Quantum Mechanics of One- and Two-Electron Atoms}, Springer-Verlag, Berlin/New York, 1957.
\end{itemize}
This reprint of the authors' article in the \textit{Handbuch der Physik} is an elaborate, detailed, definitive treatment of the problem at hand. It is a book about atoms and not about quantum mechanics, and the level is high. It is an excellent reference book.
\begin{itemize}
\item[] D. Bohm, \textit{Quantum Theory}, Dover, New York, 1989.
\end{itemize}
The book is discursively written, on a level comparable to the present book. The author pays much attention to the principles of quantum theory and gives an excellent discussion of the quantum theory of the measurement process. There are few applications and not many problems.
\begin{itemize}
\item[] S. Borowitz, \textit{Fundamentals of Quantum Mechanics}, W. A. Benjamin, New York, 1967.
\end{itemize}
This is a well-written book, about half of which is devoted to the theory of waves and to classical mechanics. The level is comparable to that of the present book.
\begin{itemize}
\item[] C. Cohen-Tannoudji, B. Diu, and F. Laloe, \textit{Quantum Mechanics}, John Wiley, New York, 1977.
\end{itemize}
This is an encyclopedic book of more than a thousand pages. The student will find detailed coverage of many aspects of atomic physics. The mathematical level is quite a bit above that of \textit{Quantum Physics}.
\begin{itemize}
\item[] R. H. Dicke and J. P. Wittke, \textit{Introduction to Quantum Mechanics}, Addison-Wesley, Reading, Mass., 1960.
\end{itemize}
I enjoyed this book very much. It is on a level comparable to the present book, and discusses a few topics, notably quantum statistics, that are not treated here. The problems are excellent.
\begin{itemize}
\item[] P. A. M. Dirac, \textit{The Principles of Quantum Mechanics} (4th edition), Oxford University Press (Clarendon), Oxford, England, 1958.
\end{itemize}
This is a superb book by one of the major creators of quantum mechanics. The student who has studied the material in this book will have no trouble with Dirac; if at all serious about mastering quantum mechanics, he or she should sooner or later go through Dirac's book.
\begin{itemize}
\item[] R. P. Feynman and A. R. Hibbs, \textit{Quantum Mechanics and Path Integrals}, McGraw-Hill, New York, 1965.
\end{itemize}
In 1948, R. P. Feynman proposed a different formulation of quantum mechanics. In this book the equivalence of this formulation to the standard theory is demonstrated, and the "path integral" expression for the general amplitude is exploited in a number of calculations. The selection of material is very interesting, and the point of view is different from the one developed by the author. Thus this

somewhat more advanced book presents an excellent

R. P. Feynman, R. B. Leighton, and M. Sands, \textit{The}
\textit{Feynman Lectures on Physics}, Vol. 3, \textit{Quantum}
\textit{Mechanics}, Addison-Wesley, Reading, Mass., 1965.

In this introduction to quantum mechanics, Feynman
abandons the path integral and approaches the
subject from the point of view of state vectors. A
large number of fascinating examples are discussed
with the minimum of formal apparatus. A superb
complementary book, whose only shortcoming is
the absence of problems.

K. Gottfried, \textit{Quantum Mechanics}, Vol. 1,
\textit{Fundamentals}, W. A. Benjamin, New York, 1966.

This is a very advanced book, distinguished by the
care with which the various topics are discussed.
The treatment of the measurement process and of
invariance principles is excellent. The student who
has mastered the material in this book should be able
to read Gottfried's book, provided he or she has
acquired the necessary mathematical equipment.

D. Griffiths, \textit{Introduction to Quantum Mechanics},
Prentice Hall, Englewood Cliffs, N.J., 1995.

This well-written, attractive book is roughly on the
level of Dicke and Wittke or Saxon. It contains a
nice selection of topics, including a discussion of
the geometric phase.

G. Greenstein and A. G. Zajonc, \textit{The Quantum}
\textit{Challenge}, Jones and Bartlett, Sudbury, Mass.,
1997.

This is a fine book that deals with the foundations of
quantum mechanics from the point of view of basic
experiments. It is a real pleasure to read and makes
few mathematical demands on the reader.

W. Heisenberg, \textit{The Physical Principles of the}
\textit{Quantum Theory}, Dover, New York, 1930.

This reprint of some 1930 lectures given by
Heisenberg on the physical significance of the
quantum theory still makes good reading. The
discussion of the uncertainty relations is particularly
useful.

T. E. Jordan, \textit{Quantum Mechanics in Simple Matrix}
\textit{Form}, John Wiley, New York, 1986.

This is a very interesting book in that it deals with
quantum mechanics in the form originally created by
W. Heisenberg, M. Born, and P. Jordan. Calculations
became much simpler with the (equivalent) wave
mechanics approach of Schrödinger, but as this brief
book shows, one can do a lot with simple matrices.
This is the place where one can find the matrix
solution to the hydrogen atom, and there is a nice
discussion of Bell's inequalities.

\begin{flushright}
References \textbf{331}
\end{flushright}

H. A. Kramers, \textit{Quantum Mechanics}, Interscience,
New York, 1957.

This book by one of the founders of the subject is at
its best in the discussion of spin and the introduction
to relativistic quantum theory, both rather advanced
subjects. The student who is comfortable with
quantum mechanics will find browsing through this
book enjoyable and rewarding.

L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz, \textit{Quantum}
\textit{Mechanics (Nonrelativistic Theory)} (2nd edition),
Addison-Wesley, Reading, Mass., 1965.

The book by Landau and Lifshitz is one of a series
of superb books covering all of theoretical physics. It
is hard to think of this as a textbook for any but the
most sophisticated students. Any student, however,
once he reaches the advanced level, will find much
that is useful in this book. There is an assumed
mathematical facility on the part of the student.

R. L. Liboff, \textit{Introductory Quantum Mechanics},
Addison Wesley Longman, Reading, Mass., 1998.

This is a very attractive book, written on roughly the
same mathematical level as \textit{Quantum Physics}. It is
an excellent alternative reference, with a more
detailed treatment of solid state physics applications.

H. J. Lipkin, \textit{Quantum Mechanics-New}
\textit{Approaches to Selected Topics}, North-Holland,
Amsterdam, 1973.

Lipkin's book deals with a number of advanced
topics in the application of quantum mechanics, in a
simple way. The physics is always at the forefront of
the discussion, and a student who has a good
command of \textit{Quantum Physics} will get much benefit
and pleasure out of this book.

A. Messiah, \textit{Quantum Mechanics} (in 2 volumes),
John Wiley, New York, 1968.

This book gives a complete coverage of quantum
theory from the treatment of one-dimensional
potentials through the quantization of the
electromagnetic field and the relativistic wave equation
of Dirac. It is an advanced book, and it assumes a
mathematical sophistication that few first-year graduate
students possess. It is an extremely worthwhile book.

E. Merzbacher, \textit{Quantum Mechanics} (3rd edition),
John Wiley, New York, 1998.

Together with the books of Schiff and Sakurai, this is
the standard first-year graduate text in quantum
mechanics. Recent editions have enlarged it, but the
standard of economy and taste have been maintained.

R. Omnes, \textit{Understanding Quantum Mechanics},
Princeton University Press, Princeton, N.J., 1999.

This excellent book covers a great deal of the work
done in recent years on extending or modifying the
